entries.content:
In my previous article, I explored operational conformance: how to evaluate whether observed evidence satisfies an operational specification.

That gives us a useful point-in-time question:

Does the system satisfy the specification right now?

But production systems don't stay still.

Traffic changes. Dependencies degrade. Certificates expire. Configuration is modified. Feature flags move. Data grows. People make manual changes. Agents take actions. Infrastructure is replaced. And so on.

A system can be conformant immediately after a deployment and stop being conformant hours or days later.

That's the problem I want to explore here.

Operational drift is the divergence between the operational specification and the state we continue to observe over time.

This is broader than configuration drift. Configuration drift asks whether infrastructure or configuration differs from a declared state.

Operational drift asks whether the system still behaves within the boundaries we intended, even if the configuration has not changed at all.

A service can have exactly the same configuration it had yesterday and still drift operationally because latency increased, error rate degraded, replica availability fell, a dependency became unhealthy, a policy is no longer being enforced, or evidence disappeared.

In this article, I’ll show you how to model operational drift, establish a conformance baseline, reevaluate a system over time, distinguish temporary noise from meaningful divergence, preserve drift evidence, classify severity, and decide when drift should trigger an alert, an investigation, or an automated response.

The central idea is this: conformance tells you whether reality matches intent at a point in time. Drift tells you whether that relationship is changing.

Prerequisites

You should be comfortable with:

  • software architecture

  • TypeScript or a similar language

  • observability

  • operational specifications

  • evidence-based evaluation

  • conformance

  • basic monitoring concepts

You don't need a specific infrastructure platform.

The examples use a deployment scenario, but the same model applies to infrastructure, data pipelines, backup systems, access controls, AI agents, and other operational workflows.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites

  • What Operational Drift Means

  • Operational Drift Isn't the Same as Configuration Drift

  • Start with a Conformance Baseline

  • Observe the Same Constraints Over Time

  • Model Drift Explicitly

  • Temporary Variation Isn't Always Drift

  • Use Windows Instead of Single Samples

  • Distinguish Drift from Missing Evidence

  • Add Severity and Persistence

  • Detect Directional Drift Before a Threshold Fails

  • Preserve the Evidence Behind Drift

  • A Reusable Drift Evaluator

  • A Small End-to-End Example

  • How Drift Detection Applies to Multiple Executors

  • How Drift Detection Applies to AI Agents

  • When Drift Should Trigger Action

  • What Operational Drift Can't Tell You

  • A Practical Drift Detection Workflow

  • From Point-in-Time Conformance to Continuous Verification

  • Conclusion

What Operational Drift Means

Suppose a deployment finishes at 10:00.

The operational specification says:

version = v42
available replicas >= 3
error rate <= 1%
p95 latency <= 400 ms

Immediately after deployment, the evidence says:

version = v42
available replicas = 3
error rate = 0.4%
p95 latency = 280 ms

The system is conformant.

Now suppose that at 14:00 the evidence says:

version = v42
available replicas = 3
error rate = 0.8%
p95 latency = 370 ms

The system is still conformant, but something has changed.

The error rate and latency are moving toward their limits.

At 16:00:

version = v42
available replicas = 3
error rate = 1.4%
p95 latency = 460 ms

Now the system is no longer conformant.

The operational specification didn't change. The executor did not necessarily run again. But reality moved.

That's operational drift.

A useful way to think about it is:

Specification
      ↓
Expected operational boundaries
      ↓
Observed state at T0
      ↓
Observed state at T1
      ↓
Observed state at T2
      ↓
Drift evaluation

The key idea is temporal: conformance is a snapshot, while drift is a relationship across snapshots.

Operational Drift Isn't the Same as Configuration Drift

Configuration drift is likely a familiar infrastructure concept to you.

By configuration drift, I mean a difference between the configuration or infrastructure state you declared and the state that actually exists in the environment.

For example:

desired replicas = 3
actual replicas = 2

Here, the declared state says the service should have three replicas, but the running environment only has two. The configuration and the actual state no longer match.

Or:

Terraform state != deployed infrastructure

In that case, infrastructure has changed outside the expected Terraform-managed state, or Terraform's record no longer matches what's actually deployed.

Those are both configuration drift because the mismatch is between a declared configuration and the environment that should reflect it.

That's useful, but it's narrower.

Operational drift can exist even when configuration is unchanged.

Consider this specification:

error rate <= 1%

The deployment configuration may still be identical to yesterday.

Yet traffic mix may have changed, a downstream API may have slowed down, a database index may have degraded, a certificate may be approaching expiration, or a queue backlog may have grown.

So:

configuration drift
=
declared configuration != actual configuration

while:

operational drift
=
observed operational state != intended operational boundaries

The two can overlap, but they're not the same thing.

That distinction matters because production failures are often behavioral before they are configurational.

Start with a Conformance Baseline

Drift needs a reference point. The easiest reference is a known conformant state.

For example:

type DeploymentEvidence = {
  version?: string;
  replicas?: number;
  errorRate?: number;
  p95LatencyMs?: number;
};

Suppose the system was evaluated after deployment:

const baseline: DeploymentEvidence = {
  version: "v42",
  replicas: 3,
  errorRate: 0.004,
  p95LatencyMs: 280,
};

and all required constraints passed.

That baseline gives you two useful things.

First, you know the system satisfied the specification at that point. And second, you have a concrete evidence snapshot against which later observations can be compared.

This doesn't mean later evidence must match the baseline exactly. That would be too strict.

It means later evidence can be evaluated in two ways:

Does it still satisfy the specification?

How is it changing relative to the baseline?

Those are different questions. Both are useful.

Observe the Same Constraints Over Time

Suppose you collect evidence every hour:

type TimedEvidence = {
  timestamp: string;
  evidence: DeploymentEvidence;
};

For example:

const observations: TimedEvidence[] = [
  {
    timestamp: "10:00",
    evidence: {
      version: "v42",
      replicas: 3,
      errorRate: 0.004,
      p95LatencyMs: 280,
    },
  },
  {
    timestamp: "12:00",
    evidence: {
      version: "v42",
      replicas: 3,
      errorRate: 0.006,
      p95LatencyMs: 320,
    },
  },
  {
    timestamp: "14:00",
    evidence: {
      version: "v42",
      replicas: 3,
      errorRate: 0.008,
      p95LatencyMs: 370,
    },
  },
];

Each observation can be evaluated against the same specification.

This gives you a conformance sequence:

10:00  PASS
12:00  PASS
14:00  PASS

At first glance, everything looks healthy. But a closer look reveals that the evidence is moving in one direction.

That's where drift detection becomes more interesting than ordinary threshold monitoring.

Model Drift Explicitly

A minimal drift result might look like this:

type DriftStatus =
  | "STABLE"
  | "DEGRADING"
  | "VIOLATED"
  | "UNKNOWN";

This gives the evaluator four explicit states. 

STABLE
means the observed behavior remains within the expected range without meaningful deterioration. 
DEGRADING
means the system is still within its allowed boundary but is moving in an unfavorable direction. 
VIOLATED
means the current evidence has crossed the specification's limit. 
UNKNOWN
means there's not enough evidence to classify the state safely.

Then:

type DriftResult = {
  constraint: string;
  status: DriftStatus;
  baseline?: number;
  current?: number;
  limit?: number;
};


DriftResult
keeps the classification together with the values that explain it. 
baseline
is the known-good reference, 
current
is the latest observation, and 
limit
is the boundary defined by the specification. Those fields are optional because some constraints may not be numeric or some evidence may be missing.

For latency:

baseline = 280
current = 370
limit = 400

This example says latency started from a known-good value of 280 ms, is now 370 ms, and must remain at or below 400 ms. The constraint hasn't failed, but the current value is much closer to the boundary.

That may be worth labeling:

DEGRADING

A drift model therefore doesn't replace conformance. It adds another dimension.

You can have:

conformance = PASS
drift = DEGRADING

That combination is often more actionable than either signal alone.

Temporary Variation Isn't Always Drift

Production systems are noisy.

One slow request doesn't mean the system is drifting. One missing sample doesn't mean the service is unhealthy. And one temporary spike doesn't necessarily justify intervention.

Suppose latency samples are:

280
290
420
285
295

The 

420
sample crosses the limit. But the system immediately returns to normal.

Compare that with:

280
310
340
370
395

The second sequence may never cross the limit. But it shows persistent degradation.

That's why drift shouldn't be defined as:

current != baseline

or even:

one sample crossed threshold

Drift is more useful when it accounts for persistence and direction.

Use Windows Instead of Single Samples

A better approach is to evaluate observations over a window.

For example:

function average(
  values: number[]
): number {
  return (
    values.reduce(
      (sum, value) => sum + value,
      0
    ) / values.length
  );
}

Now suppose you evaluate the last five latency observations:

const latencyWindow = [
  300,
  320,
  340,
  360,
  380,
];

const currentAverage =
  average(latencyWindow);

This smooths temporary noise.

You can compare that window with an earlier window:

const baselineWindow = [
  270,
  275,
  280,
  285,
  290,
];

const baselineAverage =
  average(baselineWindow);

The earlier window gives you a short historical reference for typical behavior. The later window represents the more recent operating state. Comparing the two averages helps you see whether the whole signal has shifted, rather than reacting to one unusual sample.

Then calculate the change:

const delta =
  currentAverage -
  baselineAverage;

If 

baselineAverage
is 280 ms and 
currentAverage
is 340 ms, the delta is 
+60 ms
. That doesn't mean the latency constraint has failed, but it does show that recent latency is materially worse than the earlier window.

This doesn't prove a problem exists, but it gives you a more stable signal.

The exact window size should come from the operational context.

A five-minute window may make sense for latency. A one-day window may make more sense for storage growth.

Distinguish Drift from Missing Evidence

This follows the same principle as conformance.

Suppose latency evidence disappears.

That's not the same as:

latency is stable

and it's not the same as:

latency violated the threshold

It is:

UNKNOWN

For example:

function evaluateLatencyDrift(
  baseline: number | undefined,
  current: number | undefined,
  limit: number
): DriftStatus {
  if (
    baseline === undefined ||
    current === undefined
  ) {
    return "UNKNOWN";
  }

  if (current > limit) {
    return "VIOLATED";
  }

  if (current > baseline) {
    return "DEGRADING";
  }

  return "STABLE";
}

The function evaluates the cases in a deliberate order. First, if either the baseline or the current observation is missing, it returns 

UNKNOWN
because there's not enough evidence to make a safe comparison. If evidence exists and the current value is already above the allowed limit, it returns 
VIOLATED
. If the value is still below the limit but worse than the baseline, it returns 
DEGRADING
. Only when none of those conditions apply does it return 
STABLE
.

This is still simplistic because any increase over the baseline becomes 

DEGRADING
, even if the change is tiny or temporary. In a real system, you would usually combine this with tolerances, windows, persistence, or trend rules. But it preserves an important rule: absence of evidence isn't evidence of stability.

That becomes especially important when the observability system itself is degraded.

Add Severity and Persistence

Drift becomes more useful when you know how important the constraint is and how long the drift has persisted.

For example:

type DriftSeverity =
  | "INFO"
  | "WARNING"
  | "CRITICAL";

type DriftObservation = {
  constraint: string;
  status: DriftStatus;
  severity: DriftSeverity;
  consecutiveWindows: number;
};

Here, 

severity
describes the operational impact of the affected constraint, while 
consecutiveWindows
records how many observation windows have produced the same drift condition in a row. Keeping both matters because one brief warning is different from a warning that has persisted for eight consecutive windows, and a critical replica violation may deserve action even if it has only appeared twice.

Now you can distinguish:

latency
DEGRADING
WARNING
1 window

from:

latency
DEGRADING
WARNING
8 windows

and:

replicas
VIOLATED
CRITICAL
2 windows

The second signal is more persistent, but the third is more severe.

That helps determine what response is appropriate.

Detect Directional Drift Before a Threshold Fails

One of the most useful aspects of drift detection is recognizing directional movement.

Suppose the error-rate limit is:

1%

and observations are:

0.2%
0.4%
0.6%
0.8%

Nothing has failed yet, but the trend is clear.

A simple slope can capture that direction.

For example:

function slope(
  values: number[]
): number {
  if (values.length < 2) {
    return 0;
  }

  return (
    values[values.length - 1] -
    values[0]
  ) / (values.length - 1);
}

This helper looks at the first and last values in the series and divides their difference by the number of intervals between them. It's a deliberately simple trend indicator: a positive result means the metric increased across the window, a negative result means it decreased, and a value near zero means it stayed roughly flat.

Then:

const errorRates = [
  0.002,
  0.004,
  0.006,
  0.008,
];

const trend =
  slope(errorRates);

Here, the error rate rises from 

0.002
to 
0.008
, so 
trend
is positive. The code isn't trying to predict the future or perform full statistical analysis. It's only making the direction of change explicit so the system can notice sustained movement toward the 
1%
boundary before the boundary is actually crossed.

A positive trend doesn't automatically mean failure, but it tells you the system is moving toward the boundary.

This is where drift detection differs from basic alerting.

Basic threshold alert:

tell me when error rate > 1%

Drift detection:

tell me when error rate is persistently moving toward 1%

The second can give you time to investigate before the system becomes non-conformant.

Preserve the Evidence Behind Drift

A drift result should be explainable.

For example:

{
  "constraint": "error-rate",
  "status": "DEGRADING",
  "baseline": 0.004,
  "current": 0.008,
  "limit": 0.01,
  "window": "10m",
  "consecutiveWindows": 4,
  "observedAt": "2026-10-13T18:00:00Z"
}

This is better than:

drift detected

because someone can answer:

what changed?
compared with what?
how close are we to the limit?
how long has this been happening?
when was it observed?

That matters for debugging, as well as for auditability.

A Reusable Drift Evaluator

We can generalize the model.

First define a drift rule:

type DriftRule = {
  name: string;
  severity: DriftSeverity;
  evaluate(
    baseline: T,
    current: T
  ): DriftStatus;
};

Then define a drift specification:

type DriftSpec = {
  name: string;
  rules: DriftRule[];
};

And an evaluator:

type DriftRuleResult = {
  name: string;
  status: DriftStatus;
  severity: DriftSeverity;
};

function evaluateDrift(
  spec: DriftSpec,
  baseline: T,
  current: T
): DriftRuleResult[] {
  return spec.rules.map(
    (rule) => ({
      name: rule.name,
      status:
        rule.evaluate(
          baseline,
          current
        ),
      severity:
        rule.severity,
    })
  );
}

The evaluator doesn't need to understand latency, error rate, replicas, or certificates.

Each rule owns its own comparison logic. That makes the engine reusable.

A Small End-to-End Example

Let’s create a drift specification for a deployment.

Start with evidence:

type DeploymentEvidence = {
  replicas?: number;
  errorRate?: number;
  p95LatencyMs?: number;
};

Now define rules:

const driftRules:
  DriftRule[] = [
    {
      name: "replicas",
      severity: "CRITICAL",
      evaluate: (
        baseline,
        current
      ) => {
        if (
          baseline.replicas === undefined ||
          current.replicas === undefined
        ) {
          return "UNKNOWN";
        }

        if (current.replicas < 3) {
          return "VIOLATED";
        }

        if (
          current.replicas <
          baseline.replicas
        ) {
          return "DEGRADING";
        }

        return "STABLE";
      },
    },
    {
      name: "error-rate",
      severity: "CRITICAL",
      evaluate: (
        baseline,
        current
      ) => {
        if (
          baseline.errorRate === undefined ||
          current.errorRate === undefined
        ) {
          return "UNKNOWN";
        }

        if (current.errorRate > 0.01) {
          return "VIOLATED";
        }

        if (
          current.errorRate >
          baseline.errorRate * 1.5
        ) {
          return "DEGRADING";
        }

        return "STABLE";
      },
    },
    {
      name: "latency",
      severity: "WARNING",
      evaluate: (
        baseline,
        current
      ) => {
        if (
          baseline.p95LatencyMs === undefined ||
          current.p95LatencyMs === undefined
        ) {
          return "UNKNOWN";
        }

        if (
          current.p95LatencyMs > 400
        ) {
          return "VIOLATED";
        }

        if (
          current.p95LatencyMs >
          baseline.p95LatencyMs * 1.25
        ) {
          return "DEGRADING";
        }

        return "STABLE";
      },
    },
  ];

Create the drift specification:

const driftSpec:
  DriftSpec = {
    name: "orders-runtime-drift",
    rules: driftRules,
  };

Now define baseline and current evidence:

const baseline:
  DeploymentEvidence = {
    replicas: 3,
    errorRate: 0.004,
    p95LatencyMs: 280,
  };

const current:
  DeploymentEvidence = {
    replicas: 3,
    errorRate: 0.007,
    p95LatencyMs: 360,
  };

Evaluate:

const drift =
  evaluateDrift(
    driftSpec,
    baseline,
    current
  );

Possible output:

replicas     STABLE      CRITICAL
error-rate   DEGRADING   CRITICAL
latency      DEGRADING   WARNING

The system may still be conformant, but it's no longer operationally stable relative to its baseline.

That's valuable information.

How Drift Detection Applies to Multiple Executors

Suppose two executors both successfully deployed the same service.

Immediately after deployment:

Executor A → conformant
Executor B → conformant

That doesn't mean their long-term operational behavior is identical.

Over time:

Executor A
error rate stable
latency stable
replicas stable

Executor B
error rate rising
latency rising
replicas stable

Both executors satisfied the initial specification, but their downstream operational behavior is different.

Drift gives you another comparison dimension.

You can ask:

Which executor produces more stable outcomes?
Which one drifts more often?
Which one produces more unknown evidence?
Which one needs recovery more frequently?

This is especially useful when executor choice is dynamic.

How Drift Detection Applies to AI Agents

AI agents introduce another kind of variability.

An agent may produce different plans for the same objective.

For example:

Run 1:
scale
deploy
observe

Run 2:
deploy canary
observe
expand

Run 3:
create parallel environment
switch traffic

Each plan may be valid, and each may initially conform.

But the long-term outcomes can differ.

One plan may produce a stable system, while another may create a system that slowly moves toward a boundary.

This gives us a useful separation:

agent chooses the execution path
specification defines acceptable boundaries
evidence describes the observed state
conformance evaluates the current state
drift evaluates how that state changes over time

That allows agent autonomy without making the agent the only judge of its own outcomes.

When Drift Should Trigger Action

Not every drift signal should trigger automation.

A useful response model might be:

STABLE
→ no action

DEGRADING + low severity
→ observe

DEGRADING + persistent
→ investigate

VIOLATED + warning
→ alert

VIOLATED + critical
→ rollback / remediate / escalate

UNKNOWN
→ collect evidence / block risky automation

The exact policy depends on the operation.

For example, automatically restarting a stateless service may be acceptable. But automatically rolling back a database migration may not be.

Drift detection should therefore produce evidence and classification. Policy should decide what action is permitted. That keeps observation, evaluation, decision, and execution separate.

What Operational Drift Can't Tell You

Operational drift doesn't automatically tell you why the system changed.

Suppose latency rises from:

280 ms

to:

390 ms

Drift detection can tell you:

latency is degrading

It can't automatically prove the cause.

The cause might be traffic growth, database contention, a downstream dependency, network degradation, a code regression, or resource exhaustion.

Drift is therefore a detection mechanism. It's not root-cause analysis.

The baseline can also be wrong.

If the baseline was captured during an unusually good period, normal behavior may look like degradation.

So drift quality depends on good specifications, good evidence, good baselines, appropriate windows, and correct rules.

A Practical Drift Detection Workflow

If you want to introduce operational drift detection into an existing system, I would use this sequence.

1. Start with a Conformant Operation

Pick an operation where you already know the system satisfies the specification.

2. Preserve the Baseline Evidence

Store the evidence associated with that known-good state.

3. Identify Drift-Sensitive Constraints

Not every constraint needs trend analysis.

Start with things like:

latency
error rate
capacity
queue depth
availability
certificate age
backup freshness

4. Define Observation Windows

Choose windows based on operational behavior.

5. Define Stable, Degrading, Violated, and Unknown

Make the states explicit.

6. Add Severity

Separate informational drift from critical drift.

7. Add Persistence

Avoid reacting to one noisy sample.

8. Preserve Evidence

Store baseline, current state, thresholds, windows, and timestamps.

9. Separate Detection from Response

Don't make every drift signal trigger an automatic action.

10. Revisit the Model

If the system produces constant false positives, improve the rule. If it misses real degradation, improve the evidence or the window.

Don't simply widen thresholds until everything looks stable.

From Point-in-Time Conformance to Continuous Verification

Conformance gives us this:

Specification
+
Evidence
↓
Evaluation
↓
PASS / FAIL / UNKNOWN

Drift adds time:

Specification
+
Evidence at T0
+
Evidence at T1
+
Evidence at T2
↓
Drift Evaluation
↓
STABLE / DEGRADING / VIOLATED / UNKNOWN

That changes the operational model.

We're no longer asking only:

Did the operation succeed?

or:

Is the system conformant now?

We can also ask:

Is the system moving away from the intended state?

That's a much stronger foundation for operational control, especially when systems become more autonomous.

Conclusion

Operational conformance tells us whether observed evidence satisfies the specification at a point in time.

Operational drift tells us whether that relationship is changing.

A useful drift model should preserve:

baseline evidence
current evidence
constraint boundaries
observation windows
direction of change
severity
persistence
unknown states
timestamps

That gives us a way to distinguish temporary noise, persistent degradation, actual violation, and missing evidence.

The executor doesn't need to know any of this. The executor performs the work. The specification defines the intended boundaries.

Evidence tells us what's happening. Conformance tells us whether the current state is acceptable. Drift tells us whether the system is moving away from that acceptable state.

At this point, the pieces are starting to form a larger operational model:

Intent
↓
Specification
↓
Executor
↓
Evidence
↓
Conformance
↓
Drift
↓
Governed response

The next step is to put those pieces together explicitly.

That's where I want to define Specification-Driven Operations, or SDOps, as a complete operating model.

entries.title: How to Build a Website User Interface Faster Using AI Prompts
entries.summary: A website user interface (UI) used to take hours of writing HTML, CSS, and component code by hand. Now you can describe a page in plain words and let an AI coding tool write the first version. But the
entries.content:
A website user interface (UI) used to take hours of writing HTML, CSS, and component code by hand. Now you can describe a page in plain words and let an AI coding tool write the first version.

But the result depends on your prompt. A short, vague prompt gives you a generic page with random colors and repeated code. A clear prompt with your stack, your files, and your rules gives you code you can use.

In this tutorial, you'll learn how to write that kind of prompt. You'll use it to build a full-screen hero section with a sticky, animated navbar, using Next.js, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui components.

By the end, you'll know how to:

  • Write a UI prompt that covers layout, components, colors, spacing, and responsive behavior.

  • Generate a UI from a prompt and inspect the code the tool creates.

  • Use reusable shadcn/ui components and ready-made blocks instead of repeated AI-written code.

  • Improve the result with small follow-up prompts.

  • Run, test, and customize the final page.

Table of Contents

  • Prerequisites

  • Why shadcn/ui?

  • What is ShadcnSpace?

  • What You'll Build

  • Step 1: How to Write an Effective UI Prompt

  • Step 2: How to Generate the First UI

  • Step 3: How to Build with Reusable shadcn/ui Components

  • Step 4: How to Improve the Result with Follow-Up Prompts

  • Step 5: How to Run and Customize the Final UI

  • How I Check AI-Generated Code Before Deployment

  • Key Concepts Recap

  • Conclusion

  • Resources

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have:

  • A current LTS version of Node.js installed

  • A code editor

  • An account with an AI coding tool such as Cursor, Claude, or v0

  • Basic knowledge of React and TypeScript

  • Basic knowledge of Tailwind CSS class names

You don't need to know Motion, the animation library used in this tutorial. You'll see how it works as you go.

Why shadcn/ui?

Shadcn UI is a collection of accessible React components styled with Tailwind CSS. It works differently from a normal component library. You don't install it as a package. Instead, you use a CLI to copy the component source files into your project.

This matters when you work with AI tools. The code lives in your own 

components/ui
folder, so the tool can read it, and so can you. When you ask a tool to "use the dropdown menu," it can follow the exact component in your project instead of inventing a new one.

Some key benefits:

  • Accessible by default, so menus and buttons handle keyboard use and focus

  • Built with Tailwind CSS, so there are no extra style files

  • Shared theme variables, so colors stay the same across every component

  • No lock-in, because the code is in your project and you can edit it

What is ShadcnSpace?

ShadcnSpace is a collection of 1000+ beautifully designed, accessible, and composable free and Pro Shadcn UI blocks, components, and templates for your React/Next.js apps. Supporting both Base UI and Radix UI, styled with Tailwind CSS, it is ready to copy-paste or install via the Shadcn CLI.

A block is a larger piece of UI, such as a hero section, a navbar, or a full page layout, built from shadcn/ui components.

Each block page shows a live preview. You can look at any free or pro block and copy its prompt. You then paste that prompt into any AI tool, and the tool creates the files in your project.

This tutorial uses a hero block as the example. You'll see exactly what a complete prompt looks like and why it works.

What You'll Build

You'll build a hero page with these parts:

Hero section

  • A full-screen section with a looping background video

  • A dark overlay so the text stays readable

  • A rotating icon next to a short line of text

  • A large headline that fades in when it enters the screen

Navbar

  • A sticky header with a logo on the left and a round menu button on the right

  • A background that fills in after you scroll 80px

  • A dropdown menu with five links, a dark blurred overlay, and contact details

Navigation link

  • A link that reveals a spinning icon on hover

  • An active state for the current page

The project needs this stack:

  • A shadcn/ui project structure

  • React

  • Next.js

  • Tailwind CSS

  • TypeScript

If you don't have a project yet, create one and set up shadcn/ui:

npx create-next-app@latest hero-demo --typescript --tailwind --eslint --app
cd hero-demo
npx shadcn@latest init

Current versions of 

create-next-app
ship with React 19 and Tailwind CSS 4.

Step 1: How to Write an Effective UI Prompt

A good prompt works like a short spec. It tells the tool what to build, which parts to use, and which rules to follow.

Cover these five points:

  • Layout: Say what goes where. For example, "a sticky navbar on top and a headline at the bottom left."

  • Components: Name the parts you want, such as a dropdown menu for the mobile navigation.

  • Colors: Name a main color and where it appears. Ask for theme tokens such as 

    text-foreground
    where you can.

  • Spacing: Give a rule, such as "keep content inside a max width of 7xl with horizontal padding."

  • Responsive behavior: Say what changes on a phone.

There are two ways to get a prompt for your page.

Option 1: Generate a Prompt with an AI Tool

Describe the page in your own words and follow the five points above. Here's an example:

Create a full-screen hero section for a Next.js project with
TypeScript and Tailwind CSS.

Layout:
- A sticky navbar with a logo on the left and a round menu button on the right.
- The menu button opens a dropdown with five links.
- A looping background video with a dark overlay so the text stays readable.
- A large headline and a short line of text at the bottom left.

Rules:
- Use the shadcn/ui DropdownMenu for the menu.
- Use Motion for a fade-in on the headline and the navbar.
- Keep content inside max-w-7xl with horizontal padding.
- On small screens, reduce the headline size and stack the content in one column.

Split the code into small files: page, navbar, nav link, hero, and index.

Notice what this prompt leaves out. It doesn't say "make it modern" or "make it beautiful." Those words give the tool nothing to act on.

Option 2: Copy a Prompt from a Block Page

The second way is faster when a block is already close to what you need. Open the ShadcnSpace website and pick any free or pro block from the Shadcn block library. Copy the block's prompt, and paste it into any AI tool.

That prompt already holds your project requirements, every file path, and the full code. The next step shows what it looks like.

Step 2: How to Generate the First UI

This tutorial uses Option 2 so you can study a complete prompt. Paste a prompt like this into your AI tool, and open your project folder so the tool can create files:

Create a Shadcn block in the codebase.
The codebase should support following:
- Shadcn project structure
- React ^19
- Tailwind CSS ^4
- TypeScript ^5

If it doesn't, provide instructions on how to setup project via shadcn CLI, install Tailwind CSS v4 or Typescript.

Here are the files for the block:

File path: app/hero-03/page.tsx
(code for this file)

File path: components/shadcn-space/blocks/hero-03/hero.tsx
(code for this file)

File path: components/shadcn-space/blocks/hero-03/navbar.tsx
(code for this file)

File path: components/shadcn-space/blocks/hero-03/navlink.tsx
(code for this file)

File path: components/shadcn-space/blocks/hero-03/index.tsx
(code for this file)

## Implementation Steps
1. Inspect components.json. Determine the correct aliased paths for components, utils, ui, lib, and hooks. Update all import statements and file paths in the code above to match before creating any files.
2. Install dependencies. Using the project's package manager (npm / yarn / pnpm / bun), install any dependencies and devDependencies listed in the block files.
3. Install shadcn/ui components. Using the appropriate shadcn CLI runner for the project (npx / pnpm dlx / bunx --bun), add any required shadcn/ui components.
4. Add global styles. Append only the CSS variables and custom styles referenced by this block to globals.css. Do not add unrelated styles.
5. Create block files. Write each file to the exact target path shown above. Do not rename or restructure files.
6. Verify imports. Ensure every import resolves correctly against the project's alias configuration. Fix any broken paths before finishing.

The component must be fully functional and visually match the provided code. Once all steps are complete, the block is ready to use in the project.

In the real prompt, the full code of each file sits under its file path. You'll see all five files below.

This prompt works for four reasons:

  • It states the exact stack, so the tool doesn't guess versions.

  • It lists exact file paths, so the tool doesn't restructure your project.

  • It gives ordered steps, so the tool checks your 

    components.json
    before it writes any file.

  • It defines "done" in the last line, so the tool knows when to stop.

You can reuse this pattern for your own prompts.

The Generated Files

After the tool finishes, you should have five files. Read each one before you run the page.

app/hero-03/page.tsx
import HeroPage from "@/components/shadcn-space/blocks/hero-03/index";

const Page = () => {
  return (

};

export default Page;

/hero-03
route and renders the block.

How the hero works:

1. The video background: The 

video
element uses 
loop
, 
autoPlay
, 
muted
, and 
playsInline
. Browsers only allow autoplay when the video is muted, and 
playsInline
stops iPhones from opening the video in full screen. The 
object-cover
class makes the video fill the section without stretching.

2. The overlay: The 

bg-black/50
layer sits on top of the video. This keeps the white text readable on any frame of the video.

3. Animation on scroll into view: The 

useInView
hook returns 
true
when 10 percent of the section is visible (
amount: 0.1
). The option 
once: true
makes it fire one time, so the headline doesn't fade in again every time you scroll back.

4. Responsive headline: The headline size grows through breakpoints, from 

text-4xl
on phones to 
xl:text-9xl
on large screens. On small screens, the headline and the arrow stack in a column (
flex-col
), and from 
sm
upward they sit in a row.

5. Why 

"use client"
is needed: The file uses a hook (
useRef
, 
useInView
) and Motion, which both need the browser. In the Next.js App Router, that needs the 
"use client"
directive at the top.

How the navbar works:

1. A sticky header with a growing background: The header uses 

sticky top-0
. A 
before:
pseudo-element starts at 
before:h-0
and grows to 
before:h-full
when 
sticky

2. Scroll detection with cleanup: The 

handleScroll
function sets 
sticky
to 
true
after 80px of scrolling. The 
useEffect

3. A controlled dropdown: The 

open

onOpenChange

menuOpen

4. An animated overlay: 

AnimatePresence

5. Theme tokens in the menu: The menu uses 

bg-background
, 
text-foreground
, 
text-muted-foreground

border-border

    1. Group hover: The 

    group

    2. A reveal without layout jumps: The icon wrapper goes from

    components/shadcn-space/blocks/hero-03/index.tsx

export default HeroPage;

    How the index file works:

    1. Data lives in one place: The 

    navigationData
    array holds the links. The navbar only displays what it receives, so you can change links without touching the navbar.

    2. A negative margin pulls the hero under the navbar: The navbar is 

    h-20
    (80px). The 
    -mt-20
    class on 
    main
    moves the hero up by the same amount, so the video fills the full screen behind the sticky header.

    What to Check Before You Run It

    Before you open the page, read the code and check:

    • Imports: Each import path should match your 

      components.json
      aliases.

    • Dependencies: The tool should have installed 

      motion
      and 
      lucide-react
      .

    • shadcn/ui components: The 

      dropdown-menu
      component should exist in 
      components/ui
      . If it doesn't, run 
      npx shadcn@latest add dropdown-menu
      .

    • Class names: Tailwind ignores classes it doesn't know, so a typo fails without any error. In 

      navbar.tsx
      , the 
      nav
      element has 
      item-center
      , and the correct class is 
      items-center
      . You'll fix this in Step 4.

    Spending a few minutes on this check saves much more time later.

    Step 3: How to Build with Reusable shadcn/ui Components

    AI tools often repeat the same markup. A menu, a button, and a card each get their own hand-written styles, and no two look the same. Shared components fix this problem.

    This block shows three habits you can copy.

    Use One Component for Each Job

    The menu uses shadcn/ui 

    DropdownMenu
    instead of a hand-built menu. You get keyboard support, focus handling, and correct accessibility attributes from one tested component. If you add a second dropdown on another page, it looks and behaves the same.

    Use 
    cn()
    for Conditional Classes

    The navbar and the navigation link both use 

    cn()
    from 
    @/lib/utils
    . It merges class names and handles conditions, such as 
    sticky && "before:h-full"
    . It also removes conflicting Tailwind classes, which plain template strings don't do.

    Keep Data Apart from Markup

    The links live in the 

    navigationData
    array and the 
    NavLink
    component renders them. To add a page, you add one object to the array. You don't write any new JSX.

    When to Start from a Block

    A hero and a navbar are just the start. A real product also needs sidebars, tables, and charts. Writing all of these from prompts takes time, and the output often looks different from page to page.

    A block gives you a tested starting point, and prompts handle the changes. If you build an admin area, look at the shadcn dashboard blocks. They give you layouts for the sidebar, the header, and the content areas.

    The hero in this tutorial uses Motion for fade-ins, a spinning icon, and a scroll-based reveal. If your page needs more motion, the shadcn animated blocks collection shows how animation is structured in blocks like this one.

    Before you use any block, read its code and check its license, as you would for any package.

    Step 4: How to Improve the Result with Follow-Up Prompts

    Treat the first result as a draft. Change one thing per prompt, so you can see what each prompt did. If a change breaks something, undo it with Git and make the next prompt narrower.

    Fix a Typo

    Start with the class name from Step 2:

    In components/shadcn-space/blocks/hero-03/navbar.tsx, change the class "item-center" to "items-center" on the motion.nav element.
Do not change anything else.

    Make Colors Consistent

    The block uses fixed 

    teal-400
    classes in several places. A theme token is easier to change later:
    Replace every teal-400 class in the hero-03 block files with the primary theme token. If needed, add the color to the CSS variables in globals.css. Do not change anything else.

    After this change, you can restyle the whole block by editing one CSS variable.

    Improve Responsive Behavior

    In hero.tsx, make the headline wrap on screens narrower than 640px and keep the arrow button below the headline. Keep desktop styles unchanged.

    Handle a Slow Video

    The video loads from a remote URL. Until it loads, the user sees the section background. Ask for a clear fallback:

    In hero.tsx, add a poster attribute to the video element. Keep the
bg-black background on the section so the text stays readable while the video loads or if it fails.

    Handle an Empty Menu

    The navbar maps over 

    navigationData
    . If the array is empty, the menu opens with no links. Ask the tool to handle that case:
    In navbar.tsx, if navigationData is empty, do not render the menu button.

    The tool should wrap the dropdown in a check like this:

    {navigationData.length > 0 && (
  
    {/* trigger and content stay the same */}
  
)}

    Move Fixed Content into Props

    The navbar has a phone number and an email address written inside the component. Props make the navbar reusable:

    In navbar.tsx, add two props: phone and email. Use them in place of the hard-coded phone number and email address. Update index.tsx to pass the values. Keep all styles unchanged.

    After each prompt, review the changed files, run the page, and commit when it works.

    Step 5: How to Run and Customize the Final UI

    Start the development server:

    npm run dev

    Open 

    http://localhost:3000/hero-03
    in your browser. This is the route that 
    app/hero-03/page.tsx
    creates.

    Run These Checks

    • Resize the window to about 375px wide: The headline should shrink, and the content should stay on screen.

    • Open the menu: Close it with the close button, the overlay, and the Escape key.

    • Use the keyboard: Press Tab and confirm that the menu button shows a visible focus state.

    • Scroll down: The navbar should stay at the top, and its teal background should slide in after 80px.

    • Hover a link: The spinning icon should appear next to it.

    • Check for errors: Run these two commands:

    npx tsc --noEmit
npm run lint

    Customize the Page

    You can customize the page by updating its navigation, content, assets, contact details, and theme styles.

    1. Update Navigation Links

    Open 

    index.tsx
    and edit the 
    navigationData
    array to change menu labels and URLs.
    const navigationData = [
  { title: "Home", href: "/" },
  { title: "Features", href: "/features" },
  { title: "Pricing", href: "/pricing" },
  { title: "Contact", href: "/contact" },
];

    Make sure each link points to a valid route in your application.

    2. Change the Headline and Text

    Open 

    hero.tsx
    and replace the existing heading, description, and button labels with your content.
    Build Your Next Project Faster
    

    Explore reusable UI components for your next web application.

    Keep the existing layout and component structure intact.

    3. Replace Images, Videos, and Icons

    Add your assets to the 

    public
    directory and update their paths in the relevant components.

    For example, 

    public/images/logo.svg
    is accessible at 
    /images/logo.svg
    .

    4. Update Contact Details

    Open 

    navbar.tsx
    and replace the existing phone number and email address.
    +1 (555) 123-4567
hello@example.com

    Use your actual contact details and update any other components that display them.

    5. Change Theme Colors

    Edit the CSS variables in 

    globals.css
    to update your page colors.
    :root {
  --primary: #2563eb;
  --background: #ffffff;
  --foreground: #111827;
}

    Use the variable names already defined in your project, and update the dark theme variables if your application supports dark mode.

    6. Customize Dropdown Styles

    Open 

    components/ui/dropdown-menu.tsx
    and update the relevant Tailwind CSS classes.

    For example, change 

    rounded-sm px-2 py-1.5
    to 
    rounded-md px-3 py-2
    to adjust the dropdown item's corners and spacing.

    Changes to this shared component may affect every dropdown that uses it, so test the menus across your application.

    7. Run and Test Your Changes

    Start the development server and check that everything works as expected.

    npm run dev
npm run lint
npm run build

    Check 

    package.json
    for the available scripts before running lint and build commands.

    Always test AI-generated code before shipping it. Code that looks correct can still fail to build, load assets incorrectly, or behave unexpectedly in the browser (more on this below).

    Live Preview:

    How I Check AI-Generated Code Before Deployment

    AI coding agents can create or modify multiple files, install dependencies, and run terminal commands. I treat the agents' output as a starting point, not production-ready code. Before deploying, I review the changes and verify that the application behaves as expected.

    Here are the checks I recommend before shipping AI-generated code:

    1. Review the Changes

    Check which files the agent created or modified. Review the code to understand what changed, whether it follows your existing project structure, and whether it introduces unnecessary dependencies or unrelated modifications.

    With Git, you can inspect the changes using:

    git diff
git status

    If you don't understand a change, ask the agent to explain its purpose and potential side effects before accepting it.

    2. Run the Application and Test Key Interactions

    Start the development server and open the application in your browser. Test the features you changed instead of checking only whether the page loads.

    For example, verify that navigation links work, dropdowns open and close, buttons perform their intended actions, forms validate input, and images or videos load correctly. Also check how the page behaves on mobile and desktop screen sizes.

    Open the browser's developer console and look for JavaScript errors, failed network requests, and missing assets.

    3. Run Automated Checks

    Use the scripts available in your 

    package.json
    to check code quality, run tests, and verify the production build.
    npm run lint
npm test
npm run build

    These are common examples, not universal commands. Your project may not define a 

    test
    script, so check the available scripts first. Fix any relevant errors before proceeding.

    4. Check Security and Configuration

    Review new dependencies, API calls, environment variables, and any code that handles user input or sensitive data. Never expose API keys or secrets in client-side code, and don't run unfamiliar commands from an AI agent without understanding what they do.

    For applications handling authentication, payments, or user data, perform additional security checks appropriate to those features.

    5. Verify Before Deploying

    Before shipping, confirm that the production build succeeds, the main user flows work, and no important functionality has regressed. Review the final changes once more and deploy to a staging environment first when one is available.

    My rule is simple: if I can't explain what the generated code does, I'm not ready to ship it. AI agents can speed up development, but reviewing, testing, and taking responsibility for the final code remain the developer's job.

    Key Concepts Recap

    A Prompt Is a Spec

    A good UI prompt states the layout, components, colors, spacing, and responsive behavior. It also names the stack, lists the file paths, gives ordered steps, and defines what "done" means.

    Two Ways to Get a Prompt

    You can write a prompt with an AI tool, or copy the prompt from a free or pro block page and paste it into any AI tool.

    Read Before You Run

    Check generated code for wrong imports, missing dependencies, class name typos, and fixed values. Tailwind ignores unknown classes, so typos fail silently.

    Reuse Components

    Shared shadcn/ui components give you consistent behavior and styling. Use 

    cn()
    for conditional classes, and keep data in arrays apart from markup.

    Group Hover and Logical Layout

    The 

    group
    class lets a child respond to its parent's hover state. The navigation link uses it to reveal an icon without a layout jump.

    Scroll-Based Animation

    useInView
    with 
    once: true
    runs an animation one time when an element enters the screen.

    "use client"
    in Next.js

    Any file that uses hooks, browser events, or Motion needs the 

    "use client"
    directive at the top.

    Small Follow-Up Prompts

    Change one thing per prompt, review the diff, and commit after each good result.

    Conclusion

    In this tutorial, you learned how to build a website user interface using AI prompts. You wrote a prompt that covers layout, components, colors, spacing, and responsive behavior. You generated a hero section with an animated navbar, inspected every file, and improved the result with small follow-up prompts.

    You also saw why shared components matter. The dropdown menu, the 

    cn()
    helper, and the data-driven links keep the code consistent, and blocks give you a strong starting point for larger pages.

    On your next page, write the spec first, name your stack and your files, and read the output before you move on. This habit gives you better results from any AI coding tool.

    Resources

    • Shadcn UI: Collection of copy-paste shadcn/ui components, blocks, templates, and dashboard layouts.

    • Shadcn Space: Free and pro blocks library with copyable prompts.

    • Shadcn Dashboard Blocks: Ready-made admin layouts with sidebars and content areas.

    • Shadcn Animated Blocks: Blocks that use motion.

    • Next.js Documentation

    • Tailwind CSS Documentation

    • Motion Documentation

    • Lucide Icons

entries.title: How to Migrate an Application from AWS to GKE [Full Book]
entries.summary: This guided lab walks you through migrating a small payments app, with a React UI and Express API running on a single AWS EC2 instance, while PostgreSQL stays on AWS. You’ll move the UI and API to Goo
entries.content:
This guided lab walks you through migrating a small payments app, with a React UI and Express API running on a single AWS EC2 instance, while PostgreSQL stays on AWS.

You’ll move the UI and API to Google Kubernetes Engine without changing the public URL customers already use, gradually shifting traffic from AWS to GKE a few percent at a time.

By the end, you’ll have run the app locally, stood up AWS, built GKE in eight Terraform stages, tested the new environment, shifted production traffic to GKE, completed the cutover, and torn down what you no longer need.

The image below shows the middle of the migration, with both clouds live, customers still using one URL, and the database remaining on AWS.

Around that request path, three more systems do their jobs:

Table of Contents

Before You Start

What You Need Installed

Install each tool when its chapter needs it. You don't need everything on day one.

ChapterTools
1Docker Desktop (or Docker Engine with Compose on Linux), Git, and 
python3
4An AWS account, the AWS CLI (run 
aws configure
once), Terraform 1.5 or newer, 
rsync
, and an SSH key
6Node.js 20 or newer on your laptop. The check scripts in 
scripts/
use 
node
to read JSON
10A GCP project with billing turned on, the 
gcloud
CLI, and 
kubectl
14A GitHub account and your own copy of this repository on GitHub
19
kustomize
(install with 
brew install kustomize
on a Mac, or see kubectl.docs.kubernetes.io)

On Windows, use Git Bash or WSL for every command in this book. The commands are written for a Bash shell.

Skills You Need

Prior Kubernetes, Terraform, GCP, or load-balancer experience isn't required. Don't buy a domain. On AWS, you open 

https://
plus the Elastic IP. The browser warns about a self-signed certificate. Click through it and you get the same ClearPay login as on your laptop. On GCP you add one 
/etc/hosts
line so 
https://api.clearpay.test
points at the load balancer, unless you turn on Cloud DNS.

What This Costs

AWS costs about $1.25 per day. GCP costs about $1.60 to $3 per day once it's up. A weekend run of the whole book costs a few dollars.

Neither environment should run for a month. If you stop for more than a couple of days, tear both down:

./scripts/teardown-gcp.sh
cd infra/aws/terraform && terraform destroy

Two files hold the detailed numbers: infra/aws/COST.md and infra/gcp/COST.md. The book sends you to those two files and no other documents.

How This Book Works

Clone the repository and run every command from its root folder unless a step says 

cd
somewhere else:
git clone https://github.com/Osomudeya/migrate-api-aws-gke-devops.git

cd migrate-api-aws-gke-devops

The repository already holds the app, the Terraform, the Kubernetes files, the pipeline, and the scripts.

You won't write new code. Your work is to run each step, read what the system prints, and decide whether to continue.

This book reads like a story where you join a small payments company in week one, and every chapter is a task someone on the team hands you.

Each chapter opens with a time stamp and a scene, then follows the same loop:

Most Important Rule

Don't run a command you don't understand. If the book hasn't told you why yet, keep reading, because the "why" is the point.

This book has two kinds of steps.

The first simply asks whether the step worked, such as whether the file copied or the container started. If it did, continue.

The second asks you to think about what happened. Once the command finishes, read the output and understand what it means before moving to the next chapter.

The Chapters

Read the chapters in order and skip none. Chapter 1 doesn't ask you to install Kubernetes or open GCP. Those come later.

PartChaptersWhat happens
1. Run ClearPay and Put It on AWS1–6You run the app on your laptop, deploy it to one AWS server, and write down how fast it is
2. Plan the Move7–9You read the assignment, map what the app depends on, and read the GCP design
3. Build Google Cloud With Terraform10–11You build GCP in eight Terraform stages, one at a time
4. Get ClearPay Onto GKE Staging12–15The pipeline puts ClearPay on GKE staging, and the promotion gate checks it
5. Make GKE Production-Ready16–18You review security, set up a dashboard, and break staging on purpose
6. Move Customers to GKE19–23You deploy production and move traffic from 1 percent to 100 percent
7. Finish the Migration24–28You prove the cutover, retire AWS, tear everything down, and write it up

If Something Doesn't Work

Stay in that chapter. Use its "If it fails" steps. Don't skip ahead. A problem you carry forward gets harder to find, because the next chapter adds another cloud on top of it.

The job isn't to memorize Kubernetes or Terraform. It's to learn how to work through a real migration: understand what's running, make decisions based on what you find, verify the result, and know what to do when something breaks.

How Long This Takes

This might take more than one day. If you'll be away for more than a day or two, destroy the AWS and GCP resources so you're not billed for them while it's idle. The commands are in "What this costs" above.

The Team

This lab starts as Zee, a junior DevOps engineer on the ClearPay team, week one. You play Zee.

  • Maya is the engineering manager. She asks for evidence.

  • Daniel is a senior engineer. He pairs with you on servers, Kubernetes, and capacity.

  • Amara maintains the payments API. She cares about one thing: no customer is charged twice.

  • Chris handles customer support. He hears first when transfers fail.

Your job is to move the payments API from one AWS EC2 server to GKE without a customer-visible outage, while PostgreSQL stays on AWS.

Part 1. How to Run ClearPay and Put It on AWS

A migration needs a starting point you trust. In this part, you run ClearPay on your laptop, deploy it to AWS the way the company runs it today, and write down how fast it is. Every later chapter compares GKE against those numbers.

Chapter 1. Run ClearPay on Your Laptop

Week one, Monday, 9:05 a.m.

Your laptop is new. The Wi-Fi password is on a sticky note. The first message in your inbox is from Maya, the engineering manager, and it's short.

Maya: "Get ClearPay running on your laptop first. Log in, send $20, and then we'll talk about moving the API to GKE."

The code is in the repository: 

api/
, 
ui/
, and 
db/
. Nothing is running yet.

Why This Matters

Later chapters need a picture of a good login and a good $20 send. When something fails on AWS or GKE, you compare it with this.

What You're About to Run

ClearPay has three parts, and each part has one job.

  • The UI is what a customer sees and taps: the login page, the balance, and the Send button. UI stands for user interface.

  • The API is the part that does the work. It has no screen. The UI sends it a message, such as "send $20 to Bob". The API checks the message, does the work, and sends back a reply, such as "done". API stands for application programming interface. Think of it as a door with rules. The UI asks in a fixed way, and the API answers in a fixed way.

  • The database is where ClearPay writes everything down: every account, balance, and payment. PostgreSQL is the database program ClearPay uses.

  • A server is a computer that stays on all day and waits for requests. The API runs on one.

A café works the same way. The menu is the UI. The waiter is the API. The kitchen and its records are the database. A customer never walks into the kitchen. The customer tells the waiter what they want.

This chapter runs all three on your laptop. Later chapters move the UI and the API to Google Cloud. The database stays on AWS.

Steps

Start Docker Desktop. Don't install Node or PostgreSQL for this chapter. They run inside the containers.

From the folder that holds 

docker-compose.yml
:
docker compose up --build

The first build takes a couple of minutes. This terminal keeps printing logs and doesn't give you a prompt back until you press Ctrl+C. Leave it running.

Wait until all three of these lines appear. The names on the left may start with your folder name:

Container -postgres-1 Healthy
api-1       | {"message":"api_started", ...}
ui-1        |   ➜  Local:   http://localhost:5173/


Healthy
means Postgres is up. 
api_started
means the API is up. The 
localhost:5173
line means the UI is up.

Open a second terminal in the same folder. Create two demo accounts:

docker compose exec api node db/seed.js

This runs the seed script directly. The API image has no npm, on purpose, because the security scan in Chapter 14 flags it.

Expected output:

seeded: alice@clearpay.dev (password: password123)
seeded: bob@clearpay.dev (password: password123)

If you see 

skip (already exists): alice@clearpay.dev
, the accounts exist from an earlier run. That's fine.

This is what's now running:

Check

In the second terminal:

curl localhost:4000/health

Here's the expected output. Your 

instance
value will be a container ID:
{"status":"ok","served_by":{"platform":"aws","version":"1.0.0","instance":"14b8d5d767ea","commit":"local","rollback_active":false}}


"status":"ok"
is the check. 
served_by
names the platform that answered the request. It says 
aws
on your laptop because 
docker-compose.yml
sets 
PLATFORM: aws
. Later, GKE answers with 
gke
, and that one field tells you which cloud handled each request.

Now open http://localhost:5173 and sign in. Seed already created Alice, so don't register her:

  • Email: 

    alice@clearpay.dev

  • Password: 

    password123

Send $20 to 

bob@clearpay.dev
. The transfer appears under Recent activity as 
Sent
with a short ID, for example 
Sent · a1b2c3d4
.

Look at two places on this dashboard. You'll watch them for the rest of the book:

  • Each line under Recent activity ends with 

    served by aws/1.0.0
    . That's the platform and version of the API process that wrote the transfer. It's stored with the transfer in the database.

  • The black bar at the top says 

    All systems operational
    when 
    /health/ready
    succeeds. That means the API process is up and can reach Postgres. It says nothing about logins. A wrong password shows a red error on the form, while the bar keeps saying 
    All systems operational
    .

After Chapter 5, you open the same dashboard on the AWS address. Same login, same two places.

If it Fails:

  • failed to connect to the docker API
    or 
    docker.sock
    : Docker Desktop isn't running. Start it, wait until it is ready, and run 
    docker compose up --build
    again. 

  • email already registered
    on the Register page: Alice already exists. Go back to Sign in. 

  • invalid credentials
    : the password is the full string 
    password123
    . If that still fails, run the seed command again. A 
    skip (already exists)
    line means the account is there. 

  • docker compose up
    exits right away: run 
    docker compose logs api
    in the second terminal. On a slow first boot the API can start before Postgres accepts connections. Run 
    docker compose up
    again.

  • Port 

    4000
    or 
    5173
    already in use: another program on your machine holds that port. Stop it, or change the port mapping in 
    docker-compose.yml
    .

Decision

If the transfer went through, the application works. Continue.

If it didn't, fix it here, on the laptop. AWS and GKE are harder to debug. On this machine, the answer is one 

docker compose logs
command away.

Done When:

  • docker compose up
    runs without errors

  • The seed reports two accounts, created or skipped

  • You sent $20 in the UI and saw it under Recent activity

Chapter 2. Read the Code That Matters

Monday, 11:30 a.m.

The $20 went through. You're still looking at the transfer line when a chair rolls up next to yours. Daniel, the senior engineer at the next desk, has his coffee and no hurry.

Daniel looks over at your screen. "You don't need to memorize every line. Know which file does which job, so you can open it fast during the migration."

Why This Matters

Every later chapter touches one of these four files. Five minutes now saves you a search under pressure later.

Steps

Open these files in this order:

  • api/src/index.js
    starts the API and connects every route: health checks, 
    /api/info
    , login, and transactions. 

  • api/src/servedBy.js
    is 17 lines long. It reads 
    PLATFORM
    , 
    APP_VERSION
    , and 
    ROLLBACK_ACTIVE
    from environment variables. The dashboard uses it to print 
    served by aws/1.0.0
    . 

  • api/src/routes/transactions.js
    handles sending money. Find the 
    idempotency_key
    check near the top. It runs before anything else. 

  • api/src/db.js
    connects the API to Postgres. Find 
    DB_POOL_SIZE || '10'
    .

Daniel stops you on the last file.

"A connection is an open line to the database. One API process can hold up to ten of those lines at the same time. Remember that number."

What You Now Know

index.js                 → starts the API and connects the routes
servedBy.js              → says which cloud answered (aws or gke)
routes/transactions.js   → sends money, checks the idempotency key first
db.js                    → talks to Postgres, up to 10 connections per process


servedBy.js
fills the dashboard line 
served by aws/1.0.0
. That's which cloud answered, not who logged in.

Today there's one API process, so ten connections is the whole pool. On GKE, several copies of the API run at once. Kubernetes calls each copy a pod. Each pod gets its own pool of ten, and every pod shares the same database. Chapter 22 comes back to that math.

Done When:

  • You can say, without looking, which file sets the connection limit and which file names the platform

Chapter 3. Prove a Retry Never Charges Twice

Monday, 2:10 p.m.

After lunch, you get a message from someone you haven't met yet. Amara maintains the payments API. Maya told her you have ClearPay running on your laptop, so she skips the greeting.

Amara: "Send $20 twice with the same key. Alice's balance should drop by $20, not $40."

Why This Matters

Alice sends $20 to Bob. She taps Send, and the screen freezes. She doesn't know if the payment worked, so she taps Send again.

Without protection, the API sees two requests and takes $20 two times. Alice loses $40 for one payment.

The 

idempotency_key
stops this. "Idempotent" means safe to repeat: doing it twice gives the same result as doing it once.

The key is a label the app puts on each payment, for example 

round-a
.

  • The first request arrives with the label 

    round-a
    . The API takes $20 and saves the label.

  • The second request arrives with the same label. The API sees 

    round-a
    again. It knows this is the same payment, so it takes no money. It sends back the first result.

Same label means same payment.

This matters more during the migration. Sometimes the first tap goes to AWS and the retry goes to GKE. Those are two different servers, but they use one database. GKE looks in that database, finds 

round-a
, and doesn't charge again. One shared database keeps the customer safe on both clouds.

Use 

curl
for this chapter, not the Send money button. The UI gives every click a new key, so every click is a new transfer.

For a deeper walk-through of idempotency, see PayFlow: A Production-Grade Fintech System for Learning Real DevOps.

Steps

Stay in the second terminal, in the folder with 

docker-compose.yml
. Run one command at a time and read the output before the next one.

Log in as Alice. This stores her login token in a shell variable called 

TOKEN
. A token is proof that Alice signed in. Later commands send it with 
$TOKEN
.
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST localhost:4000/api/auth/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"alice@clearpay.dev","password":"password123"}' \
  | python3 -c "import sys, json; print(json.load(sys.stdin)['token'])")

This prints nothing when it works. Run 

echo $TOKEN
to confirm. You should see a long string.

Then read Alice's account. Write down the 

balance_cents
number.
curl -s localhost:4000/api/accounts/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

This is the expected shape. Your numbers and 

id
will differ:
{"account":{"id":"...","balance_cents":"94000","currency":"USD"},"served_by":{"platform":"aws","version":"1.0.0","instance":"...","commit":"local","rollback_active":false}}


94000
means $940.00. If you haven't sent anything yet, you'll see 
100000
($1,000.00). If the command says 
missing_token
or 
invalid_token
, run step 1 again.

Now pick a label you haven't used yet:

LABEL=round-a

Send $20 to Bob. 

2000
is $20.00 in cents.
curl -s -X POST localhost:4000/api/transactions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"to_email\":\"bob@clearpay.dev\",\"amount_cents\":2000,\"idempotency_key\":\"$LABEL\"}"

Look for 

"replayed"
in the reply:

  • "replayed":false
    means this send took $20. Continue. 

  • "replayed":true
    means this label was used before, probably in an earlier run. No money moved. Set 
    LABEL=round-b
    and send again until you see 
    "replayed":false
    .

Send the exact same request again. Don't change 

LABEL
.
curl -s -X POST localhost:4000/api/transactions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"to_email\":\"bob@clearpay.dev\",\"amount_cents\":2000,\"idempotency_key\":\"$LABEL\"}"

Now you should see 

"replayed":true
, and the transaction 
id
matches the first send.

Read the account again:

curl -s localhost:4000/api/accounts/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"

Check

balance_cents
is 2000 lower than the number you wrote down, not 4000 lower. If you started at 
94000
, you now see 
92000
.

If it Fails:

  • echo $TOKEN
    is empty: run the login command again.

  • The second send still shows 

    "replayed":false
    : 
    LABEL
    changed between the two sends. Run 
    echo $LABEL
    , then send again.

  • Both sends showed 

    "replayed":true
    : the balance won't change. Pick a new 
    LABEL
    and repeat steps 3 and 4.

Done When:

  • One send returned 

    "replayed":false
    and the next returned 
    "replayed":true
    for the same label 

  • balance_cents
    fell by 2000, not 4000

Chapter 4. Build the AWS Server With Terraform

Tuesday, 9:15 a.m.

Maya stops at your desk on her way to a meeting. Yesterday you told her that ClearPay runs on your laptop and that a retried payment charges only once.

Maya: "Good. Now, localhost isn't a baseline. Get ClearPay onto AWS and prove a customer can complete a transaction there. Then we can talk about leaving AWS. Daniel will work with you on this one."

Daniel rolls his chair over from the next desk.

Daniel: "One rule before you start. Don't skip 

terraform plan
."

Why This Matters

This book starts from the setup many small companies run: one Linux server with no Docker on it.

systemd, the Linux service manager, starts the Node API when the server boots. nginx sits in front of it and handles HTTPS on port 443. PostgreSQL runs on Amazon RDS, the managed database service.

There's no AWS load balancer. A load balancer spreads traffic across several servers, and this setup has one. Adding one would add an hourly bill for no gain. The numbers are in 

infra/aws/COST.md
.

The file 

api/Dockerfile
exists, but only your laptop uses it. The AWS server never runs Docker.

Daniel: "The EC2 server won't have Docker. systemd starts Node on boot, next to nginx. That's the server you're inheriting."

The diagram above shows how a customer request reaches ClearPay on AWS. The Elastic IP provides a fixed public address for the EC2 server. Chapter 7. Read the Migration Assignment

Wednesday, 4:00 p.m.

Maya forwards the assignment with one line on top: "Read all of it before you open Terraform."

The Assignment: Migrate the ClearPay API from AWS EC2 to GKE.

ClearPay runs on one EC2 server. It works, but it has no autoscaling, no staged rollout, and a deploy process that lives in one person's head. You ran that process by hand in Chapter 5, so you know what it lacks.

The business wants the API on Kubernetes: a staging environment, automated deploys, and room to grow. Again, the database isn't part of this assignment.

Current Architecture

ClearPay lives in one AWS account, in the default VPC from Chapter 4: one EC2 server and one RDS database.

What Can't Change

  • The database. Moving Postgres is a separate, later project.

  • The API contract. The same paths return the same JSON: 

    /health
    , 
    /api/auth/login
    , 
    /api/transactions
    . A browser or script that works on AWS must work on GKE with no changes.

  • Customers see no lasting outage at any point.

Acceptance Criteria

Done means this, in order:

  • GKE serves all production traffic, and it stays that way. Errors and latency stay inside the limits you wrote in Chapter 6.

  • While AWS still exists, rollback to AWS still works.

  • Then you retire AWS, after GKE has proven itself.

What moves and what stays:

The diagram shows the migration from AWS to GCP. The ClearPay UI and API move from the EC2 server to Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), where staging and production run. PostgreSQL remains on Amazon RDS in AWS, so both environments use the same database during the migration.

The whole book follows one path:

AWS only  →  AWS and GKE together  →  GKE only, then EC2 gone

The middle step is where the work happens. Both clouds run the same app, both talk to the same database, and traffic moves between them in small steps.

How Traffic Will Move

Today, customers type the Elastic IP and every request goes to AWS.

  • You put a Google load balancer in front, and customers switch to its address once. They keep using that address for the rest of the migration.

  • The load balancer then sends some requests to AWS and the rest to GKE. It starts with 100% AWS and 0% GKE.

  • You raise the GKE share by hand with 

    scripts/shift-traffic.sh
    , a few steps at a time, checking numbers after each step.

  • If something goes wrong on GKE, you send 100% of the traffic back to AWS with 

    shift-traffic.sh 100 0
    . The rollback takes seconds.

The diagram above shows how customers reach ClearPay through one public address while the UI and API run on both AWS and GKE during migration. Both environments connect to the same PostgreSQL database on Amazon RDS in AWS. Keeping the database in one place avoids migrating payment data alongside the application.

Why not use DNS to split traffic? DNS is the lookup that turns a name into an IP address. Laptops and internet providers cache the answer.

After you change a DNS record, some customers keep going to the old place for minutes or hours. A rollback that takes an hour isn't a rollback. The load balancer changes the split in seconds.

Rollback Requirement

At every stage of the shift, going back to 100 percent AWS must be fast and safe. Not a redeploy. Not a DNS change that takes an hour to spread. Chapter 20 tests exactly that, before the first shift.

What "Zero Downtime" Means Here

It doesn't mean zero failed requests, ever. No real system can promise that.

It means no customer sees a lasting outage. A few failed requests are allowed if they stay under the limits you wrote in Chapter 6.

Why the API Moves First

If the API and the database move together and something breaks, the fault could be in either one, or in how they interact. Moving only the API keeps the question small: can this API run on GKE without hurting customers?

That's an answerable question. "Can you move everything at once safely?" is much harder to answer, and much worse to debug live.

Why the Database Stays on AWS

Chapter 13 shows what connecting across clouds involves. For now: PostgreSQL doesn't move in this project.

A future, separate project handles that, most likely with Google's Database Migration Service, continuous replication, and its own cutover. This project ends with the API on GKE and the database still on AWS. That's the plan, not an unfinished loose end.

Why Both Clouds Must Run at the Same Time

The rollback plan depends on it. You send a little traffic to GKE and keep AWS ready. If GKE fails, AWS takes everything back. That only works while AWS still exists.

Do this now, before Chapter 9. Write four numbers in your notes. They decide how much this move may cost you.

Standard or Autopilot

GKE is Google's managed Kubernetes. It runs in two modes:

  • Standard: you choose the virtual machines, grouped in a node pool. Google bills those machines whether the app is busy or idle.

  • Autopilot: Google hides the machines. You say how much CPU and memory each container needs, and Google bills that.

This repo uses Standard. The reason isn't cost. It keeps node pools, machine sizes, and autoscaling visible, and those are what this book teaches. Autopilot would hide them.

Work out both costs yourself. Standard bills the machines. One 

e2-medium
running all day is about $1.44 in 
infra/gcp/COST.md
, plus Cloud NAT.

Autopilot bills the CPU and memory each pod reserves. 

k8s/base/deployment.yaml
reserves 
250m
CPU (a quarter of one CPU core) and 
256Mi
of memory per API pod. Using the Autopilot rates in 
infra/gcp/COST.md
, three API pods cost roughly:
0.25 vCPU × 3 × $0.0445/hour × 24  ≈  $0.80 / day
0.25 GiB  × 3 × $0.0049/hour × 24  ≈  $0.09 / day

That's about $0.89 a day for three API pods, before the UI pods. Autopilot can cost less than one Standard machine. The lab still uses Standard so you can see the node pool.

Tell Maya both numbers and the reason.

How Many API Processes

AWS runs one API process. On GKE, a HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) adds or removes API pods based on CPU use. Each pod is one API process with its own pool of ten database connections.

This lab's cluster is three small 

e2-medium
machines. The production HPA in 
k8s/overlays/production/patch-hpa.yaml
runs between 1 and 3 API pods, because three machines of that size can't fit more alongside GKE's own system pods.

Answer Daniel: "One to three API pods on GKE, plus one on AWS while both run. Each can open ten connections."

A company with bigger machines would set a higher ceiling, such as 3 to 8 pods. Chapter 22 shows why that ceiling needs checking against the database limit before traffic moves.

A Designed Network

On AWS, this lab used the default VPC that AWS created for you. Nobody designed it.

On GCP, 

infra/gcp/terraform/02-network
builds its own VPC with a named subnet and Cloud NAT. The cluster's machines get private addresses only. They reach the internet, and later the AWS database, through Cloud NAT, which gives all of them one shared public IP.

Region

01-foundation/variables.tf
sets the region to 
us-east4
, the Google region closest to AWS's 
us-east-1
. Every database query from GKE crosses between the two clouds, so a short distance keeps that trip short. If your AWS setup isn't in 
us-east-1
, change this before you build anything.

The Map

The left side is what exists. The right side is what Part 3 builds.

The diagram above maps the migration from AWS to GCP. Customers use one public address, managed by the GCP load balancer, which splits traffic between the existing AWS EC2 server and GKE. GKE runs the UI and API in private nodes, with Cloud NAT providing outbound internet access. Both environments connect to the same PostgreSQL database on AWS. Traffic shifts gradually to GKE while the database stays in place.

You'll meet three public IP addresses, in this order:

  • The Elastic IP. That's the EC2 server. Customers use it today.

  • The GKE Gateway IP. The load balancer sends GKE's share of traffic to it. Customers never type it.

  • The load balancer IP from 

    08-edge
    . Customers switch to this address once, and the traffic split happens behind it.

Part 3 doesn't need AWS running every minute. AWS is needed again in Chapter 11 (to copy the database URL into Secret Manager) and Chapter 13 (to open the database to GKE).

Don't stop the EC2 server and leave RDS running. RDS is most of the daily AWS bill, a stopped RDS restarts itself after seven days, and the Elastic IP bills either way.

To come back, run
