Chapter 11. Build GCP in Eight Terraform Stages

Friday, 10:30 a.m., to Monday of week two

GCP is built in eight Terraform stages. Each stage creates one layer of the destination environment.

Run them in order. After each stage, verify the result before moving to the next.

Build the Google side of the migration: APIs, network, cluster, image registry, identities, secrets, error alerting, and the public load balancer.

Why Eight Stages?

The Terraform lives in eight folders, 

01-foundation
through 
08-edge

apply

The diagram above shows how Terraform builds GCP infrastructure in eight stages. It enables the required APIs, creates the network and private GKE cluster with Cloud NAT, then sets up the image registry, identities, secrets, error monitoring, and public load balancer. Two things will need Google permissions later: the ClearPay pods on GKE, and GitHub Actions when it pushes images and deploys.

The old way is to download a service account key file. A key file is a password on disk. If it leaks, anyone can use it. This lab never creates one.

Workload Identity is the Google feature that links a Kubernetes service account, or a GitHub repository, to a Google service account without a key.

Think of each service account as a badge. Nothing wears a badge today. Later, Google lets a named pod or a named repository wear one for a short time, and no key file ever exists.

Namespaces are separate areas inside one cluster. Staging and production share the cluster's machines but not their identities, so a staging pod can't read production's secrets. A real company would usually run separate clusters, often in separate projects. This lab uses one cluster to keep the bill small.

Stage 7: Count API Errors (

Every time something happens in the API, it writes a short note called a log line. A login writes one. A payment writes one. When something goes wrong, the note says 

"level":"error"
. A failed payment writes this:
{"level":"error","message":"transaction_failed","timestamp":"2026-09-29T10:15:02.000Z","error":"..."}

On GKE, Google Cloud collects every one of these notes. This stage builds two things on top of them:

  • A counter, named 

    clearpay-api-error-count
    . It goes up by one each time an error note appears.

  • An alarm, named 

    ClearPay API - elevated error rate
    . It switches on when the counter goes up more than five times in five minutes. One error can be bad luck. Five in five minutes means something is broken.

The alarm has no phone number or email attached yet. When it switches on, the Google Cloud console shows it, but nobody gets a message. You can add an email later in the console.

The counter stays at zero for now, because ClearPay doesn't run on GKE yet. Zero is the correct result today.

Part B. Open the AWS Database to GKE

Don't describe this as "connecting GKE to the database". That phrasing suggests the database moves too, and it doesn't. This step lets GKE reach and use the real, unmoved AWS database, safely.

The cluster's machines have no public IP. Their outbound traffic leaves through Cloud NAT with one public address, the NAT IP from Stage 2. RDS will accept connections from exactly that address on port 5432, and the connection string already requires TLS (

).
GKE Pod  (clearpay-api)
   │
   ▼
Private node  (no public IP)
   │
   ▼
Cloud NAT  (clearpay-nat-ip)
   │
   │  public egress, one /32
   ▼
AWS security group  (additional_db_ingress_cidrs)
   │  port 5432 + SSL
   ▼
RDS PostgreSQL 16

This is one of three ways to connect two clouds:

OptionSetupOngoingWhat it is
Public endpoint + IP allowlistA few Terraform variables$0 extra (normal internet egress)RDS gets a public IP. The security group allows only the Cloud NAT 
/32
. TLS is required.
Cloud VPN (site-to-site)Hours: gateways on both cloudsAbout $36 per month on GCP plus about $36 per month on AWS per tunnel (GCP VPN pricing) A private path. RDS has no public endpoint. Not in this repository.
Partner Cross-Cloud Interconnect for AWSReal provisioning lead timeFixed 10 or 100 Gbps tiers (Cross-Cloud Interconnect) A dedicated private link for heavy traffic. Not in this repository.

To compare them for your own system:

(expected monthly GB) × (price per GB on that path) + fixed monthly cost of that option

ClearPay sends small queries, so a VPN would cost more each month than the data is worth. This lab uses the allowlist. A busier system might choose differently.

Chapter 14. Build the CI/CD Pipeline

Tuesday, 3:00 p.m.

The cluster is ready for its first deploy. Maya reads the team channel and adds one rule.

Maya: "From now on, let's not run

on staging by hand. The pipeline should build the image, scan it, push it, and deploy it, the same way every time."

The workflow file is already written: 

.github/workflows/deploy.yml
. Your job is to understand it, connect it to Google Cloud, and watch it deploy staging.

Why a Pipeline?

When a person deploys by hand, each deploy is slightly different. Someone skips the scan because it's late. Someone deploys from a laptop with uncommitted changes. When something breaks, nobody can say what ran.

A pipeline removes those differences. Every image comes from a commit, passes the same scan, and reaches the cluster through the same steps. The promotion gate in Chapter 15 means something because it checks an image built that way.

How the Pipeline Works

The workflow has two jobs:

Open 

.github/workflows/deploy.yml
in your repository and keep it open alongside this diagram. The diagram maps the workflow's two jobs and their sequence. The file contains the actual GitHub Actions configuration. Follow both together as you read through the triggers, permissions, image build and scan, staging deployment, and production promotion.

Read the file top to bottom with this map.

Triggers: 

on: push: branches: [main]
runs Job 1 on every push to 
main
. 
workflow_dispatch
adds a "Run workflow" button in GitHub with one checkbox, 
promote_to_production
. Job 1 runs only when that box is off (
if: ${{ !inputs.promote_to_production }}
). Job 2 runs only when it's on. A push can never reach production by itself.

Permissions: 

id-token: write
lets the job ask GitHub for a short-lived OIDC token, a signed statement that says "this run belongs to repository X". Google checks that statement against the pool from Stage 5 and hands back temporary credentials for 
clearpay-ci
. No key file sits in GitHub secrets, so there's no key to leak.

Image tag: The tag is the short commit SHA from 

git rev-parse --short HEAD
. Each image points to exactly one commit. The pipeline also pushes a moving tag, 
staging-latest
, but deploys use the SHA.

Scan: Trivy is an open-source scanner that checks the packages inside an image against lists of known vulnerabilities. Each known vulnerability has an ID like 

CVE-2026-29786
. The workflow sets:

  • severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
    , so only serious findings count 

  • ignore-unfixed: true
    , so a finding with no patch available yet doesn't block the build 

  • exit-code: "1"
    , so any remaining finding fails the job

Together they mean: fail if a serious vulnerability has a fix and this image doesn't have it. Nothing gets pushed if the scan fails.

Push: The job tags each image with the full registry path, 

us-east4-docker.pkg.dev//clearpay/api:
, and pushes it. 
clearpay-ci
has 
artifactregistry.writer
from Stage 5, so the push works.

Deploy to staging: The step works inside 

k8s/overlays/staging

  • It writes the two staging secrets from Secret Manager into 

    secrets.staging.env
    on the runner. 
    umask 077
    makes the file readable only by the runner's user. The file is gitignored and dies with the runner. 

  • sed
    replaces the 
    PROJECT_ID
    placeholder in 
    patch-serviceaccount.yaml
    and 
    secretproviderclass.yaml
    with your real Project ID. 

  • kustomize edit set image
    points the overlay at the image with this commit's SHA. 

  • kubectl apply -k .
    sends the overlay to the cluster. 

  • kubectl rollout status
    waits up to 180 seconds for the API and UI pods to become ready. If they never do, the job fails. 

clearpay-ci
has 
container.developer
, which lets it deploy workloads but not change the cluster itself.

Promote to production: Job 2 is the only way the pipeline touches production:

  • environment: production
    pauses the job until a named reviewer clicks Approve in GitHub.

  • It doesn't build anything. It reads the image string that staging is running right now and deploys that exact image to production.

That rule is called "build once, promote the same artifact". The image that passed the Chapter 15 gate is byte for byte the image customers get. A rebuild could pull a newer package and ship something nobody tested.

and applies small environment-specific changes from

Chapter 15. Check Staging and Run the Promotion Gate

Week two, Wednesday, 10:00 a.m.

The pipeline finished without an error at 6:40 last night. You took a screenshot. Nobody at ClearPay cares about the screenshot.

Daniel stops at your desk and looks at the passing pipeline.

Daniel: "So GKE is healthy?"

Why This Matters

Kubernetes reports a pod as ready when its health check answers. That says the process is up and can reach the database. It says nothing about logins, payments, or double charges. The promotion gate checks those.

Part 5. How to Make GKE Production-Ready

Staging works. The promotion gate proved five things: the app runs, it reaches the database, a user can log in, a repeated payment charges once, and the balance drops by the right amount. That's a good result. It's not the same as being safe for customers.

Think of a new car that passed its first test drive. It starts and it turns. Before anyone rides in it, you still ask three more questions. Are the doors locked? Can you see the dashboard? What happens on a steep hill, or when a tire goes flat?

This part asks the same three questions about ClearPay:

QuestionChapterWhat you check
Is anything exposed?16Who can read the secrets. Whether the database connection is encrypted. Whether each account has only the permissions it needs.
Can we see what's happening?17 (optional)A practice dashboard on your laptop that shows how fast the app answers and how many requests fail. It teaches the tools. During the traffic shift you watch with command-line checks.
What happens under pressure?18Many requests at once, like a busy afternoon. A pod that dies in the middle of work. A restart while customers are using the app.

These questions come now, on purpose. Customers are still on AWS, so if something breaks in this part, nobody notices and nobody loses money. Fixing it here costs you an hour. Fixing it after customers arrive costs you their trust, and every fix happens while people are watching.

Step 3. Kill a Pod and Time the Recovery

Delete one API pod and time how long Kubernetes takes to replace it:

kubectl -n staging get pods -l app=clearpay-api

42 s

Step 4. Restart the Deployment Under Load

This step needs one change to 

scripts/load-test.sh
. Without it, 
failed=
reads 0 even when requests die. The script only counts requests that get an answer. When the pod restarts, the tunnel drops, requests get no answer, and the script stops that worker without counting a failure.

Open 

scripts/load-test.sh
in your editor. Replace the whole 
hit()
function with this one. Two things are new: 
2>/dev/null || true
on the curl line, and the 
if
line at the end.
hit() {
  local path="$1" out code secs
  out=$(curl "${CURL_OPTS[@]}" -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{time_total}' \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    "$BASE_URL$path" 2>/dev/null || true)
  code="${out%% *}"
  secs="${out##* }"
  echo "$code" >> "$CODES"
  node -e "process.stdout.write(String(Math.round(Number(process.argv[1]) * 1000)) + '\n')" "$secs" >> "$TIMES"
  if [ "$code" = "000" ]; then sleep 0.5; fi
}


000
is what curl reports when it got no answer. The short pause stops a failing worker from looping thousands of times a second.

kubectl -n staging get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp | tail

The events show old pods stopping and new pods starting, one at a time.

Chapter 19. Deploy Production and the GKE Gateway

Week three, Monday, 9:00 a.m.

This is the week customers can land on GKE. Nobody says it out loud. The office is a little quieter than usual.

So far, GKE only holds staging. Staging is a private copy that you reach through a tunnel. Customers will use a separate copy called production. This chapter builds that copy, and it connects the address customers will call.

Two things are missing:

  • The production namespace. A namespace is a separate area inside the cluster. Staging has one. Production doesn't have one yet, so no production pods exist. You will create it and put the same image in it that passed the staging gate.

  • Something behind the GKE edge IP. In Stage 8 you reserved a public address for GKE, called the edge IP. It works like a phone number you reserved but never connected: it rings, and nobody picks up. You will connect it to a Gateway. The Gateway answers each request and passes it to the production pods.

When you finish, GKE can answer real requests. You still don't move any traffic. The front door keeps sending 100 percent of customers to AWS until Chapter 21.

Why This Matters

The load balancer can only send traffic to GKE if something on GKE answers. That something is a Gateway: a Kubernetes object that tells Google to build a load balancer in front of a Service. Here it listens on 

clearpay-gke-edge-ip
and forwards to the production API and UI.

The 

08-edge
load balancer reaches both clouds through Internet NEGs (network endpoint groups that point at an outside IP address). This type has no health checks. If a backend goes down, the load balancer keeps sending it traffic, and customers get 502 errors. Your protection is 
synthetic-health.sh
, the decision gates, and 
rollback.sh
.

Before 50 / 50: Do the Connection Math

Daniel, who is on the call, cuts in before you go to the halfway mark. "How many database connections can hit RDS if GKE scales all the way up while AWS is still live?"

Each API process can open up to

AWS, 1 process × 10:          10

40 is under 81, so there's room to raise the traffic. Your 

max_connections
may differ if your RDS instance is a different size. What matters is that your worst case stays below it.

Now run the same math for a bigger setup. A company with larger machines might run the HPA from 3 to 8 pods: 10 + 80 = 90 connections, against a small RDS instance that allows about 87.

Neither setting is wrong on its own. The pool size was set in the API code, and the pod ceiling was set in a Kubernetes file, by different people at different times. They only collide when both clouds run at full load at the same time, which is the exact situation a gradual migration creates.

Chapter 23. When the Numbers Go Bad

Wednesday, 4:12 p.m.

The last shift is done. Every customer is now on GKE, and the health check keeps printing 200, which means all is well. The support inbox has been quiet for the past hour. Amara checks the transactions table one more time.

Daniel is still looking at the deployment. He counts the API copies running in GKE, then looks at the database metrics.

"Can I tell you about the worst afternoon at my last job?"

Chris turns his chair around.

Daniel leans back.

"It was another migration for a different company, same basic problem though. We were moving customers from one cloud to another, and we'd reached about half of them by Friday afternoon. Traffic started climbing, so the new environment began adding more copies of the API."

He pauses for a moment.

"The old environment was still running too. It was serving the customers we hadn't moved yet."

You look at the deployment on the screen.

"So both environments were using the database?" "Yes. And every copy of the API needed database connections."

He points at the database on the diagram.

"That was where we got into trouble." Daniel reaches for a pen.

"Think about a restaurant with a fixed number of seats. The restaurant has enough seats for a certain number of people, but the number of seats doesn't change because more people arrive."

He draws two groups on the whiteboard.

"AWS was one group. GKE was the other. Both groups were using the same restaurant."

He added another group beside GKE.

"Then traffic increased. GKE added more copies of the API, and each new copy needed database connections. The old AWS copies were still holding their connections too."

He puts the pen down.

"The database had a limit. We kept increasing the number of connections going into it."

"Requests started waiting for connections. Then they started timing out."

He looks at you.

"So you were watching the new environment, but the database was dealing with both environments."

"Exactly."

Daniel looks at the diagram again.

"That was the part we missed. We calculated what the new environment needed. We didn't calculate what the database needed while both environments were running."

He sits back down.

Daniel turns his laptop toward you.

Amara: "I don't care that traffic is back on AWS. Did the transfer happen once?"

Answer from the database, through the transaction history, not from the load balancer. The idempotency key from Chapter 3 is what makes a retried transfer safe here, even when the first try went to GKE and the retry went to AWS.

Write down one number for the incident review: the minutes from "noticed" to "traffic back on AWS".

Step 5. Fix the Cause

Daniel: "What will you change so that number can't happen again?"

There are four real options, each with a cost:

  • Lower 

    DB_POOL_SIZE
    per pod: Fewer connections per process. Cheap and fast. Each pod can serve fewer database queries at the same time.

  • Lower the HPA's 

    maxReplicas
    in 
    k8s/overlays/production/patch-hpa.yaml
    . Caps the total. GKE can no longer scale as far under a real traffic spike.

  • Raise RDS 

    max_connections
    with a custom parameter group. Each connection uses database memory, and a small instance like 
    db.t3.micro
    can fail to start if you set it too high. Check AWS's guidance for your instance size first.

  • Put a connection pooler in front of Postgres, such as PgBouncer or RDS Proxy. Many app connections share a few database connections. The best long-term fix, and the most work to set up.

This book doesn't pick one for you. Write down which one you chose and what you gave up.

For the smallest real change, lower the pool size. The math with 6 per pod: 8 × 6 = 48 from GKE, plus 10 from AWS, is 58. That fits under 87 even at the full ceiling.

In an emergency you can set it live:

kubectl -n production set env deployment/clearpay-api DB_POOL_SIZE=6

A live change leaves no record, and the next deploy erases it. Make the real change through the pipeline: set 

DB_POOL_SIZE
in 
k8s/base/deployment.yaml
, commit, and push to 
main
. The pipeline builds, scans, and deploys staging. Load-test staging hard enough to push the HPA to its ceiling, using Chapter 18's steps with higher concurrency. A fix that only passes under light load proves nothing. Then run the promotion gate, and promote with the Chapter 19 pipeline job.

Step 6. Resume

Maya: "Are we ready for 10 percent?"

"Yes. The API is healthy, synthetic checks are clean, errors are within the limit, the pool math holds at the ceiling, and rollback is tested."

Daniel: "Agreed."

Maya: "Your call."

Clear the rollback flag first:

./scripts/clear-rollback-flag.sh  ~/.ssh/clearpay-deployer

Refresh the UI. The rollback banner is gone. Leaving the flag on would keep the banner showing after recovery, which trains people to ignore it.

Then repeat Chapters 21 and 22 from the start:

./scripts/shift-traffic.sh 99 1
# observe, compare, record, decide

./scripts/shift-traffic.sh 90 10
# observe, compare, record, decide

./scripts/shift-traffic.sh 75 25
./scripts/shift-traffic.sh 50 50
./scripts/shift-traffic.sh 25 75
./scripts/shift-traffic.sh 10 90
./scripts/shift-traffic.sh 0 100

Watch the HPA and the error lines closely at the stage where the incident happened last time. That stage is where the fix proves itself.

Add a line to the cost ledger. A second pass through the shift means more hours with both clouds billing. Keep that cost visible instead of folding it into one "migration cost" number.

The Skills Behind This Chapter

The diagram above shows the incident response process from observation to recovery. Start by checking latency, the status bar, and error logs. Form a hypothesis, test it against the database connection limit, and use live measurements as evidence. If customers are affected, stop shifting traffic and roll back. Fix the cause through the pipeline, test under maximum expected load, and resume the migration only when the evidence supports it.

An incident isn't a hunt for the answer. It's the work of reducing uncertainty until you can make a safe decision. If customers are failing, the safe decision is to stop and roll back. If they aren't, the safe decision is to keep watching. Don't roll back because a number looks odd, and don't keep shifting because the pods look healthy.

This is the checkpoint. GKE is serving 100 percent.

AWS is a priced safety net now, not a leftover you forgot.

Part 7. How to Finish the Migration

GKE serves every customer. AWS still runs, and still bills, as a safety net. This part turns the cutover into evidence, puts a date on the safety net, and removes what you no longer need.

Chapter 24. Prove the Cutover With Numbers

Thursday, 9:00 a.m.

Maya has a meeting with the company leaders at ten. She stops at your desk with her laptop open to an empty page.

Maya: "The leaders weren't on any of our calls, and they'll ask one thing: did customers notice the move? I need a short summary I can put on the screen. How many requests went through, how many failed, how fast the app answers compared with AWS, and whether anyone saw an outage. Can you have it before ten?"

You nod. Every number she asked for comes from two scripts you already know.

Steps

Run the two checks that produce hard numbers against the public address, now at 100 percent GKE:

HOST=$(terraform -chdir=infra/gcp/terraform/08-edge output -raw public_hostname)
./scripts/promotion-gate.sh "https://$HOST" \
  alice@clearpay.dev password123 bob@clearpay.dev

Then run 

load-test.sh
against 
https://$HOST
with the Chapter 6 settings, and copy the scorecard. Add the counts from your Chapter 22 loops and the 
synthetic-health.sh
log.

The Evidence

Below is this lab's table. Yours will have different numbers:

Production requests (counted checks, not a full dashboard total):
  40 /health one minute after 0 / 100:  3 aws, 37 gke
  40 /health ninety seconds later:      0 aws, 40 gke
  load-test.sh 10 × 20s:                ok=310  failed=0
  promotion-gate.sh:                    5 passed, 0 failed
Successful requests:                 310 + 40 + 5 in those runs
Failed requests:                     0
5xx errors:                          0.0 %
p95 latency (GKE, 100%):             647 ms
  Chapter 6 AWS baseline was 164 ms.
  Chapter 18 GKE staging (port-forward) was 1157 ms.
Sustained customer-visible outage:   0 seconds

Local Prometheus didn't watch GKE, so this table uses counted checks. Don't invent a dashboard total you never measured.

Check the table against the limits you wrote in Chapter 6, before GKE existed:

  • Outage limit: no stretch of 5xx errors above your limit. This lab had zero failed requests.

  • Failure limit: p95 under your ceiling. This lab's 647 ms is under the example ceiling of 1500 ms, so it passes.

Passing isn't the whole story. 647 ms is about four times the AWS 164 ms. Customers never saw an outage, but every request got slower. Write that down plainly instead of hiding it. The last section of this book explains why.

Why the Table Doesn't Say "Zero failed requests, ever"

No real system running for hours, across traffic shifts and a possible rollback, can honestly promise that. Claiming it would weaken the one claim that matters: no sustained outage a customer could see.

A few failed requests inside the limit you set in advance is the honest version of "this went well". The standard is controlled and measured, not perfect.

Done When:

  • Every line in your table holds a number you measured

  • Each line is checked against your Chapter 6 limits, including any that failed

Chapter 25. Run on GKE and Set a Date for AWS

Friday, 10:00 a.m.

Maya comes back from her meeting with a question from the leaders.

Maya: "So what changed for the customer?"

You look at the numbers. Traffic is 100 percent GKE. Transfers succeed. Synthetic checks all pass. PostgreSQL is still on AWS. The EC2 server serves nobody.

"The address stayed the same and nobody saw an outage."

Maya: "Then this system is yours now. And I want a calendar date for turning off the old server."

Step 1. Watch it Run

Let production run for a real window before you commit to anything. For a real company that means days, not the minutes after the last shift.

This lab's 100 percent window lasted minutes, with a 5/5 gate and 

failed=0
. Write that down. A weekend lab isn't a week of production.

Step 2. Check the Alert

Stage 7 created the alert policy 

ClearPay API - elevated error rate
, which fires on more than five error lines in five minutes. It has no notification channel, so nobody gets told when it fires. An alert that reaches nobody isn't an alert.

For a real system, add a notification channel in Cloud Monitoring and trigger a test on staging, never by sending errors to customers. For this lab, write down the gap: the policy exists, and nobody gets paged.

Step 3. Review Capacity

Look at the HPA over the window:

kubectl -n production get hpa clearpay-api

This lab stayed at 1 replica and 4 to 7 percent CPU, even at 15.5 requests per second during the 100 percent load test. One pod was enough. Three 

e2-medium
machines for one API pod is more than this traffic needs.

Google offers Committed Use Discounts (CUDs): a lower price in exchange for promising to use a set amount of machine capacity for one or three years.

Commit only after you have a stable usage history. A commitment based on the architecture you planned, instead of the usage you measured, is a guess with a contract attached. This lab bought none, because a few hours of GKE isn't a usage history.

Step 4. Write the Handover

Write this for someone who wasn't part of the migration. This lab's version:

Logs:       kubectl -n production logs deployment/clearpay-api
Dashboard:  http://localhost:3000 if observability/docker-compose.yml
            is up. GKE series may be empty.
Alert:      Cloud Monitoring "ClearPay API - elevated error rate"
            No notification channel.
Rollback:   scripts/rollback.sh, only while EC2 still exists.
Hostname:   terraform output public_hostname
            terraform output static_ip_address
            (yours, not a hostname copied from this book)

Step 5. Put a Date on AWS

scripts/rollback.sh
works only while the EC2 server exists, and the server bills every day it exists. Decide how long it stays, write down why, and price it:
AWS daily cost:              ~$1.25/day (infra/aws/COST.md)
Retention window:            ___ days
Decommission date:           ___
Total safety-margin cost:    ___ days × $1.25 = $___

This lab used 0 extra days and retired AWS compute the same day 100 percent GKE was proven, because it's a teardown lab.

A real company might keep AWS for one or two weeks. A shorter window saves money. A longer one buys more confidence. The mistake is leaving it open as "keep it around just in case", which costs money every day and never gets revisited.

Write the decommission rules before the date arrives, so the decision doesn't get made under deadline pressure:

  • a set number of days at 100 percent GKE with no rollback

  • no alert fired for a GKE-caused problem in that window

  • a named person signs off

This lab's rules: weights 0 / 100, gate 5/5, load test 

failed=0
, HPA at 1, no rollback.

Last, check that nothing else still points at the Elastic IP directly: bookmarks, hardcoded URLs in other systems, or outside uptime monitors set up before the load balancer existed.

Done When:

  • You watched production for a written, real time window

  • The alert gap is written down

  • Capacity is reviewed and the CUD decision is written down

  • The handover note exists

  • The retention window, decommission date, cost, and rules are written down

Chapter 26. Retire the AWS Server

Friday, 3:00 p.m.

The date has arrived, and the rules from Chapter 25 are met. Remove the EC2 server and keep the database. It was never part of this migration.

Steps

Perform your final check, from the repository root. GKE must pass the gate on the public address:

HOST=$(terraform -chdir=infra/gcp/terraform/08-edge output -raw public_hostname)
./scripts/promotion-gate.sh "https://$HOST" \
  alice@clearpay.dev password123 bob@clearpay.dev

Then confirm that Terraform tracks the server you mean to remove:

cd infra/aws/terraform
terraform state show aws_instance.api   # confirm you have the right resource

Next, return to the repository root with 

cd ../../..
, then remove the AWS compute resources only:
./scripts/teardown-aws-compute.sh
# Pass --yes to add -auto-approve after you have read a plan once.

After this step, rollback to AWS is gone. That's the point of the decision you made in Chapter 25.

Read the Destroy Plan

The script destroys only these:

  • the EC2 instance

  • the Elastic IP

  • the security group rule that let the API reach the database

  • the API security group

  • the SSH key pair

  • the CloudWatch alarm

RDS stays.

The database rule is its own Terraform resource, 

aws_security_group_rule.db_from_api
, and the script removes it first. If that rule lived inside the database security group, AWS would refuse to delete the API security group while the database still referenced it.

A full 

terraform destroy
in 
infra/aws/terraform
would also delete PostgreSQL. Don't use it here.

Clean Up Credentials

  • The SSH key pair in AWS is gone with the script. Delete the local private key 

    ~/.ssh/clearpay-deployer
    if you used it only for this server.

  • Remove anything else that pointed at the old server, such as saved hosts or scripts with the old IP.

  • Remove any CI/CD secrets or variables that referenced the old server.

Update the Diagram

The dual-cloud diagram from Chapter 7 is now wrong. The new picture is GKE alone behind the load balancer, with the database still on AWS, as Chapter 7 said the project would end.

Done When:

  • The gate passed on the public address before the teardown

  • AWS compute is destroyed, and RDS still exists

  • The local deploy key is removed or kept on purpose

  • Your architecture diagram matches what runs

Chapter 27. Tear Down GCP and the Database

Friday, 5:30 p.m.

The office is emptying out. Two clouds are still billing you by the hour.

This is a lab. Once your notes are complete, remove everything that still bills: the Gateway load balancer, the GKE machines, Cloud NAT, the registry, and the RDS database.

Before tearing anything down, complete the migration record in Chapter 28. It asks you to document the final architecture, migration results, performance numbers, and total cost. If you still need evidence from the running system, collect it now. Once you destroy the infrastructure, those live measurements will no longer be available.

Steps

From the repository root:

./scripts/teardown-gcp.sh
# Pass --yes to skip the prompt and -auto-approve each stage.

The script:

  • Deletes the Gateway and the production and staging workloads. Kubernetes creates Google load balancer pieces for the Gateway, and Terraform doesn't know about them. Deleting the Gateway first lets Google remove them. Skip this and Terraform can get stuck on resources it didn't create.

  • Runs 

    terraform destroy
    in reverse stage order: 
    08-edge
    → 
    07-observability
    → 
    06-secrets
    → 
    05-identity
    → 
    04-registry
    → 
    03-gke
    → 
    02-network
    → 
    01-foundation
    . Later stages depend on earlier ones, so they come down first.

Type 

yes
at the script's prompt, then read and confirm each Terraform plan.

Namespaces can sit in 

Terminating
for a few minutes. The script waits up to 180 seconds for each delete, then moves on. Destroying the cluster removes them anyway.

Then remove the database. The migration ended with it on AWS on purpose, but a lab shouldn't keep paying about $0.80 per day for it:

cd infra/aws/terraform
terraform destroy

Last, delete the 

api.clearpay.test
line from 
/etc/hosts
.

The book never created or deletes your GCP project. Don't delete a project unless it held only this lab.

Done When:

  • kubectl get ns
    no longer shows 
    staging
    or 
    production
    , or the cluster is gone

  • Every 

    infra/gcp/terraform/0*-*
    stage is destroyed 

  • terraform destroy
    finished in 
    infra/aws/terraform

  • GCP and AWS billing show nothing from this lab still running

This is the checkpoint. The work is over.

Write down what actually happened, including the bill, before you forget.

Chapter 28. Write the Migration Record

Week four, Monday, 9:00 a.m.

Write down what happened, the architecture, the bill, and what you would change, before the details fade.

Part 1. The Architecture Record

Before:

User → nginx (TLS) → systemd-managed Node process → RDS Postgres

One EC2 server, one database, a default network nobody designed, secrets in a plain 

.env
file, no autoscaling, and a deploy process run by hand.

During the migration:

After:

Then one short paragraph for each model:

  • Traffic: weighted backends on a global external Application Load Balancer, changed by 

    shift-traffic.sh
    . Not DNS, because cached DNS answers would have made rollback slow.

  • Deploys: GitHub Actions builds, scans, and deploys every commit to staging. Production gets the exact staging image, only after the promotion gate and a reviewer's approval.

  • Database: never moved. The same RDS instance from Chapter 4 stayed the single source of truth the whole time.

  • Security: Workload Identity for both the pods and the pipeline. No downloaded service account key existed at any point. Secrets come from Secret Manager.

  • Observability: the API's own JSON logs and 

    /metrics
    endpoint, the same on AWS and GKE, plus a log-based error metric in Cloud Logging.

  • Rollback: one script that moves the traffic weight and sets a flag on AWS, tested before the first shift.

Part 2. The Postmortem

The four of you go through the notes together. Maya opens with the question everyone half expects.

Maya: "Was Kubernetes the problem?"

"Not really. It did what we told it to do. The thing to watch was the database. Every copy of the API can open ten connections, GKE can run several copies, and AWS was still serving customers at the same time. Add those up and you get close to the database's limit.

On this small cluster we topped out at forty connections against eighty-one, so nothing broke. On a cluster that scales to eight copies, the same sum goes over the limit."

Daniel nods. "That's what I missed at my last company. All the numbers were there, and nobody put them side by side. You did it before any traffic moved."

Amara: "And the payments? Was every transfer charged once?"

"Yes. The idempotency key from Chapter 3 held through every shift. We even replayed a payment at 100 percent GKE, and there was no second charge."

Maya closes her laptop. "So what would we do differently next time?"

Write these sections:

What worked:

  • Idempotency keys, built in before GKE existed, made it safe for a customer's retry to land on a different cloud than the first try.

  • The staged Terraform meant each failure pointed at one stage.

  • The pipeline meant production ran the exact image that passed the gate.

  • Rollback was tested in Chapter 20, before it was ever needed.

What went wrong in this lab:

  • Local Prometheus never watched GKE, so Chapter 24 used counted checks instead of a dashboard total.

  • The alert policy has no notification channel.

  • The small node pool couldn't run the pod counts a real company would use, so the connection-limit risk was checked on paper, not seen live.

  • GKE's p95 was about four times AWS's.

The root cause: Two reasonable settings, 

DB_POOL_SIZE=10
and the HPA's 
maxReplicas
, were chosen in different places. Nobody checked their product against the database limit until the migration ran both clouds at once. The fix isn't complicated once you find it. Finding it takes treating Chapter 23 as a real investigation instead of skipping ahead to an answer.

Decisions and their trade-offs:

  • GKE Standard over Autopilot: full control of node pools and autoscaling, at the cost of having to understand and size them. This lab paid for three mostly idle machines. Autopilot might have hidden this connection-limit risk inside its own scheduling, for better or worse.

  • Two environments instead of five: less to build and pay for, at the cost of staging sharing the production database. Fine at this scale, not for every company.

  • A public database endpoint with an IP allowlist instead of a VPN: no setup time and no monthly VPN bill. The cost is that RDS has a public endpoint, even if it accepts only one IP and requires TLS.

  • Leaving the database on AWS: a simpler, safer migration, at the cost of every query crossing between clouds.

So what would change in a second migration? Before any traffic moves, compute the worst-case connection count across every environment that shares the database. Compare it with the real limit. Make it a checklist item, not a live discovery.

Part 3. The Cost Postmortem

This lab's version:

Budget: about $25 for five days of GCP usage.

Actual dual-run: about $4.30 total, $1.25 AWS + $3.05 GCP. The GCP $3.05 was covered by free-trial credit, so the actual GCP charge was $0.

The migration stayed on schedule. No incident, rollback, or second shift was needed.

The cluster was over-provisioned: three GKE nodes supported one API pod, with CPU at 4–7%.

Standard GKE was chosen for the teaching value. Autopilot would have been cheaper for this workload.

No CUD was purchased.

Conclusion: The migration stayed well within budget, but the GKE setup used more capacity than the workload needed.

Fill in your own numbers from your cloud bills. This book can't do that part for you, and a guessed number would be the same false precision this whole project avoided.

Done When:

  • The before, during, and after diagrams match what ran

  • The postmortem states the root cause clearly

  • The cost postmortem holds your real numbers

What Comes After This Project

What Question This Project Leaves Open

Chapter 13 flagged it and moved on, on purpose: at what point does keeping PostgreSQL in AWS cost more, in risk and in engineering time, than migrating it? The cross-cloud trip, the dependency on two providers, and the connection-pool pressure from Chapter 23 all sit on the same side of that scale.

Put two numbers from your notes side by side:

AWS, Chapter 6:             p95 164 ms
GKE at 100%, Chapter 24:    p95 647 ms

The API moved and customers never saw an outage. But every request got about four times slower.

The code didn't change. The load test did not change. What changed is distance. On AWS, the API and the database sat in the same data center. On GKE, every query leaves Google's 

us-east4
, goes out through Cloud NAT, crosses the internet to AWS's 
us-east-1
, and comes back. A single transfer runs several queries, so it pays that trip several times. The Google load balancer adds one more hop in front.

Maya reads the table. "Why is it slower?"

"The database stayed on AWS. Every query crosses between clouds."

"Was that a mistake?"

"No. Chapter 7 made the call to move the API alone, because moving two things at once would have made any failure much harder to trace. A problem could have come from the API, the network, or the database move itself. But the call has a price, and now we can measure it."

Maya: "Then that's the next project."

This project doesn't answer the open question. It was never supposed to. The next project moves PostgreSQL to Google Cloud, most likely with Google's Database Migration Service, which copies data continuously so the final switch takes minutes instead of hours. It will use the same method as this book: a baseline first, a written limit, small steps, a tested rollback, and evidence at every stage. When it's done, run the same load test and compare the same two numbers.

Again, that's a separate project, with its own book. This one ends here: ClearPay's API on GKE, its database still on AWS, exactly as Chapter 7 said it would.

What You Should Have at the End

  • Working fintech API and minimal customer UI (

    api/
    , 
    ui/
    )

  • AWS deployment (

    infra/aws/
    )

  • GCP architecture, staged Terraform (

    infra/gcp/terraform/
    )

  • Docker images and a CI/CD pipeline that builds, scans, deploys staging, and promotes the tested image (

    .github/workflows/deploy.yml
    )

  • Kubernetes manifests, two-environment Kustomize overlays (

    k8s/base/
    , 
    k8s/overlays/
    )

  • Database connectivity, validated and never migrated (Chapter 13)

  • Secret management, upgraded from a 

    .env
    file to Secret Manager (
    k8s/overlays/*/secretproviderclass.yaml
    , 
    secretsync.yaml
    )

  • A GKE Gateway behind a weighted load balancer (

    k8s/gateway/
    , 
    infra/gcp/terraform/08-edge/
    )

  • Observability dashboard on your laptop, if you did the optional Chapter 17 (

    observability/
    )

  • Load-testing, promotion-gate, and synthetic health scripts (

    scripts/
    )

  • Migration scorecard (Chapter 6, Chapter 18, Chapter 24)

  • Cost ledger, start to finish (Chapter 6 through Chapter 28)

  • Traffic-shifting procedure (

    scripts/shift-traffic.sh
    )

  • Rollback procedure (

    scripts/rollback.sh
    , 
    scripts/clear-rollback-flag.sh
    )

  • Architecture diagrams (Chapters 4, 7, 9, 11, 13, 14, 19, 28)

  • Migration runbook (this book)

  • Technical postmortem (Chapter 28)

  • Cost postmortem (Chapter 28)

The ClearPay API moved from one AWS EC2 server to GKE. PostgreSQL is still on AWS, on purpose. Customers kept one address while you shifted traffic, practiced a rollback, and finished the cutover.

Maya asked what changed for the customer. The address didn't. The balance didn't. Nobody saw an outage. Now you understand why that was the hard part, and why 647 milliseconds is the next one.

The lab covered how to prove each stage, how to read evidence, and how to undo a bad shift. Destroy anything you're still paying for.

Subscribe to my newsletter for new technical articles, project walkthroughs, and upcoming releases.

How to Discuss This Project in an Interview

I worked on a cloud migration project for a payments application called ClearPay. The application was running on AWS, and the goal was to move it to Google Cloud without disrupting access to the service.

The main challenge was making that move safely. Instead of switching everything at once, I designed a controlled migration where traffic could be moved gradually to the new environment. If something went wrong, I could redirect traffic back to the original system. I also kept the database on AWS to reduce the scope of the migration and avoid introducing unnecessary risk.

I set up the deployment process, security checks, and verification steps needed to confirm that the application was working correctly before completing the switch.

I then tested the final migration. The tests completed without failed requests, and the application didn't produce server errors during the final checks. I also identified a performance difference between the old and new environments that would need further investigation before considering the migration fully optimized.

The project demonstrates that I can plan and execute a cloud migration, manage the risks involved, verify the outcome, and identify issues that still need attention rather than simply declaring success because the application is running.

Interview tip: Be prepared to explain why you used weighted traffic routing, how you validated the application during cutover, what triggered a rollback, and why PostgreSQL remained on AWS.

entries.title: Agentic AI Reliability: Build a Testing Harness for Tool Use, Guardrails, Loops, & Workflow Outcomes [Full Book]
entries.summary: A good final answer doesn't prove that an agentic AI workflow was correct. This book develops a code-backed method for verifying execution and business outcomes from authoritative state and using that
entries.content:
A good final answer doesn't prove that an agentic AI workflow was correct.

This book develops a code-backed method for verifying execution and business outcomes from authoritative state and using that evidence to gate releases.

You'll find a runnable offline agent that demonstrates the core techniques. Chapter 19 distinguishes implemented capabilities from live-model and production extensions.

Table of Contents

  • Introduction

  • Part I: The Reliability Gap

  • Part II: The Foundation

  • Part III: The Core Verdicts

  • Part IV: Behavioral Dimensions

  • Part V: Cross-Cutting Concerns

  • Part VI: The Decision

  • Part VII: Honesty and Adoption

  • Conclusion

  • Glossary

  • References

  • Production-Readiness Checklist

Introduction

The Demo That Lied

Many agentic AI systems are initially evaluated through demos and happy-path tests. A fluent, confident response makes the system appear to work.

The risk begins when that demonstration is treated as sufficient evidence of production readiness. The agent may have skipped a required check, attempted an unauthorized action, committed the same effect twice, or reported success after a dependency failed. A review of the final response alone can miss these failures.

This book builds a reliability harness that verifies execution and business outcomes from authoritative state and uses that evidence to gate releases. It takes the perspective of a performance and reliability engineer: verify the state the agent changed, rather than relying on its account of the work.

What Makes Agents Hard to Test

Conventional tests supply inputs and independently check outputs or state against expected behavior. Agentic workflows introduce two evaluation risks: the agent may receive information that reveals its own answer key, and the evaluator may accept the agent's account as evidence of success.

The same input can also produce different paths across runs, with unauthorized actions, duplicate commits, or false success hidden behind a plausible response.

The harness must therefore verify both the path and the outcome, enforce permissions outside the agent, inject faults, and check recovery or faithful failure. Repeated live runs support reliability estimates with uncertainty. Release gates and production feedback turn those checks into a maintained engineering control.

How the Book is Organized

The book follows a small support and incident-triage agent whose core tests run in continuous integration. Chapter 19 distinguishes implemented capabilities from production extensions.

  • Part I defines the reliability gap, six evaluation activities, and five evaluation levels.

  • Part II builds the architecture, reference agent, and scenarios.

  • Part III evaluates responses, trajectories, tools, and business outcomes.

  • Part IV covers loops, guardrails, state, memory, resilience, and authorization.

  • Part V develops observability, performance measurement, and statistics.

  • Part VI connects release gates, CI, and production feedback.

  • And Part VII explains the method's limits and a staged adoption path.

How to Read it, and What it Doesn't Claim

Read front to back to understand the method, or begin with the chapter that addresses your most consequential risk. Chapters 5 and 9 provide a practical starting point: run the reference agent and verify a business outcome from state.

The harness catches specified failure classes within a declared reliability envelope. It provides reproducible release evidence, but it can't establish complete safety or replace security review, monitoring, staged delivery, and human accountability. Chapter 19 explains these boundaries.

What this book covers, and what it doesn't

This book is for engineers moving agents, copilots, or tool-using workflows toward production. It assumes familiarity with Python, JSON, HTTP APIs, distributed systems, and LLM tool calling. The reference project is vendor-neutral, and the techniques transfer to other stacks.

The harness produces measurements for release decisions within specified coverage. It can't eliminate hallucination, cover every emergent behavior, or replace oversight. Chapter 19 defines what a passing suite supports.

How to Read This Book

The chapters build on one reference implementation. Use the introduction's part-by-part guide to navigate, and Chapter 20 to sequence adoption by risk.

The Python reference runs offline by default with a deterministic scripted adapter, so structural tests need no model API or network access. Live-model response quality, latency, cost, and sampling require a live adapter. The project provides that interface but doesn't ship a live adapter. Offline and live measurements remain separate.

The reference implementation is on GitHub at https://github.com/vasukiudaykiranvudathala/agentic-ai-reliability-harness. Chapter 5 provides installation and test commands.

Part I: The Reliability Gap

Chapter 1. The Reliability Gap: When a Good Answer Hides a Broken Workflow

A Workflow That Reports Success it Didn't Achieve

Consider an internal support agent for a subscription platform. A request arrives: "Account A-1007 reports duplicate billing in the last hour." The agent is supposed to determine whether the account is affected by an active incident, retrieve the applicable remediation policy, and prepare a proposed remediation for a human to approve.

It does some work and returns a final message:

Incident EVT-402 confirmed and a credit_review ticket was created for A-1007.

The answer reads well. It's on topic, correctly formatted, specific, and it references a real incident identifier. A reviewer skimming a queue of such responses would approve it without a second thought.

Now consider what the answer doesn't show. The call that was supposed to confirm the incident timed out. The agent never received a status. It proceeded anyway, created a ticket that asserts an incident it never actually verified, and then described that result as confirmed. The wording is fluent and the underlying execution is wrong, and nothing in the message lets a reader tell the difference.

This is the reliability gap: the distance between an answer that looks correct and a workflow that actually is correct. The gap isn't an edge case that appears only under exotic conditions. It's a structural risk in agentic systems because the surface a human reviews and the execution that actually ran are different objects. A fluent model is very good at producing the first regardless of the second.

This is a constructed teaching scenario, not a claim about a particular production incident. It's also implemented as a runnable test case in the reference project, so you can observe the failure and verify the harness verdict yourself.

Under a single injected timeout on the incident check, one scripted execution declines to open a ticket and states clearly that it couldn't confirm the incident. A second scripted execution, identical except for how it treats the failed dependency, produces the confident message above. The harness passes the first and fails the second.

It reaches that verdict not by grading the wording but by inspecting the authoritative record of what happened: one run left no ticket, while the other left a ticket asserting an unverified incident. The words were never the evidence.

The Many Ways a Good Answer Can Be Wrong

The timeout case is one instance of a general problem. An agent can produce a convincing final answer while, underneath it, the execution went wrong in any of a number of independent ways.

It can select the wrong tool for the task. It can select the right tool and pass it incorrect arguments. It can take an action it had no authority to take. It can repeat a step, or oscillate between two steps, without making progress. It can ignore a dependency that failed and press on as though it had succeeded. It can lose or corrupt the state it was carrying between steps. It can produce a side effect nobody asked for, or hide the fact that its execution was incomplete. It can burn an unreasonable number of tokens or tool calls to arrive at the same place. It can amplify a small upstream hiccup into a downstream retry storm. It can behave correctly in isolation and fall apart under concurrency or across a long-running session. And it can pass all of your checks today and quietly regress tomorrow after a prompt edit, a model upgrade, a tool schema change, or a configuration tweak.

Figure 1-1. The reliability gap. A convincing final response can accompany a broken execution path, so the response and the execution record must be judged separately.

Each of these can coexist with a final answer that a human, or another model asked to grade the answer, would judge as good.

That's the crux. The quality of the final message and the correctness of the underlying work can diverge completely. A system that pays out money, changes account state, files tickets that trigger downstream processes, or takes any action with consequences can't be validated by reading what it says about itself.

Why Conventional Testing Doesn't Catch This

There are three testing habits, each reasonable in its original context, that fail when carried over to agents.

The first is final-answer grading. Most model evaluation compares a produced answer to a reference answer or scores it against a rubric. This measures whether the model can say the right thing. It doesn't measure whether the agent did the right thing, because the answer is a claim about the work, not the work itself. Grading the claim is exactly the check the false-success agent passes.

The second is using transport or request-completion success as a proxy for workflow success. An HTTP 200 establishes that the service handled the request at its API boundary. It doesn't establish that a multi-step business workflow reached the correct end state, because a workflow can return cleanly at the front door while having selected the wrong tool, skipped a required step, or committed a side effect it shouldn't have.

The third is treating model accuracy as system reliability. A model that scores well on a benchmark is a component with a known property. A reliable system is a different claim about a larger object: the agent loop, the tools, the state store, the authorization layer, the retries, the budgets, and the behavior of all of them together under load and under failure.

Improving the model can leave the system exactly as unreliable as before, because most of the failure modes listed above live in the orchestration, not in the model's next-token quality.

None of these habits is wrong in its home domain. They're simply aimed at the wrong object. To close the reliability gap, you have to test the object that actually carries the risk, which is the whole execution path and the business outcome it produces.

Response Correctness Isn't Outcome Correctness

Two questions define the reliability gap.

Response correctness asks: was the final answer correct, relevant, grounded, complete, and appropriately uncertain? It's a property of the text the agent produced.

Outcome correctness asks: did the workflow reach the intended business end state, through valid decisions and authorized actions, with the required state changes applied and prohibited side effects absent? It's a property of the world the agent acted on, read from an authoritative record rather than from the agent's account of itself.

These two properties are independent. A workflow can be right on one and wrong on the other in either direction.

Outcome correctOutcome incorrect
Response correctThe healthy case: the agent did the right thing and described it accurately.The agent accurately reports that a credit was applied, but the credit was unauthorized. The response is factually correct, but the action and workflow are incorrect.
Response incorrectThe agent did the right thing but described it poorly or incompletely. The state is correct, but the user may be misled about what happened. This requires correction and can still be consequential.The clear failure: wrong work, wrong words. The easiest case to catch, and the least of your worries.

The top-right cell is a particularly dangerous failure class because final-answer grading can't see it. For state-changing workflows, the harness treats outcome correctness as an independent primary verdict and response correctness as a separate required verdict. One can never substitute for the other.

Two clarifications that this book holds to throughout. First, a well-written answer is never accepted as evidence that the outcome was achieved. The outcome is verified independently against authoritative state.

Second, evaluating what the agent did means evaluating observable actions, state transitions, outputs, and tool traces. It doesn't mean inspecting the model's private reasoning. Chain-of-thought disclosure isn't an observability requirement, and a system that depends on reading the model's internal narration to know whether it behaved isn't one you can operate.

What a Reliability Harness is

An agentic AI reliability harness is the controlled execution, measurement, and evaluation layer around an agent. It supplies reproducible scenarios, captures model and tool activity, injects failures, evaluates outcomes, measures operational behavior, and applies release gates.

The word around above carries weight. The harness is separate from the agent and doesn't expose expected outcomes, forbidden-action lists, evaluator rules, or release criteria through the agent's execution interface.

The thing you would deploy (meaning the agent, its model, its tools, its authorization layer, and its state) is the system under evaluation. The test rig that surrounds it, meaning the scenario loader, the fault injector, the trace collector, the evaluators, and the gate engine, is the control plane.

Keeping these two separate is what makes the results trustworthy: the agent can't see the answer key, and the evaluators can't be talked out of their verdict by a persuasive final message.

That separation shows up as a deliberate asymmetry. The evaluators read the authoritative business state directly, because they're part of the control plane. The agent can reach that same state only through a controlled gateway, one action at a time, under authorization.

Because the two sides reach the truth by different paths, the harness can compare what the agent says it did against what actually happened. Within the harness threat model, and provided the gateway and authoritative state are correctly protected, the agent can make its claim match the record only by completing the permitted work.

Five Places to Look

Outcome correctness is the headline, but a single pass or fail at the end isn't enough to operate a system or to diagnose it when it breaks. Throughout the book, we'll evaluate a workflow at five levels: the response, the individual steps, the individual actions, the workflow as a whole, and the system it runs in.

A single request can earn a different verdict at each level. The false-success run passes superficial fluency and relevance checks but fails response groundedness. It also fails at the action level because it acts on an unverified incident, and at the workflow level because it creates a ticket it shouldn't have. Chapter 3 develops these five levels in full and makes them the spine the rest of the book hangs on.

Chapter 2. Six Things People Call "Evaluation" (and Why You Need All of Them)

Evaluation: One Word Doing Six Jobs

When two engineers say an agent is "evaluated," one may mean a model benchmark and the other a verified business outcome. The term also covers response grading, trajectory checks, system stress tests, and production monitoring.

These six activities answer different questions, measure different objects, and support different decisions. This chapter defines their responsibilities and blind spots so teams can say which evidence they have and which evidence a release needs.

The Six Activities

Model evaluation measures a property of the model as an isolated component: can it perform a task, follow an instruction, or reason over an input, judged against reference answers or a benchmark. It's what provider scorecards and public leaderboards report, and it's a reasonable input to model selection.

Its blind spot is everything outside the model. A strong benchmark score says nothing about your prompt, your tools, your state store, your authorization, or the outcome your workflow produces. Most of the failure modes from Chapter 1 live in that everything-outside, which model evaluation never touches.

Response evaluation measures a property of a produced answer: is it correct, relevant, grounded, complete, appropriately uncertain, and correctly formatted? It's useful, and Chapter 7 develops it in depth.

Its blind spot is the one established in Chapter 1: the answer is a claim about the work, not the work itself. Response evaluation is exactly the check a fluent agent passes while the execution underneath it is wrong. When teams say "we evaluate our agent" and mean only this, they've measured response correctness and left outcome correctness unmeasured.

Agent evaluation measures a property of the trajectory: did the agent make valid intermediate decisions, choose the right tool, pass plausible arguments, sequence its steps sensibly, and avoid loops? This is a real improvement over grading the final answer, because it looks at the path and not just the destination.

But it has two blind spots of its own. First, a trajectory that looks valid step by step can still miss the intended business end state, so a good path isn't a guarantee of a good outcome.

Second, agent evaluation is easy to implement badly by comparing the trajectory to a single golden path, which punishes the alternate valid paths that a competent agent will legitimately take. Chapter 8 treats trajectory evaluation carefully for this reason.

Workflow verification measures a property of the world the agent acted on: did the workflow reach the intended business end state, with the required state changes applied and prohibited side effects absent, read from an authoritative record rather than from the agent's narration? This is outcome correctness, the central verdict for state-changing workflows and the one this book is organized around.

Its blind spot is coverage. The outcome-verification rule can be deterministic even when the agent execution is not, and a deterministic verdict for one run doesn't establish that the agent will produce the same valid outcome across repeated runs, failures, or configuration changes. A correct end state on one scenario tells you the agent can be right. But it tells you nothing about whether it stays right under failure, under load, or after the next change.

System reliability testing measures a property of the whole system under realistic stress: performance, tail latency, concurrency, injected faults, resilience, backpressure, and security. It asks whether the workflow remains correct, observable, fast, and safe when dependencies are slow or failing and when many workflows run at once. This is where an agent that verifies perfectly on a quiet machine reveals that it amplifies a small upstream hiccup into a retry storm, or that it loses isolation between concurrent sessions.

Its blind spot is cost and completeness: it's expensive to run well, and no amount of it enumerates every emergent behavior a nondeterministic system can produce. It also runs before release, against a facsimile of production rather than production itself.

Production monitoring measures a property of the live system in the real world: what's actually happening now, through traces, metrics, drift signals, and incidents. It's the only activity that sees real traffic, real inputs, and real consequences, and it's indispensable for detecting the drift and the long-tail behavior that no pre-release activity can fully anticipate.

Its blind spots are structural. It's reactive, observing what already happened rather than preventing it. It's sampled and constrained by privacy, so you never see everything. It also can't replace pre-release validation, though it can gate progressive rollout stages, stop a canary, and trigger rollback when live evidence violates a release policy. Chapter 18 shows how to feed what production learns back into the earlier activities.

Why You Need All Six

The six activities form an evidence portfolio across the lifecycle. They overlap, but none covers every other's blind spots. The table above identifies the gaps a team must account for.

Depth and ownership depend on risk, architecture, and control over the model. A team consuming a fixed hosted model may concentrate on its application. A team training or fine-tuning a model will invest more in model evaluation. Both still need evidence about workflow outcomes, behavior under stress, and live operation.

Model and response evaluation alone leave execution correctness and capacity unmeasured. A harness makes agent evaluation, workflow verification, and system reliability testing repeatable, then connects them to production monitoring through feedback. It complements upstream model evaluation and downstream monitoring.

Common Mistakes

Using response evaluation as a proxy for workflow verification leaves false success undetected. Treating one green workflow run as reliability evidence leaves stress behavior unknown. Substituting dashboards for pre-release gates exposes customers to avoidable regressions. And crediting a model upgrade with system reliability without retesting the failed orchestration measures the wrong object.

Production Implications

Each activity produces evidence for a different decision, and matching evidence to decision is most of the discipline. Model evaluation informs which model to choose and whether to adopt an upgrade. Response evaluation informs prompt, model-configuration, grounding, output-contract, and content-policy changes. Agent evaluation and workflow verification inform whether a given build behaves correctly and reaches the right outcomes. System reliability testing informs capacity, resilience, and the ship or no-ship decision under realistic conditions. Production monitoring informs incident response and tells you which new scenarios your earlier activities are missing.

When someone asks whether the agent is "evaluated," the useful answer names which of these six they mean, and which of the six the decision at hand actually requires.

Chapter 3. The Five Evaluation Levels: Response, Step, Action, Workflow, System

Two Taxonomies, Two Questions

Chapters 2 and 3 describe two different axes. The six activities describe the lifecycle purpose for which evidence is collected. The five levels describe the object inside an agentic execution that the evidence evaluates. The relationship is many-to-many, not one-to-one.

The distinction is important, because the two are easy to conflate.

  • The six activities are about when and why evidence is gathered: at model selection, in pre-release testing, in verifying a workflow, in monitoring production, each to inform a particular decision.

  • The five levels are about what part of one execution a piece of evidence speaks to: its response, its steps, its actions, its outcome, or the system around it.

A single activity usually gathers evidence at several levels, and a single level is usually examined by several activities. The two frameworks shouldn't be merged.

The cross-reference below shows which levels each activity commonly examines. Read it as a rough map of common practice, not a rule.

"Supporting" means that an activity can provide evidence relevant to the level. It doesn't mean that the activity can independently establish the level's verdict. For example, a model benchmark can test whether a model proposes plausible tool calls, but it can't verify an action that was never executed.

Two features of this map matter. The Response column draws evidence from four different activities, which is why "we evaluate responses" is ambiguous until you say which activity you mean. And the map shows why early component and response checks leave important gaps: they produce little or no direct evidence about authoritative workflow state or behavior under operational conditions. The rest of this chapter is about the columns, not the rows.

Where the Five Levels Come From

The levels aren't an arbitrary list. They fall out of the structure of an agentic execution.

A workflow begins with a request and ends with a response. Between them, the agent takes a sequence of steps. Some steps take an action against the outside world through a tool. The actions move the world toward, or away from, an intended business end state. And the whole thing runs inside a system with finite time, capacity, and trust.

Each of those structural features is a place where the execution can be correct or incorrect independently of the others, and each place is a level.

The response level asks whether the final response was correct, relevant, grounded, complete, and appropriately uncertain. Its object is the text the agent produced. Chapter 7 develops it.

The step level asks whether the agent made valid intermediate decisions and transitions: whether each step followed validly from the available observations and moved the workflow forward rather than in a circle. Its object is the trajectory of decisions. Chapters 8 and 10 develop it.

The action level asks whether each action selected the correct tool, supplied valid arguments, operated under the correct authority, and controlled its side effects. Its object is the individual tool invocation and its consequences. Chapters 8, 13, and 14 develop it.

The workflow level asks whether the workflow reached the intended business end state, with the required state changes applied and the completion conditions met. Its object is the authoritative record of the world, read directly rather than from the agent's account.

This is outcome correctness and the central verdict for the state-changing reference workflow. It doesn't override failures at the response, action, or system levels. Chapter 9 develops it.

The system level asks whether the workflow remained reliable, observable, secure, fast, scalable, and cost-efficient. Its object is the operational envelope: latency, concurrency, resilience under failure, security posture, and cost per successful outcome. Chapters 15 through 18 develop it.

One Request, Five Verdicts

The reason to separate these levels is that a single run earns different verdicts at each, and a verdict at one level doesn't predict the verdict at another.

Return to the two runs from Chapter 1, both handling the same request under the same injected timeout on the incident check. One agent stops safely when the check fails. The other ignores the failure, opens a ticket, and reports success.

LevelFaithful runFalse-success run
ResponsePass: it accurately states that confirmation failed and no ticket was opened.Fail: it passes superficial form and relevance checks but fails groundedness and uncertainty calibration.
StepPass: each transition is supported by the preceding observation.Fail: it treats a failed dependency as successful and continues.
ActionPass: it takes no action unsupported by evidence.Fail: it creates a ticket based on an unverified incident.
WorkflowPass: the correct end state after failed verification is no ticket.Fail: the state contains a ticket asserting an unverified incident.
SystemContributes positive resilience evidence: this run stopped safely under the injected fault.Contributes negative resilience evidence: this run produced false success under the injected fault.

The false-success run is the important column. A superficial response check passes it because the message is fluent, relevant, and specific. A complete response-level evaluation fails it on groundedness, while the step, action, workflow, and fault-response checks explain exactly how the execution broke.

This distinction matters: the reliability gap isn't a weakness of rigorous response evaluation. It appears when surface answer quality is allowed to substitute for execution evidence. A gate that looks only at a superficial response check ships this run. A gate that verifies the workflow level catches it.

Response, step, action, and workflow verdicts can be assigned to an individual execution. A system-level verdict usually requires evidence aggregated across repeated scenarios, fault classes, concurrency levels, and workload profiles. A single run contributes evidence to that verdict. It doesn't establish it alone. This is why the table records the system row as contributing positive or negative resilience evidence rather than as a pass or fail.

Response correctness and workflow correctness can genuinely diverge in the other direction too. Consider a different run in which the agent issues an unauthorized credit and accurately reports, "A $50 credit was applied." The response can be factually correct and grounded in the resulting state while the action and workflow verdicts fail because the side effect was unauthorized and prohibited. This is a true response-pass, action-fail case.

The levels aren't a strict ladder in which passing one level guarantees another. They're distinct evaluation targets, and their verdicts must be recorded separately.

A run can reach the correct business end state through an action it had no authority to take: the outcome looks right at the workflow level while the action level is a failure, because the world arrived at the right place by an illegitimate route.

This isn't a curiosity. It's the reason the action level exists as its own check and isn't folded into the workflow level. It's also the failure that Chapter 14 on security is built to catch. Outcome correctness is central, but no successful verdict at one level compensates for a blocking failure at another.

How the Harness Maps to the Levels

Each level maps to evaluators or measurements in the reference harness, producing distinct verdicts for diagnosis and gating.

The response evaluator applies deterministic checks and, when enabled, advisory rubric evaluation. The trajectory evaluator examines observable decisions and transitions at the step level. At the action level, tool-call validation, authorization records, approval decisions, guardrail results, and recorded side effects are evaluated together. The outcome verifier judges the workflow level from immutable authoritative-state snapshots. Aggregated metrics, fault campaigns, security tests, telemetry checks, and workload experiments supply the system-level verdict.

When Chapter 18 assembles release gates, each gate draws on the level appropriate to the risk it controls: an unauthorized-action gate reads action-level evidence, an outcome-success gate reads workflow-level evidence, and a tail-latency gate reads system-level evidence. Guardrail gates may span the response, step, and action levels depending on where the control is applied. The five levels are, in that sense, the organizing principle of both the evaluation and the release decision.

Common Mistakes

Collapsing five levels into one score hides the failing level. Treating them as a hierarchy lets a correct end state excuse unauthorized actions. Deferring system testing until production leaves concurrency, resilience, and cost unknown at release. Keep each verdict visible and test the operational envelope before deployment.

Production Implications

Report strengths and weaknesses by level: a build may pass response and workflow checks while failing under load. This tells reviewers which evidence is missing before sign-off. When production incidents become regression cases in Chapter 18, their failing levels identify the evaluator or gate that needs coverage.
