The exit criteria make each claim checkable.

Level 1 is reached when there's at least one state-based golden outcome and one negative outcome, and no success is inferred from response text alone.

Level 2 is reached when every state-changing tool is routed through an enforced gateway, identity is obtained outside the model's context, authorization and approval decisions are recorded, and the bypass architecture test passes.

Level 3 is reached when the consequential failure classes have scenarios, the evaluators' own positive and negative controls pass, and loop, fault, state, and guardrail evidence is complete.

Level 4 is reached when the required CI gate is enabled, seeded mutants are rejected, live rates meet confidence-aware gates, representative capacity objectives are met, and exceptions are owned and expiring.

Level 5 is reached when the shadow and canary process is operational, rollout has pass, fail, and inconclusive handling, drift monitoring is active, production failures are clustered and reviewed, and rollback, reconciliation, and incident procedures have been tested.

A team that has written a loop detector but never proven it fires hasn't reached Level 3. A team with a gate that has never blocked a seeded regression hasn't reached Level 4.

Maturity isn't Deployment Authorization

A level is a defensible improvement over the one below it, but reaching a level isn't permission to ship. The minimum acceptable level depends on the workflow's consequences, reversibility, exposure, and threat model, and Level 0 is never acceptable for production while Level 1 may be unacceptable for anything that moves money or acts on the outside world.

Workflow riskMinimum evidence before production
Text-only, low consequenceResponse evaluation, monitoring, bounded live testing
Read-only enterprise assistantGrounding, isolation, live evaluation, observability
State-changing workflowOutcome verification, external enforcement, resilience, gated release
Financial or irreversible actionApproval, security testing, live statistics, capacity, progressive rollout, human oversight

Maturity is also assessed per workflow or consequential capability, not per organization, because a platform is rarely at one level across everything. When the dimensions differ, report the profile rather than averaging it into one flattering number, and for a production decision, the weakest required dimension governs.

A platform whose ticket creation is Outcome 5, Security 4, Resilience 4, Performance 4 while its credit issuance is Outcome 3, Security 2, Resilience 2, Performance 1 is not a Level 5 platform. It's a mature ticketing capability sitting next to an immature and far more dangerous one. Calling the whole thing Level 5 because of the safe workflow is exactly the self-flattery this model exists to prevent.

Step 0: Define the Workflow and Risk Contract

Before the first scenario, define what matters, because a scenario written without it may encode the wrong definition of success. This is the oracle limitation from Chapter 19.

The contract documents the business objective, the authoritative state, the allowed and prohibited effects, the identity and tenant boundaries, which actions are reversible and which are not, the approval requirements, the expected failure behavior, the threat model, the latency, capacity, and cost objectives, and the human owner and escalation path.

This is a page of writing, not a project, and it's the difference between a suite that verifies the right thing and one that consistently enforces a mistake.

Build State-Based Outcome Verification

With the contract in hand, write one golden scenario and make its success a predicate over authoritative state. Don't read the final message to decide whether it passed. Read the ticket, the credit, and the record. This single step reorients the whole effort around state rather than story, and on many real systems it immediately catches a false success the demo hid.

Add a negative scenario the agent must refuse and an alternate that shouldn't be flagged, so a pass isn't a tautology and legitimate variation survives. That is Level 1.

Establish External Enforcement

Put enforcement where the agent can't reach it. Route every action through a gateway the agent can't bypass, obtain identity from a trusted context rather than from model output, decide authorization outside the agent and fail closed, require a trusted approval for sensitive actions, and prove with an architecture test that the agent holds no direct path to a tool.

Record the authorization and commit decisions, so a control can be shown to have been exercised rather than merely present. That's Level 2, and it's the level that removes the largest remaining source of false confidence after outcome verification.

Add Behavioral and Resilience Evaluation

Now judge the path, not just the endpoint, in the order your consequential risks demand rather than in chapter order. A money-moving agent adds guardrails and fault injection first, because a committed prohibited credit or a false success under a fault is its worst day. A read-heavy assistant adds trajectory evidence and grounding first, because acting on a read that never succeeded is its worst day.

Add loop detection where runaway cost or non-termination is a real risk, and state verification where stale or poisoned context could drive a decision. Give the evaluators their own positive and negative controls, because an evaluator that has never been shown a real defect is unproven. That's Level 3.

Validate Observability, Performance, and Capacity

Two foundations underpin the gate.

First, observability: emit the trace and assemble the execution record from independent evidence paths, so the same instrumentation that debugs the agent produces the evidence the harness verifies, and a missing span is a caught telemetry gap rather than a hidden action.

Second, performance and capacity, which a functionally correct single-user system hasn't yet earned. Build a representative workflow mix, and measure model, gateway, tool, queue, and commit latency separately. Compute amplification per dependency, test both open and closed workloads, and run stress, spike, endurance, and fault-under-load tests. Locate the saturation knee, verify that outcome, safety, and isolation hold under load, establish cost per successful outcome, and define a sustainable capacity with headroom.

A system that's correct only at one user isn't production-ready, and this step is where that gap is closed.

Gate Merge, Promotion, and Rollout

Wire a calibrated gate into CI and prove it fails: confirm the baseline passes and a seeded regression fails, then make the job a required status check so a failing gate blocks a merge rather than merely printing red. Turn on live mode for the questions a scripted model can't answer, and treat its numbers statistically, rates with intervals, safety targets as zero observed plus a rule-of-three bound, comparisons as paired repeated runs against a practical margin.

That combination (a required deterministic gate plus confidence-aware live and performance evidence) is Level 4, and it's the target before broad production exposure of a consequential workflow. Then gate the rollout itself, with hysteresis and a safe rollback path, remembering that rollback limits new harm but doesn't reverse effects already committed.

Close the Production Feedback Loop

The loop is what makes the method adaptive. Monitor production with the same metric contracts where the evidence exists, separating immediate online signals from delayed authoritative outcomes, and watch for drift across inputs, behavior, outcomes, dependencies, and cost. When a real failure occurs, relevant incidents are sanitized, clustered, minimized, and converted into versioned regression cases where reliable reproduction and a valid expected outcome are possible.

Not every incident becomes a test: some can't be reproduced, some lack enough evidence, some duplicate an existing failure family, some lose critical detail through redaction, some become obsolete after an architecture change, and some call for a monitoring or operational control rather than another scenario.

What the loop guarantees isn't that every failure is captured forever, but that the ones that can be are turned into durable coverage. That's Level 5.

Adoption Anti-Patterns

The failures of adoption are as predictable as the failures of agents. Boiling the ocean (building everything before shipping any control) produces a long project and no protection.

Gating on the response reintroduces false success. A gate never shown to fail is trusted on faith. Copying a threshold profile without calibration ships a policy nobody chose. Turning on live mode before the offline structure is stable means debugging model variance and structural bugs at once. Keeping one golden scenario forever leaves no failure coverage and no false-positive guard. Building the harness but leaving it advisory guarantees it's skipped under deadline pressure. And declaring a platform-wide maturity level because one low-risk workflow reached it hides the dangerous workflow that didn't.

Required Production-Readiness Artifacts

A mature program is legible, and the artifacts below are what a reviewer, auditor, or future maintainer should be able to find. They turn "we tested it" into a defensible record.

ArtifactPurpose
Workflow contractDefines success, prohibited effects, and ownership
Threat modelDefines adversaries and trust boundaries
Scenario catalogDefines covered behavior
Dataset manifestPins test data and provenance
Execution-record schemaDefines observable evidence
Evaluator registryLists evaluators and versions
Authorization policyDefines permitted actions
Workload modelDefines representative demand
Performance baselineDefines latency, capacity, amplification, and cost
Gate profileDefines ship or no-ship policy
Evidence scorecardRecords achieved results and uncertainty
Exception registerRecords temporary accepted risks
Rollout and rollback planControls production exposure
Incident-to-test registerTracks production feedback

What Good Looks Like

A mature program has a specific shape. Every identified consequential failure class has representative positive, negative, boundary, and recovery coverage appropriate to its risk. The release gate is a required check, calibrated, versioned, and proven to fail against a seeded regression, with no unresolved blocking or inconclusive gates.

Safety-critical rates are reported as zero observed with a confidence bound sized to the assurance they need, and live evidence is within its validity window. There's representative capacity headroom and security-control exercise coverage, and irreversible effects have tested reconciliation.

Production failures are reviewed, clustered, and converted into versioned regression cases or operational controls when doing so adds durable coverage. Scenarios, policies, and exceptions have current owners.

And running through all of it is the honesty of Chapter 19: the team treats the harness as a foundational control that raises the floor, not as a proof of safety, and pairs it with the security review, monitoring, staged delivery, and human accountability it can't replace.

The Argument, Restated

The reference demonstrates how to verify execution and business outcomes, enforce permissions, and gate releases in a small CI-ready system. Its deterministic results remain scoped to the encoded fixtures and assertions. The maturity model turns that method into a staged, per-workflow adoption path. Maturity alone doesn't authorize deployment.

The goal is maintained evidence that covered workflows reach intended outcomes through permitted actions within a defined reliability envelope.

Chapter 20 Checklist:

  • You can place a workflow on the five-level model by its exit criteria, not by whether a component exists.

  • You can read a maturity dimension row and name the highest-priority next step.

  • You can explain why maturity is per workflow and isn't deployment authorization.

  • You can write a Step 0 workflow and risk contract and say why it precedes the first scenario.

  • You can order the behavioral evaluators and the performance work by a system's consequential risks.

  • You can name the production-readiness artifacts a reviewer should find.

  • You can state what good looks like and the honest posture that runs through it.

Key Takeaway

Adopt controls by risk and assess maturity per workflow against evidence-based exit criteria. Begin with a workflow contract and state verification, then add external enforcement, behavioral tests, observability, capacity evidence, and required release gates. Maintain coverage through production feedback. The weakest required dimension governs the decision. Maturity alone isn't deployment authorization.

Conclusion

What the Book Argued

The handbook turns a reliability question into an engineering method: did the workflow reach the intended business outcome through permitted actions?

The method separates the agent from its evaluators, records independent execution evidence, verifies outcomes, and checks responses, trajectories, guardrails, state, and fault handling. Observability supports diagnosis and evidence reconciliation, statistics quantify live uncertainty, and release gates apply the resulting policy on each change.

What the Reference Proved, and What it Didn't

The small support agent, scripted model, and virtual clock demonstrate implemented checks reproducibly: gateway authorization, idempotent effects, evidence ordering, prohibited-action detection, faithful fault handling, and rejection of seeded regressions. A failing CI job blocks merging only when configured as a required check.

These results describe the tested fixtures and controls. They don't establish live-model behavior, unseen-scenario reliability, or security beyond the declared threat model.

Production extensions, including richer authorization, memory at scale, representative capacity testing, and tamper-evident auditing, are distinguished from shipped capabilities in Chapter 19.

The Real Goal

The goal is a reproducible, gated, continuously maintained body of evidence that covered workflows reach their intended outcomes through permitted actions within a defined reliability envelope.

Begin with one consequential workflow, define its acceptance conditions, and prove the harness detects a known defect. Add controls in the order its risks demand. Maintain the evidence as the model, prompts, tools, policies, and production conditions change.

Glossary

I've defined terms here as the handbook uses them. Where a term has a broader meaning elsewhere, the definition here is the one intended in this book.

Acceptable outcomes: The set of end states a scenario will accept. A scenario passes if any one alternative is fully satisfied, so an ambiguous request can have more than one correct end state. See Chapter 9.

Action journal: The append-only record of every state-changing attempt, committed or rejected, with its tool, idempotency key, principal, authorization and approval references, and before and after state hashes. It answers "what ever committed," as distinct from the snapshot's "what is true now." See Chapters 5, 9, and 15.

Amplification: The fan-out of one workflow into downstream work, reported as a vector of ratios per dependency (model-call, tool-call, retry). It measures demand, not directly cost. See Chapters 10 and 16.

Approval: A trusted, out-of-band grant that a specific sensitive action instance is sanctioned, bound to an authenticated approver, an action digest, a scope, and an expiry. The agent may request one but can never create or interpret its own as approval. See Chapters 6 and 14.

Authoritative state: The business state that's the source of outcome truth: accounts, incidents, tickets, and credits. Verdicts about outcomes are read from it, never from the agent's account of what it did. See Chapters 5 and 9.

Confidence interval: The reported uncertainty around a live rate. Proportions use a Wilson interval, which behaves well near zero and one and for small samples. See Chapter 17.

Control plane: The test rig that observes and judges: scenario loader, evaluators, immutable evidence store, metrics, reports, and gates. It's trusted, so it is part of the trusted computing base. See Chapters 4 and 19.

Effectively-once: The property that a workflow produces a single committed business effect within a tool's documented idempotency boundary, even under a retry. It's not universal exactly-once execution, which distributed systems rarely provide. See Chapters 5, 9, and 13.

Evaluation activity (the six): The six activities are model evaluation, response evaluation, agent evaluation, workflow verification, system reliability testing, and production monitoring. See Chapter 2.

Evaluation level (the five): The five levels at which behavior is judged: response, step, action, workflow, and system. Distinct from the six activities. Together they form a two-axis view. See Chapter 3.

Evidence requirement: A trajectory expectation that a successful, matching read of the state preceded the action that depended on it, judged by event sequence so a retry can't fool it. A timed-out or mismatched read isn't evidence. See Chapter 8.

Execution record: The assembled, control-plane artifact the evaluators read, built from independent sources (runner events, gateway outcomes, authorization decisions, the action journal, state snapshots). The OpenTelemetry trace is a view of it, not its source. See Chapter 15.

Fail closed: A control that can't produce a trustworthy decision denies the action rather than allowing it. An unavailable decision point blocks, it never passes by default. See Chapters 11, 13, and 14.

False success: A fluent, confident final response that accompanies a wrong or missing business outcome. The central failure the method exists to catch, by reading state rather than the response. See Chapters 1, 7, and 9.

Faithful failure: A run that can't complete but reports so honestly, changing nothing it shouldn't and claiming nothing it didn't do. Acceptable under a fault, unlike a false success. See Chapter 13.

Gate decision (three-state): A release gate returns pass, fail, or inconclusive: a measured blocking failure is fail, a blocking gate with missing or insufficient evidence is inconclusive, and both block a release while only fail claims a regression. See Chapter 18.

Gateway: The single enforcement path from an agent's requested action to tool execution, the policy enforcement point. It validates arguments, authorizes, requires approval for sensitive actions, and only then executes. See Chapters 4 and 14.

Guardrail. A safety control along the path from input to committed effect. The guardrail evaluator verifies safety held (pass), a bypass occurred (fail), or the control had no opportunity (not_exercised). See Chapter 11.

Identity: The trusted, request-scoped execution context bound to the gateway, carrying the caller and granted authority. It's never supplied or expanded by the agent. See Chapter 14.

Idempotency key: A stable key required on every write, by which the store enforces uniqueness per tool and key so a retry doesn't create a duplicate effect. See Chapters 5 and 13.

Indeterminate: An outcome or control result that couldn't be established because the authoritative state or the control's decision was unavailable. Never treated as a silent pass. See Chapters 9, 14, and 17.

Invariant: A must-never condition checked after each observable transition. It detects a violation immediately and stops further actions. It doesn't unwind an effect that already committed. See Chapters 4 and 9.

Maturity level (the five): The five levels of adoption above a demo-only baseline: outcome-aware, controlled, evaluated, evidence-gated, and production-adaptive, reached by meeting exit criteria and assessed per workflow. See Chapter 20.

Mode A, B, C: The execution modes: A is deterministic and offline (scripted model, virtual clock), B is a controlled live model, and C is a representative system under load. A number from one mode is never reported as if from another. See Chapters 5 and 16.

not_evaluated: A metric with no eligible denominator or that wasn't scheduled. Reported as such, never as a passing zero. See Chapter 17.

not_exercised: A control that had no relevant safety opportunity in a run. Distinct from a pass: the control didn't fail, but it was never tested. See Chapter 11.

PDP and PEP: The policy decision point that decides whether an action is authorized, and the policy enforcement point (the gateway) that enforces the decision. See Chapter 14.

Progress: A verified change toward at least one acceptable outcome, measured from authoritative state and newly satisfied evidence, not from activity, novelty, or mutation. The discriminator for non-progress detection. See Chapter 10.

Provenance and trust level: The origin and trustworthiness of a memory entry (authoritative_fact, user_statement, retrieved_content, model_inference, summary, security_decision). A non-authoritative entry can never be silently promoted to fact. See Chapter 12.

Redaction seam: The point at which sensitive fields are removed before anything is persisted to the record or a span, applied recursively by policy, with the correlation digest computed over the redacted values. See Chapter 15.

Rule of three: The result that zero events in n independent trials bounds the true rate at about three over n with 95% confidence. It bounds only the tested distribution, never an unexercised class. See Chapter 17.

Scenario: A single typed record, grouped by visibility class, that configures a world (stimulus, runtime, trusted environment) and states the correct handling (expectations) without leaking the answer to the agent. See Chapter 6.

Seeded regression: A deliberately introduced failure used to prove the gate can fail, the negative control for the gate itself. A gate never shown to fail is untested. See Chapter 18.

Self-terminated: Whether the system under evaluation stopped itself on its own budgets, or whether the independent harness watchdog had to fire. A watchdog firing is always a failure. See Chapters 4 and 8.

State snapshot: A frozen, sequenced, content-hashed value object of the outcome-relevant state at a point in the run. Immutable evidence the evaluators read. The hash is an integrity checksum, not tamper-evidence. See Chapters 4 and 12.

System under evaluation (SUE): What you would deploy: the agent runtime, the model interface, the tool clients, the gateway, the authorization enforcement, and the production runtime limits. Distinct from the controlled test environment and the control plane. See Chapter 4.

Trace-to-test: The controlled process that turns a production failure into a versioned regression case: sanitize, cluster, minimize, define the expected outcome, and add it with provenance. See Chapters 6 and 18.

Trajectory: The observable path of decisions and actions, judged at the step and action levels against a set of valid paths rather than one golden sequence. See Chapter 8.

Watchdog: The independent outer guard whose deadline is strictly beyond the SUE's own limits. It exists only to stop a SUE that failed to stop itself, and its firing is recorded as a failure. See Chapters 4 and 10.

References

The book cites external sources for claims that rest on published standards or research rather than on the reference implementation. They're listed by the chapter that uses them.

Each title links to the publisher's canonical location. The OpenTelemetry GenAI status was verified against the OpenTelemetry documentation and repository as of September 2026. The others are stable published works.

Evaluation and Model-as-Judge (Chapter 7)

  • Zheng, L., Chiang, W.-L., Sheng, Y., et al. "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) Datasets and Benchmarks Track, 2023. Documents position bias, verbosity bias, and self-enhancement bias in LLM judges, and the value of human-labeled calibration.

Safety, Security Policy, and Risk (Chapters 11 and 12)

  • OWASP. "OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications." Open Worldwide Application Security Project. See the entries for Prompt Injection and Excessive Agency. Cited for the distinction between untrusted-instruction influence and excessive permission or autonomy, and for treating memory and context poisoning as an attack surface requiring integrity and provenance controls.

  • National Institute of Standards and Technology. "Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile." NIST AI 600-1, July 2024. Cited for the position that generative-AI controls must be measured across the lifecycle and supported by governance and monitoring rather than reduced to prompt wording.

Resilience and Idempotency (Chapters 13 and 16)

  • Stripe. "Idempotent requests." Stripe API documentation. Cited for the real-world conditions under which a retry with the same idempotency key avoids duplicate effects: key retention, parameter matching, and where the result is stored.

  • Brooker, M. "Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter." Amazon Builders' Library, Amazon Web Services. Cited for bounded retries, exponential backoff, and jitter as the difference between recovery and outage amplification.

  • Grafana Labs. "Open and closed models." k6 documentation. Cited for the distinction between open and closed workload models and the coordinated-omission failure mode of throttled load generation.

Security and Authorization (Chapter 14)

  • National Institute of Standards and Technology. "Zero Trust Architecture." NIST Special Publication 800-207, August 2020. Cited for authorization around users, assets, and resources rather than implicit trust based on location or ownership.

  • Jones, M., Nadalin, A., Campbell, B., et al. "OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange." RFC 8693, IETF, January 2020. Cited for the formal distinction between delegation and impersonation and for representing both the subject and the acting party, which fits the subject-actor model used to prevent the confused deputy.

Observability Standards (Chapter 15)

OpenTelemetry. "Semantic Conventions for Generative AI." OpenTelemetry GenAI Semantic Conventions repository and opentelemetry.io. As verified in September 2026: the GenAI, provider-specific, and MCP conventions were moved into a dedicated repository in June 2026 to version independently, and remain in Development status with no official release, under active development by the GenAI Special Interest Group formed in 2024. Cited for the recommendation to pin the semantic-convention version and treat the conventions as evolving rather than settled.

Statistics (Chapter 17)

  • National Institute of Standards and Technology. "Confidence Intervals for a Proportion." NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods. Cited for the established methods of computing a binomial confidence interval, including the Wilson score interval.

  • Hanley, J. A., and Lippman-Hand, A. "If Nothing Goes Wrong, Is Everything All Right? Interpreting Zero Numerators." Journal of the American Medical Association, 1983;249(13):1743-1745. The origin of the rule of three: with zero events observed in n trials, the upper bound on the true rate is approximately three over n.

Release, CI/CD, and Progressive Delivery (Chapter 18)

  • GitHub. "About protected branches" and "About status checks." GitHub Documentation. Cited for required status checks as the mechanism that turns a failing CI job into a merge block.

  • Argo Project. "Analysis" and progressive-delivery documentation. Argo Rollouts. Cited for distinguishing successful, failed, and inconclusive analysis and for consecutive-success and failure-limit handling in a rollout controller.

Production-Readiness Checklist

This checklist turns the method into a sign-off gate for one consequential, state-changing workflow. It's organized so the items map to the chapters that justify them and to the limitations in Chapter 19 that each item is meant to counter.

Assess it per workflow, not per platform, and let the weakest required item govern the decision. Items marked with a risk tier apply above that tier. A text-only low-consequence assistant doesn't need the capacity or approval items, while a financial or irreversible action needs all of them.

Every box is a claim you must be able to defend with an artifact, not a feeling that it's probably fine.

Contract and Specification (Chapters 6 and 19)

  • A written workflow contract exists: business objective, authoritative state, allowed and prohibited effects, identity and tenant boundaries, reversible versus irreversible actions, approval requirements, expected failure behavior, latency, capacity, and cost objectives, and a named human owner.

  • A written threat model exists: adversaries, trust boundaries, and what is and isn't in scope.

  • Expected outcomes, invariants, authorization policies, and gate thresholds have had domain-owner review. Safety-critical scenarios have had two-person review. (Counters the oracle limitation: the harness can't validate its own answer key.)

  • Expectations, policies, and thresholds are versioned and under change control.

Outcome Verification (Chapters 5, 9)

  • Success is a predicate over authoritative state, not the final message.

  • Acceptable outcomes are declared for every state-changing scenario; a scenario with none is rejected at load.

  • The count assertion is scoped to the logical operation by a stable business key, not a broad filter.

  • The outcome verifier has been shown to fail on a missing, duplicate, wrong-reference, wrong-tenant, and committed-prohibited-effect mutation.

  • The consistency point at which state is read is defined. An unreadable state returns indeterminate, not a pass.

External Enforcement (Chapters 4 and 14)

  • Every state-changing tool is reached only through the gateway. An architecture test proves the agent imports no tool implementation.

  • Identity is obtained from a trusted context bound to the gateway, never from model output, tool arguments, or conversation text.

  • Authorization is decided outside the agent and fails closed. An unavailable decision point blocks and is recorded as indeterminate, not denied-as-normal.

  • Sensitive actions require a trusted approval bound to approver, action digest, scope, and expiry. The agent can't manufacture one, and approval is subordinate to authorization.

  • Authorization and approval decisions are recorded, so a control can be shown to have been exercised.

  • (Multi-tenant) Tenant isolation holds at the identity, policy, argument, state, memory, result, response, and audit boundaries.

Behavioral and Resilience Evaluation (Chapters 8, 10, 11, 12, and 13)

  • Trajectory evidence requirements verify a successful, matching read preceded each dependent action, by event sequence.

  • The consequential failure classes have positive, negative, boundary, and recovery scenarios appropriate to their risk.

  • Loop and non-progress detection is present where runaway cost or non-termination is a risk, and legitimate fan-out isn't flagged.

  • Guardrail evaluation distinguishes pass (control held), fail (bypass), and not_exercised, and has been shown to catch a real bypass.

  • Writes are idempotent. The after-commit case has been tested and produces an effectively-once outcome, not a duplicate.

  • A fault produces recovery or faithful failure, never a false success. The false-success-under-fault rate is zero observed.

  • (Persistent memory) Memory reads are validated for freshness, provenance, and isolation, and a non-authoritative entry can't become authority.

Observability and Evidence (Chapter 15)

  • The execution record is assembled from independent evidence paths. A missing span is a caught telemetry gap, not an evidence blackout.

  • Traces, logs, metrics, records, and journals are kept distinct, with correct authority for each.

  • Secrets and personal data are redacted at the source and again at the collector. A seeded-secret test proves the redaction works.

  • Span attributes carry bounded grouping dimensions. Per-request digests and identifiers live in the record, not as indexed dimensions.

  • The semantic-convention version the telemetry targets is pinned, with compatibility mappings in one place.

  • Audit evidence for consequential actions is retained regardless of trace sampling.

Performance and Capacity (Chapter 16. Tier: State-Changing and Above)

  • A representative workload mix is defined: scenario weights, read/write ratio, tenant and account cardinality, fault and approval frequency, context sizes.

  • Latency is decomposed by layer (model, gateway, tool, queue, commit), and reported by mode, with a monotonic-clock harness-overhead benchmark kept separate from virtual-time logic.

  • Amplification is measured per dependency. Retry amplification is physical attempts over logical operations.

  • The workload model is explicit (open or closed) with offered, admitted, and completed accounting, so overload isn't hidden by coordinated omission.

  • Stress, spike, endurance, and fault-under-load tests locate the saturation knee.

  • Outcome success, safety, and isolation hold under load. The reliability knee is identified.

  • Cost per successful outcome is measured, with the numerator including failed and retried workflows, against a versioned price model.

  • Sustainable capacity is defined with headroom.

Statistics (Chapter 17. Tier: Live-Mode Measurement)

  • Live rates are reported with confidence intervals and a sample count, never as bare point estimates.

  • A safety target of zero is reported with its rule-of-three bound, and the sample is sized to the assurance required.

  • Rates are sliced by predefined risk classes with per-slice denominators and intervals, not averaged.

  • The unit of analysis is stated. Repeated trials within a scenario are treated as clustered, not independent.

  • Configuration comparisons use paired, randomized runs against a practical non-inferiority margin.

  • A model judge, if used, is calibrated against human labels and never owns the release decision.

Release Gate and CI/CD (Chapter 18)

  • The gate returns pass, fail, or inconclusive. Not-evaluated or absent blocking metric blocks by default.

  • A safety gate requires zero observed failures, a bound under target, and the adversarial slices actually exercised, not merely one attempt.

  • The gate profile is calibrated, versioned, and marked as such. Baselines record their configuration and expire.

  • The gate has been proven to fail against a seeded regression.

  • The gate runs in CI on every change and is configured as a required status check. The harness self-tests are kept separate from the release suite.

  • Exceptions are owned, expiring, visible on the scorecard, and don't rewrite the metric. Safety bypasses require elevated approval.

  • The scorecard artifact records the decision, versions, metric values and statuses, intervals, evidence achieved, baseline, exceptions, and links to sanitized evidence.

Rollout and Production Feedback (Chapters 15 and 18)

  • Pre-merge, pre-release, and rollout are gated as distinct decisions.

  • Production monitoring uses the same metric contracts where evidence exists, separating online proxies from delayed authoritative outcomes.

  • Rollout gating has hysteresis (minimum canary exposure, consecutive passing windows, a failure limit, an inconclusive timeout) and a safe halt-or-rollback path.

  • Irreversible effects have a tested reconciliation, compensation, and incident procedure. Rollback is understood not to reverse committed effects.

  • Drift is monitored across inputs, behavior, outcomes, dependencies, and cost.

  • Production failures are reviewed, clustered, minimized, and converted into versioned regression cases or operational controls where reproduction and a valid outcome are possible.

Trusted Computing Base and Governance (Chapter 19)

  • The control plane is code-reviewed and owned. Gate-profile files and baselines are protected and their changes audited.

  • CI dependencies and actions are pinned. Artifacts are integrity-protected. Exceptions have separation of duties.

  • Scenarios, policies, and exceptions have current owners and review dates.

  • The team treats the harness as a foundational control that raises the floor, not as a proof of safety, and pairs it with security review, monitoring, staged delivery, and human accountability.

Sign-Off

  • The workflow is at the maturity level its risk tier requires, assessed per workflow, with the weakest required dimension recorded.

  • No unresolved blocking or inconclusive gates. All live evidence is within its validity window.

  • A named owner has reviewed the evidence scorecard and accepts the residual risk described in the limitations.

entries.title: The Anatomy of an AI Data Center
entries.summary: Artificial intelligence models like GPT-4 and Claude require massive, highly complex physical infrastructure. We just published a new full-length course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that ta
entries.content:
Artificial intelligence models like GPT-4 and Claude require massive, highly complex physical infrastructure. We just published a new full-length course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel that takes you deep inside the data centers powering the AI revolution.

This course traces the entire journey of electricity from the utility grid all the way down to the individual GPUs executing matrix multiplications.

The course breaks down the complete anatomy of an AI factory, teaching you:

  • How high-voltage power distribution networks and backup systems route reliable electricity to server racks.

  • The mechanics of advanced liquid cooling and global heat rejection systems required to keep massive GPU clusters from overheating.

  • The complex optical networking and interconnects needed for thousands of chips to communicate during training and inference.

  • The engineering, procurement, and physical construction processes for these multi-gigawatt mega-facilities.

  • The real-world economics behind GPU cloud hosting, capacity contracts, and infrastructure investments.

Head over to the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel to watch the full course today (8-hour watch).

entries.title: Learn How to Design Software Systems Like a Senior Engineer in Our New Course
entries.summary: System design is one of the most important skills for software engineers today. Whether you're applying for senior or staff-level positions or just looking to level up your architectural knowledge, un
entries.content:
System design is one of the most important skills for software engineers today. Whether you're applying for senior or staff-level positions or just looking to level up your architectural knowledge, understanding how to design systems at scale is a deciding factor for top tech companies.

To help you master these concepts and pass your interviews, we just published a comprehensive, 3-hour course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel: Design Software Systems Like a Senior Engineer.

This complete course provides a practical, five-step framework for structuring your thinking, asking the right clarifying questions, and tackling vague requirements under pressure.

This course grounds your learning in real-world production system examples that show up most often in interviews. You will learn how to apply the framework to build high-level architectures for massive platforms, including:

  • Spotify

  • Booking.com

  • WhatsApp

You'll also learn the five dimensions you are actually evaluated on during system design interviews. You'll learn how to start with a simple architecture and naturally build upon it by identifying bottlenecks, managing your time, calculating storage and traffic estimates, and deeply discussing the trade-offs of different technical decisions (like choosing WebSockets over HTTP or adding load balancers).

Watch the full course now on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (3-hour watch).

entries.title: How to Build Ephemeral PR Preview Environments on GKE with GitHub Actions, Ingress, and Automatic TLS
entries.summary: Every team that ships software eventually builds a staging environment. And every team that builds a staging environment eventually discovers the same problem. Staging is shared. One environment, many
entries.content:
Every team that ships software eventually builds a staging environment. And every team that builds a staging environment eventually discovers the same problem.

Staging is shared. One environment, many pull requests. Someone deploys a half-finished feature to test it. Someone else deploys on top of that. A third person runs a database migration. By Thursday afternoon, nobody can tell which version of which branch is actually running, and the sentence "it works on staging" has stopped carrying any information at all.

The workarounds are familiar: a Slack channel where people claim staging like a meeting room, a rotating deploy schedule, or a second staging environment, then a third, each one drifting further from production configuration than the last.

There's a better pattern, and platform teams at companies like Vercel, Netlify, and Shopify have made it standard: give every pull request its own environment.

Open a PR, and a fresh, isolated copy of your application deploys automatically. Push another commit, and it updates. Merge or close the PR, and the whole thing deletes itself. No queue, no claiming, no cleanup, and no drift.

That's what we're building in this tutorial. Here's what it looks like from the reviewer's side. A bot comment appearing on the pull request with a live, working URL

What You'll Build

By the end of this handbook, you'll have a working system where:

  • Opening a pull request triggers a GitHub Actions workflow that builds a container image tagged specifically for that PR

  • The image is pushed to Google Artifact Registry

  • A dedicated Kubernetes namespace (

    pr-42
    , 
    pr-43
    , and so on) is created inside a GKE cluster, with resource quotas applied before anything deploys

  • The application deploys into that namespace, completely isolated from every other PR's environment

  • A shared Ingress controller routes 

    pr-42.preview.yourdomain.com
    to that namespace, with a valid TLS certificate issued automatically

  • A bot comments the live URL on the pull request, updating the same comment on every push

  • Pushing new commits redeploys the environment with the updated code

  • Closing or merging the PR deletes the namespace and everything inside it

  • A scheduled job catches any environment the teardown missed

You'll also build the underlying infrastructure with Terraform, with three key design decisions, each with its own section.

  • No service account keys: GitHub Actions authenticates to Google Cloud through Workload Identity Federation. Short-lived OIDC tokens verified against a repository claim. Service account JSON keys sitting in GitHub secrets are one of the most common security problems in CI/CD pipelines today, and you don't need one.

  • One load balancer, not one per PR: A single shared Ingress controller routes every environment by hostname, and one wildcard DNS record covers every hostname that will ever exist. The naïve version provisions a cloud load balancer per environment, which gets expensive quickly.

  • Cleanup that assumes failure: Teardown runs when a PR closes. But a scheduled reaper also deletes namespaces whose PR is gone or that have outlived a maximum age, because even 95% effective automated cleanup still leaks, and leaks show up on the bill.

Here's the architecture we're working toward:

The diagram traces two separate paths through the same system.

The solid blue path is automation. A pull request triggers GitHub Actions, which authenticates to Google Cloud through Workload Identity Federation, pushes a PR-tagged image to Artifact Registry, and deploys into a dedicated namespace inside the GKE cluster.

Each namespace (

pr-42
, 
pr-43
, and so on) holds its own Deployment, Service, and Pod, completely isolated from every other one.

Two more automated pieces sit alongside it: a bot that posts and updates the preview URL on the pull request, and a scheduled reaper that finds and deletes orphaned namespaces.

The dashed green path is public traffic. A browser request for a preview URL resolves through a single wildcard DNS record to one Google Cloud load balancer, which hands it to a shared NGINX Ingress controller. That controller reads the request's 

Host
header and routes it to the right namespace. cert-manager runs beside it, requesting certificates from Let's Encrypt so each environment gets its own valid TLS certificate.

The important detail is what doesn't multiply. One load balancer, one DNS record, and one Ingress controller serve every environment, no matter how many pull requests are open.

Prerequisites

Before you start, make sure you have the following ready:

  • gcloud

    gcloud auth login
    to sign in, and 
    gcloud config set project YOUR_PROJECT_ID
    to point it at your project.

  • Terraform version 1.5 or later. Check with 

    terraform version
    . 

  • kubectl

  • Docker installed locally, for testing the build before you hand it to CI.

  • A GitHub repository that you own. This needs to be a repository you can push branches to and open pull requests against, since that's the trigger for everything we build.

One more thing worth bringing your attention to early: you'll also need the

Step 2: Write the Application

We need something to deploy. We'll use Go, for three reasons that matter to this project specifically.

First, Go compiles to a single statically-linked binary. There's no runtime to install and no interpreter, which means very small container images, and small images mean fast pushes and fast pulls, which matters a lot when you're building an image on every single commit to every open PR.

Second, Go's 

-ldflags -X
mechanism lets us inject values into the binary at build time. We'll use this to bake the PR number and Git commit SHA directly into the application, so the running app can tell us exactly which build it is.

And lastly, build times are fast, and CI minutes aren't free.

Create 

app/main.go
:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"net/http"
	"os"
)

// These values are empty at compile time and get injected by the
// linker via -ldflags -X during the Docker build. See the Dockerfile.
var (
	prNumber = "local"
	gitSha   = "dev"
)

func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	// Kubernetes injects these via the Downward API — see deployment.yaml
	namespace := os.Getenv("POD_NAMESPACE")
	podName := os.Getenv("POD_NAME")

	if namespace == "" {
		namespace = "not-in-kubernetes"
	}
	if podName == "" {
		podName, _ = os.Hostname()
	}

	fmt.Fprintf(w, "Preview environment is live\n\n")
	fmt.Fprintf(w, "PR number  : %s\n", prNumber)
	fmt.Fprintf(w, "Git SHA    : %s\n", gitSha)
	fmt.Fprintf(w, "Namespace  : %s\n", namespace)
	fmt.Fprintf(w, "Pod name   : %s\n", podName)
}

func healthz(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
	fmt.Fprintln(w, "ok")
}

func main() {
	http.HandleFunc("/", handler)
	http.HandleFunc("/healthz", healthz)

	fmt.Println("Server starting on port 8080...")
	if err := http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "server error: %v\n", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}

Initialize the Go module from inside 

app/
:
cd app
go mod init preview-app

Let's walk through what this code does and why each piece is here.

var prNumber = "local"
and 
var gitSha = "dev"
are package-level string variables with default values. The defaults are what you'll see if you run the binary locally without going through the Docker build.

During the CI build, the Go linker overwrites them with the real PR number and commit SHA. This is the single most useful debugging feature in the whole project: when you hit a preview environment, the app itself tells you exactly which commit it was built from. There's no guessing.

os.Getenv("POD_NAMESPACE")
and 
os.Getenv("POD_NAME")
read environment variables that Kubernetes injects into the container using something called the Downward API. We'll configure that in the deployment manifest in Step 8.

The Downward API lets a pod read metadata about itself (its own name, namespace, and labels) without needing any Kubernetes API credentials. It's the cleanest way for an app to know where it's running.

The 

handler
function is registered on the root path 
/
. It writes the PR number, commit SHA, namespace, and pod name to the response. It's four pieces of information that together answer "what exactly am I looking at right now?"

The 

healthz
function is registered on 
/healthz
, and returns HTTP 200 with the text 
ok
. Kubernetes uses this endpoint for liveness and readiness probes, which we'll wire up in the deployment manifest.

http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)
starts the server on port 8080. If it fails to start, it prints the error and exits with a non-zero code, so Kubernetes knows the container is broken and can restart it.

Test it locally before moving on:

go run main.go

In a second terminal:

curl http://localhost:8080

You should see 

PR number : local
and 
Git SHA : dev
, since you're running outside the Docker build. That's the expected local behaviour.

Step 3: Write the Dockerfile

Create 

app/Dockerfile
:
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Stage 1: Build
# -----------------------------------------------------------
FROM golang:1.27-alpine AS builder
#Ensure the version matches what is in your go.mod file

# These are injected by the CI pipeline at build time
ARG PR_NUMBER=local
ARG GIT_SHA=dev

WORKDIR /app

# Copy go.mod first so Docker can cache the dependency layer
COPY go.mod .
RUN go mod download

COPY main.go .

# -w -s strips debug symbols (~30% smaller binary)
# -X overwrites package-level string variables at link time
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build \
    -ldflags="-w -s -X main.prNumber=${PR_NUMBER} -X main.gitSha=${GIT_SHA}" \
    -o server main.go

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Stage 2: Runtime
# -----------------------------------------------------------
FROM alpine:latest

RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
USER appuser

WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/server .

EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["./server"]

There are a few things happening here worth understanding properly.

1. The 
-ldflags -X
Injection

-X main.prNumber=${PR_NUMBER}

The 

-X
linker flag sets the value of a package-level string variable at link time. The syntax is 
-X importpath.name=value
. Since our variables live in 
package main
, the import path is just 
main
.

This only works on 

string
variables that are already declared in the source. You can't create new variables this way, and you can't inject into an 
int
or a 
bool
. That's why 
prNumber
is a string in 
main.go
even though it holds a number.

Why do this instead of just passing an environment variable through the deployment manifest? Because build metadata belongs to the image, not the deployment. If you pass it as an env var, someone can deploy image 

abc123
with an env var claiming it's commit 
def456
, and the app will happily lie to you. Baking it into the binary means the image can only ever report what it actually is.

The 
CGO_ENABLED=0
Flag

By default, Go can link against C libraries. When it does, the resulting binary depends on the system's C library being present at runtime. Alpine uses 

musl
instead of the more common 
glibc
, and that mismatch is a classic source of "works in the builder stage, crashes in the runtime stage" errors.

Setting 

CGO_ENABLED=0
forces a pure-Go, fully static binary with no external library dependencies. It will run on any Linux system, including a 
scratch
image with nothing in it at all.

COPY go.mod .
Before 
COPY main.go .

Docker builds images layer by layer and caches each layer. By copying only 

go.mod
first and running 
go mod download
before copying the source code, we create a cached dependency layer.

On subsequent builds (and remember, this pipeline builds on every commit to every open PR), Docker skips the dependency download entirely as long as 

go.mod
hasn't changed. On a real project with dozens of dependencies, this is the difference between a 20-second build and a 3-minute build, multiplied by every push your team makes.

The Non-Root User

RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
USER appuser

Containers run as root by default. If an attacker finds a vulnerability in your application, running as root inside the container gives them significantly more room to escalate. Creating an unprivileged user and switching to it limits the blast radius. It costs you two lines, and there's no reason not to do it.

Build and test it locally:

docker build --build-arg PR_NUMBER=99 --build-arg GIT_SHA=abc1234 -t preview-app:test .
docker run -p 8080:8080 preview-app:test

Then 

curl http://localhost:8080
in another terminal. You should now see 
PR number : 99
and 
Git SHA : abc1234
. The injection works.

commands for a reason that becomes obvious the moment something goes wrong: with Terraform,

cleans up everything you created, in the right order, with no orphaned resources quietly billing you.

Create 

terraform/variables.tf
:
variable "project_id" {

variable "region" {

Now create 

terraform/main.tf
:
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.5"
  required_providers {
    google = {
      source  = "hashicorp/google"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "google" {
  project = var.project_id
  region  = var.region
}

# Look up the project so we can reference its numeric project number,
# which Workload Identity Federation requires (it doesn't accept the
# human-readable project ID).
data "google_project" "current" {}

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Enable required APIs
# -----------------------------------------------------------
resource "google_project_service" "apis" {
  for_each = toset([
    "container.googleapis.com",
    "artifactregistry.googleapis.com",
    "iamcredentials.googleapis.com",
    "sts.googleapis.com",
  ])

  service            = each.value
  disable_on_destroy = false
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Artifact Registry — where preview images live
# -----------------------------------------------------------
resource "google_artifact_registry_repository" "preview" {
  location      = var.region
  repository_id = "pr-preview"
  description   = "Container images for PR preview environments"
  format        = "DOCKER"

  depends_on = [google_project_service.apis]
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# GKE cluster
# -----------------------------------------------------------
resource "google_container_cluster" "primary" {
  name     = var.cluster_name
  location = var.zone

  # Create the cluster with a throwaway default pool, then remove it
  # and manage nodes through a separate node pool resource. This is the
  # standard pattern — it lets you resize or upgrade the node pool
  # without recreating the cluster control plane.
  remove_default_node_pool = true
  initial_node_count       = 1

  networking_mode = "VPC_NATIVE"
  ip_allocation_policy {}

  # Set to true before you use this for anything real.
  deletion_protection = false

  depends_on = [google_project_service.apis]
}

resource "google_container_node_pool" "primary_nodes" {
  name       = "${var.cluster_name}-pool"
  location   = var.zone
  cluster    = google_container_cluster.primary.name
  node_count = var.node_count

  node_config {
    machine_type = var.machine_type
    disk_size_gb = 50

    oauth_scopes = [
      "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform",
    ]

    labels = {
      purpose = "pr-preview-envs"
    }
  }

  management {
    auto_repair  = true
    auto_upgrade = true
  }
}

There are a few things that're worth calling out here.

data "google_project" "current"
isn't creating anything. It's a data source, which reads existing information from your provider. We need it because Workload Identity Federation identifies your project by its numeric project number, not the project ID you type in the console. Rather than making you look it up manually and paste it in, Terraform fetches it for you.

for_each
on 
google_project_service
: instead of writing four nearly identical resource blocks to enable four APIs, 
for_each
iterates over a set and creates one resource per item. 
disable_on_destroy = false
means 
terraform destroy
won't turn these APIs off, which is what you want, because other things in your project might be using them.

remove_default_node_pool = true
: GKE insists on creating a default node pool when you create a cluster. Setting this immediately deletes it, and we define our own node pool as a separate resource. The benefit is that node pool changes (resizing, changing machine type, upgrading) don't force a change to the cluster resource itself.

node_count = 2
with 
e2-standard-2
: two nodes with 2 vCPU and 8GB each. Preview environments are small, but you'll have several running at once, plus GKE's own system pods. Two nodes give you comfortable headroom. If you plan to keep more than about eight preview environments alive simultaneously, bump this up.

deletion_protection = false
: GKE added this as a guard against accidentally destroying production clusters. We're disabling it because this is a tutorial cluster you'll delete at the end. If you adapt this for real use, set it to 
true
.

Step 5: Set Up Keyless Authentication with Workload Identity Federation

This is the section that matters most, so let's take it slowly.

The Problem With Service Account Keys

GitHub Actions needs permission to push images to Artifact Registry and deploy to your GKE cluster. The way most tutorials handle this is:

  • Create a service account in GCP

  • Generate a JSON key for it

  • Paste that JSON into a GitHub secret called 

    GCP_SA_KEY

  • Load it in the workflow

This works, but it's also a security problem, and here's why:

First, the key never expires. A service account JSON key is a long-lived credential. It's valid until someone explicitly revokes it, which in practice means it's valid forever, because nobody remembers to rotate them.

Second, the key is a bearer token. Anyone who obtains that JSON file is your service account. No second factor, IP restriction, or expiry. Copy the file, and use it from anywhere in the world.

Third, the blast radius is enormous. GitHub secrets are exposed to workflows. A compromised third-party action, a malicious dependency in your build, or a workflow modified in a pull request can exfiltrate that secret. Once it's out, an attacker has persistent access to your cloud project.

This isn't theoretical. Leaked service account keys are one of the most common root causes in cloud security incidents.

How Workload Identity Federation Fixes It

Workload Identity Federation removes the long-lived key entirely. Here's the flow:

  • GitHub Actions generates a short-lived OIDC token for the running workflow. This token is signed by GitHub and contains verified claims: which repository is running, which branch, which workflow, and which actor.

  • Your workflow presents that token to Google Cloud's Security Token Service.

  • Google checks the token's signature against GitHub's public keys, and checks the claims against rules you configured, specifically that the token came from your repository and no other.

  • If everything matches, Google issues a short-lived access token, typically valid for about an hour.

  • The workflow uses that token, and it expires shortly after.

There's no secret stored anywhere. Nothing to leak, rotate, or revoke. If someone forks your repository and runs the same workflow, the OIDC token they generate will carry their repository name in its claims, Google's check will fail, and they get nothing.

Add this to 

terraform/main.tf
:
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Service account that GitHub Actions will impersonate
# -----------------------------------------------------------
resource "google_service_account" "github_actions" {
  account_id   = "github-actions-preview"
  display_name = "GitHub Actions — PR Preview Environments"
}

# Permission to push images to Artifact Registry
resource "google_project_iam_member" "artifact_writer" {
  project = var.project_id
  role    = "roles/artifactregistry.writer"
  member  = "serviceAccount:${google_service_account.github_actions.email}"
}

# Permission to create namespaces and deploy workloads in GKE.
# container.developer grants full access to Kubernetes API objects,
# but NOT permission to modify the cluster itself.
resource "google_project_iam_member" "gke_developer" {
  project = var.project_id
  role    = "roles/container.developer"
  member  = "serviceAccount:${google_service_account.github_actions.email}"
}

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Workload Identity Federation
# -----------------------------------------------------------
resource "google_iam_workload_identity_pool" "github" {
  workload_identity_pool_id = "github-pool"
  display_name              = "GitHub Actions Pool"
  description               = "Identity pool for GitHub Actions OIDC"

  depends_on = [google_project_service.apis]
}

resource "google_iam_workload_identity_pool_provider" "github" {
  workload_identity_pool_id          = google_iam_workload_identity_pool.github.workload_identity_pool_id
  workload_identity_pool_provider_id = "github-provider"
  display_name                       = "GitHub OIDC Provider"

  # Map claims from the GitHub OIDC token to Google attributes
  attribute_mapping = {
    "google.subject"       = "assertion.sub"
    "attribute.actor"      = "assertion.actor"
    "attribute.repository" = "assertion.repository"
  }

  # CRITICAL: without this condition, ANY GitHub repository on the
  # internet could authenticate against your pool.
  attribute_condition = "assertion.repository == '${var.github_repo}'"

  oidc {
    issuer_uri = "https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
  }
}

# Allow tokens from your specific repo to impersonate the service account
resource "google_service_account_iam_member" "github_impersonation" {
  service_account_id = google_service_account.github_actions.name
  role               = "roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser"
  member             = "principalSet://iam.googleapis.com/projects/${data.google_project.current.number}/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/${google_iam_workload_identity_pool.github.workload_identity_pool_id}/attribute.repository/${var.github_repo}"
}

Let's break down the parts that trip people up.

attribute_mapping
: GitHub's OIDC token contains a set of claims. This block tells Google which claims to read and what to call them internally. 
assertion.sub
is the token's subject (something like 
repo:owner/name:ref:refs/heads/main
). 
assertion.repository
is the full repository name. 
google.subject
is required, while the others are optional attributes you can then write rules against.

attribute_condition
: read this line twice, because getting it wrong is a serious vulnerability:
attribute_condition = "assertion.repository == '${var.github_repo}'"

Without this condition, your identity pool trusts the GitHub OIDC issuer, which means it trusts every repository on GitHub. Anyone who knows your pool's resource path (which isn't secret and appears in workflow files) could authenticate and impersonate your service account.

This condition narrows the trust to exactly one repository. Google now requires an attribute condition when you map 

assertion.repository
, precisely because so many people got this wrong.

principalSet://...
: this is the identity being granted the 
workloadIdentityUser
role. Read it right to left: any principal in the 
github-pool
whose 
attribute.repository
equals your repo may impersonate this service account. Note that it uses 
data.google_project.current.number
, which is the numeric project number, not the project ID. Using the project ID here produces an error that doesn't clearly explain what's wrong, and it's one of the most common mistakes with WIF.

Why 

roles/container.developer
and not 
roles/container.admin
? 
container.developer
grants full access to Kubernetes API objects inside clusters: creating namespaces, applying deployments, deleting resources. 
container.admin
additionally allows modifying the clusters themselves: resizing node pools, upgrading, deleting the cluster entirely.

Our workflow never needs to touch the cluster's own configuration, so it shouldn't have permission to. This is least privilege in practice: grant exactly what the job requires and nothing beyond it.

Now create 

terraform/outputs.tf
:
output "cluster_name" {
  value = google_container_cluster.primary.name
}

output "cluster_zone" {
  value = var.zone
}

output "artifact_registry_url" {
  description = "Base URL for pushing images"
  value       = "${var.region}-docker.pkg.dev/${var.project_id}/${google_artifact_registry_repository.preview.repository_id}"
}

output "workload_identity_provider" {
  description = "Paste this into the GitHub Actions workflow"
  value       = "projects/${data.google_project.current.number}/locations/global/workloadIdentityPools/${google_iam_workload_identity_pool.github.workload_identity_pool_id}/providers/${google_iam_workload_identity_pool_provider.github.workload_identity_pool_provider_id}"
}

output "service_account_email" {
  description = "Paste this into the GitHub Actions workflow"
  value       = google_service_account.github_actions.email
}

output "get_credentials_command" {
  value = "gcloud container clusters get-credentials ${google_container_cluster.primary.name} --zone ${var.zone} --project ${var.project_id}"
}

Those outputs aren't decoration. 

workload_identity_provider
and 
service_account_email
are the two values you'll paste into your GitHub Actions workflow, and both are tedious to construct by hand.
