You can print them again any time with 

terraform output
.

Connect 

kubectl
to the new cluster using the command from the 
get_credentials_command
output:
gcloud container clusters get-credentials pr-preview-cluster \
  --zone europe-west2-a \
  --project YOUR_PROJECT_ID

Verify:

kubectl get nodes

You should see two nodes in 

Ready
state.

Step 7: Prove the Lifecycle Manually

Before automating anything, do it by hand once.

This isn't busywork. Automation is fundamentally just a script running commands you could have typed. If you don't know what the commands are, you can't debug the automation when it fails...and it will fail, usually at 11 pm before a demo. Ten minutes here saves hours later.

Create a namespace:

kubectl create namespace pr-test

Deploy a placeholder into it:

kubectl create deployment hello \
  --image=nginx:1.27-alpine \
  --namespace=pr-test

Check it:

kubectl get pods --namespace=pr-test

Now the important part – prove the isolation:

kubectl get pods --all-namespaces | grep hello

The pod exists only in 

pr-test
. Nothing in 
default
or any other namespace knows about it. That's the property the entire project is built on: a namespace is a boundary, and everything inside one PR's namespace is invisible to every other.

Now tear it down:

kubectl delete namespace pr-test

Watch what happens:

kubectl get namespace pr-test

For a few seconds, you'll see 

Terminating
, then the namespace disappears entirely. Deleting a namespace deletes every resource inside it: deployments, pods, services, config maps, secrets, everything. One command, complete cleanup.

That single property is why namespace-per-PR is such a good fit for preview environments. Teardown isn't a careful sequence of deletions you have to get right. It's one command that can't leave anything behind.

Step 8: Write the Kubernetes Manifests with Kustomize

Every preview environment deploys the same application. The only differences between 

pr-42
and 
pr-43
are the namespace and the image tag.

This is exactly the problem Kustomize solves. You write the manifests once as a base, then apply small, declarative changes on top of it (an overlay) without templating, string substitution, or 

sed
scripts mangling your YAML.

Kustomize is built into 

kubectl
(that's the 
-k
flag), so there's nothing extra to install.

Create 

k8s/base/deployment.yaml
:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: preview-app
  labels:
    app: preview-app
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: preview-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: preview-app
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: preview-app
          # This is a placeholder. The overlay replaces it with the
          # real registry path and PR-specific tag.
          image: preview-app
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8080
          env:
            # Downward API: the pod learns its own identity
            - name: POD_NAMESPACE
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.namespace
            - name: POD_NAME
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.name
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 2
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "50m"
              memory: "64Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "200m"
              memory: "128Mi"

Create 

k8s/base/service.yaml
:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: preview-app
spec:
  selector:
    app: preview-app
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 8080
  type: ClusterIP

Create 

k8s/base/kustomization.yaml
:
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

resources:
  - deployment.yaml
  - service.yaml

There are some deliberate choices here.

replicas: 1
: production runs multiple replicas for availability. A preview environment doesn't need high availability. One replica per environment, multiplied across every open PR, keeps your node count and your bill sane.

image: preview-app
: a bare placeholder with no registry and no tag. It would never pull as-is. Kustomize's image transformer matches on this name and replaces it wholesale, so the base manifest never needs to know your registry URL.

The Downward API 

env
block: this is where 
POD_NAMESPACE
and 
POD_NAME
come from. 
fieldRef
reads a field from the pod's own spec at runtime and exposes it as an environment variable. No API calls, credentials, or service account needed.

type: ClusterIP
: internal-only. Each 
LoadBalancer
service provisions a real Google Cloud load balancer with a real hourly cost and a public IP. Doing that per PR would be expensive and wasteful. We'll reach the app with 
kubectl port-forward
for now, and in Step 13 a single shared Ingress controller takes over, serving every environment through one load balancer.

Resource requests and limits: 

requests
reserve capacity so the scheduler knows how much room a pod needs. 
limits
cap what it can consume. Without limits, one runaway preview environment could starve every other one on the node. With many short-lived environments coming and going, this isn't optional.

Test the base renders correctly:

kubectl kustomize k8s/base

That prints the rendered YAML without applying it. This is useful for debugging.

Step 9: Build the Spin-Up Workflow

Now we connect everything.

Create 

.github/workflows/preview-deploy.yml
:
name: Deploy PR Preview

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]

# If someone pushes three commits quickly, cancel the older runs.
# Without this, three deploys race each other into the same namespace
# and whichever finishes last wins — which may not be the newest commit.
concurrency:
  group: preview-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write   # REQUIRED for Workload Identity Federation
  pull-requests: write

env:
  PROJECT_ID: YOUR_PROJECT_ID
  REGION: europe-west2
  CLUSTER_NAME: pr-preview-cluster
  CLUSTER_ZONE: europe-west2-a
  REPOSITORY: pr-preview
  IMAGE_NAME: preview-app

jobs:
  deploy:
    name: Build and deploy preview
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Check out code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set environment variables
        run: |
          PR_NUMBER=${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
          SHORT_SHA=$(echo "${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}" | cut -c1-7)

          echo "PR_NUMBER=${PR_NUMBER}"   >> $GITHUB_ENV
          echo "SHORT_SHA=${SHORT_SHA}"   >> $GITHUB_ENV
          echo "NAMESPACE=pr-${PR_NUMBER}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
          echo "IMAGE_TAG=pr-${PR_NUMBER}-${SHORT_SHA}" >> $GITHUB_ENV
          echo "IMAGE_BASE=${{ env.REGION }}-docker.pkg.dev/${{ env.PROJECT_ID }}/${{ env.REPOSITORY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV

      - name: Authenticate to Google Cloud
        uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
        with:
          workload_identity_provider: ${{ secrets.WIF_PROVIDER }}
          service_account: ${{ secrets.WIF_SERVICE_ACCOUNT }}

      - name: Set up gcloud
        uses: google-github-actions/setup-gcloud@v2

      - name: Configure Docker for Artifact Registry
        run: gcloud auth configure-docker ${{ env.REGION }}-docker.pkg.dev --quiet

      - name: Build and push image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --build-arg PR_NUMBER="${PR_NUMBER}" \
            --build-arg GIT_SHA="${SHORT_SHA}" \
            -t "${IMAGE_BASE}:${IMAGE_TAG}" \
            ./app

          docker push "${IMAGE_BASE}:${IMAGE_TAG}"

      - name: Get GKE credentials
        uses: google-github-actions/get-gke-credentials@v2
        with:
          cluster_name: ${{ env.CLUSTER_NAME }}
          location: ${{ env.CLUSTER_ZONE }}

      - name: Create namespace
        run: |
          # --dry-run=client | apply makes this idempotent.
          # Running it on an existing namespace is a no-op, not an error.
          kubectl create namespace "${NAMESPACE}" \
            --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

      - name: Generate Kustomize overlay
        run: |
          mkdir -p k8s/overlays/"${NAMESPACE}"
          cat > k8s/overlays/"${NAMESPACE}"/kustomization.yaml <


Add the Two Secrets
Go to your repository on GitHub and go to Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions, and New repository secret. Add:
Secret nameValue
WIF_PROVIDER

The 
workload_identity_provider
 output from Terraform		

WIF_SERVICE_ACCOUNT

The 
service_account_email
 output from Terraform		

Neither of these is a credential. The provider path and service account email are identifiers, not secrets. They grant nothing on their own, because the OIDC token and the attribute condition are what actually control access. Storing them as secrets is just tidiness. Update 
PROJECT_ID
 and the region values in the workflow's 
env:
 block to match your setup.
Understanding the Workflow
on: pull_request: types: [opened, synchronize, reopened]
: these are three distinct triggers.
  • opened
     fires when the PR is first created.

  • synchronize
     fires on every subsequent push to the branch, which is what keeps the environment current.

  • reopened
     handles a PR that was closed and then reopened. Without it, that PR would have a torn-down environment and nothing to recreate it.

concurrency
: this one saves real debugging time. Push three commits in quick succession, and you get three workflow runs targeting the same namespace. They race. The one that finishes last wins, and that's not necessarily the newest code. A fast early build can overtake a slow later one, leaving your preview environment silently running stale code while the PR shows green. Grouping by PR number with 
cancel-in-progress: true
 means only the newest run survives.
permissions: id-token: write
: without this line, nothing else works. It's what allows the workflow to request an OIDC token from GitHub. Leave it out and 
google-github-actions/auth
 fails with an error about being unable to get an ID token. This is the single most common WIF setup mistake.
$GITHUB_ENV
: writing 
KEY=value
 to this file makes the variable available in all subsequent steps. Not the current one, as a variable you write in a step can't be read later in that same step. It's why the setup happens in its own step at the top.
github.event.pull_request.head.sha
: note this rather than 
github.sha
. On 
pull_request
 events, GitHub checks out a merge commit. This is a temporary commit combining your branch with the base branch. 
github.sha
 refers to that merge commit, which doesn't exist in your repository's history and will confuse anyone who tries to look it up. 
head.sha
 is the actual last commit on the PR branch, which is what a developer expects to see.
--dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
 is a small trick worth stealing. 
kubectl create namespace
 fails if the namespace already exists, which would break every push after the first. This pipeline generates the namespace YAML without contacting the cluster, then pipes it to
apply
, which creates it if it's missing and does nothing if it isn't. Idempotent by construction.
The heredoc overlay: instead of committing an overlay per PR (impossible, as you don't know PR numbers in advance), the workflow writes one at runtime and throws it away when the runner is destroyed. It's ephemeral configuration for an ephemeral environment.
kubectl rollout status
 is what makes the workflow honest. Without it, the job succeeds the moment 
kubectl apply
 is accepted by the API server, which happens before a single pod has started. A crash-looping image would still show a green check. 
rollout status
 blocks until pods are actually ready, or fails after 180 seconds. Green means working.
A Note on Forked Pull Requests
Something is worth knowing before you deploy this anywhere public: pull requests from forks do not receive 
id-token: write
 permission, by design. GitHub blocks it so a stranger can't open a PR that steals your cloud credentials.
For a private repository or a personal project, this doesn't affect you. For a public repository accepting outside contributions, you'd need a 
workflow_run
-based pattern where a privileged workflow runs from the base repository after the untrusted build completes. That's beyond this handbook's scope, but if you're deploying this on an open-source project, don't skip it.
Step 10: Build the Teardown Workflow
Spin-up is only half the value. An environment that never disappears is just a slow leak in your cloud bill.
Create 
.github/workflows/preview-teardown.yml
:
name: Tear Down PR Preview

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [closed]

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write

env:
  PROJECT_ID: YOUR_PROJECT_ID
  CLUSTER_NAME: pr-preview-cluster
  CLUSTER_ZONE: europe-west2-a

jobs:
  teardown:
    name: Delete preview namespace
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Set namespace
        run: echo "NAMESPACE=pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}" >> $GITHUB_ENV

      - name: Authenticate to Google Cloud
        uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
        with:
          workload_identity_provider: ${{ secrets.WIF_PROVIDER }}
          service_account: ${{ secrets.WIF_SERVICE_ACCOUNT }}

      - name: Get GKE credentials
        uses: google-github-actions/get-gke-credentials@v2
        with:
          cluster_name: ${{ env.CLUSTER_NAME }}
          location: ${{ env.CLUSTER_ZONE }}

      - name: Delete namespace
        run: |
          echo "Deleting namespace ${NAMESPACE}"
          kubectl delete namespace "${NAMESPACE}" \
            --ignore-not-found=true \
            --wait=false

      - name: Confirm
        run: |
          echo "Preview environment for PR #${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} torn down."



A few details here matter more than they might seem.
First, 
types: [closed]
 covers merges too. GitHub doesn't have a separate 
merged
 event type. Merging a pull request fires 
closed
 with the payload field 
merged: true
. So this single trigger handles both "merged successfully" and "abandoned and closed." Both should tear down the environment, so we don't need to distinguish between them.
Next, 
--ignore-not-found=true
: if the namespace doesn't exist (perhaps the deploy failed, or someone deleted it manually), 
kubectl delete
 would normally exit with an error and mark the workflow red. That's a false alarm: the desired end state is "namespace doesn't exist," and it doesn't. This flag makes the step succeed when there's nothing to do.
Finally, 
--wait=false
: namespace deletion is asynchronous. Kubernetes marks it
Terminating
, then works through deleting every resource inside it. Waiting for that to complete could hold your CI runner for a minute or more, for no benefit. Fire the delete and let the cluster finish on its own time.

Commit everything and push:
git add .
git commit -m "Add PR preview environment infrastructure"
git push -u origin main



Now create a branch and make a visible change:
git checkout -b test-preview



Edit 
app/main.go
. Change the first line of the handler output:
fmt.Fprintf(w, "Preview environment is live — testing the pipeline\n\n")



Commit and push:
git add .
git commit -m "Test preview environment"
git push -u origin test-preview



Open a pull request on GitHub, then go to the Actions tab. You should see "Deploy PR Preview" running.
Watch the steps in order: authentication succeeds without a key, the image builds and pushes, the namespace is created, Kustomize renders the overlay (you'll see the fully resolved manifest printed), the deployment applies, and 
rollout status
 waits until pods are ready.
Once it's green, verify from your terminal:
kubectl get namespaces | grep pr-



You should see your 
pr-1
 (or whatever number your PR got).
kubectl get pods --namespace=pr-1



Now reach the application:
kubectl port-forward --namespace=pr-1 service/preview-app 8080:80



In a second terminal:
curl http://localhost:8080



You should see:
Preview environment is live — testing the pipeline

PR number  : 1
Git SHA    : a1b2c3d
Namespace  : pr-1
Pod name   : preview-app-7d9f8b6c4-xk2mp



The application is reporting the PR number and commit SHA that were baked into its binary at build time, and the namespace it discovered through the Downward API. Every one of those values was resolved by a different part of the pipeline, and they all agree. That's your proof the whole chain works.
Now push another commit to the same branch and watch the environment update in place.
Then close the pull request and watch the teardown workflow fire.
kubectl get namespace pr-1



Terminating
, then gone.
What You Have, and What's Still Missing
Stop and take stock, because the hard infrastructure work is done. A pull request now produces a real, isolated environment with no manual steps, and closing it removes every trace. That's the whole lifecycle, automated.
But look again at how you reached it:
kubectl port-forward --namespace=pr-1 service/preview-app 8080:80



That requires 
kubectl
 installed, credentials for the cluster, permission to use them, and knowledge of which namespace maps to which PR. This is fine for the person who built the pipeline, but it's useless for the designer checking a spacing change, the product manager reviewing a copy edit, or the QA engineer clicking through a flow before sign-off.
The whole point of a preview environment is that anyone can look at the change. An environment only engineers can reach isn't really a preview environment. It's a debugging tool.
The rest of this tutorial closes that gap, and then makes the result safe to leave running. First, we'll set up a public HTTPS URL for every environment. Then we'll build the guardrails and go through the cleanup that stop it becoming a quiet line item on your cloud bill.
Step 12: Reserve a Static IP Address
Before installing anything, you'll need to reserve an external IP address.
This matters because when you install the Ingress controller, it creates a Kubernetes Service of type 
LoadBalancer
, and Google Cloud provisions a real load balancer with a public IP. By default, that IP is ephemeral. If the Service is deleted and recreated, you get a different one.
Your wildcard DNS record points at that IP. If it changes, every preview environment breaks at once, and you won't find out until someone tells you the link is dead. Reserving the IP first means it belongs to your project, not to the load balancer, and it survives anything you do to the cluster.
Add this to 
terraform/main.tf
:
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Static external IP for the Ingress controller
# -----------------------------------------------------------
resource "google_compute_address" "ingress" {
  name         = "pr-preview-ingress-ip"
  region       = var.region
  address_type = "EXTERNAL"

  depends_on = [google_project_service.apis]
}



And add the output to 
terraform/outputs.tf
:
output "ingress_ip" {
  description = "Point your wildcard DNS record at this address"
  value       = google_compute_address.ingress.address
}



You'll also want 
compute.googleapis.com
 in the APIs list if it isn't there already. Update the 
for_each
 set in your 
google_project_service
 resource:
  for_each = toset([
    "container.googleapis.com",
    "artifactregistry.googleapis.com",
    "iamcredentials.googleapis.com",
    "sts.googleapis.com",
    "compute.googleapis.com",
  ])



Apply it:
cd terraform
terraform apply \
  -var="project_id=YOUR_PROJECT_ID" \
  -var="github_repo=YOUR_USERNAME/pr-preview-envs"



Note the IP that comes back:
terraform output ingress_ip



Write it down. You'll use it twice in the next two steps.
Important: this must be a regional address in the same region as your cluster, which is what 
region = var.region
 gives you. Google Cloud also offers global addresses, used by global HTTP(S) load balancers.
The Service type 
LoadBalancer
 that ingress-nginx creates is a regional load balancer, and it can't bind a global address. Mixing these up produces a Service stuck in 
Pending
 forever with an error that doesn't clearly explain why.
Step 13: Install the Ingress Controller
An Ingress is a Kubernetes resource that describes HTTP routing rules: "requests for this hostname go to that Service." But the Ingress resource is only a description. Something has to actually read those rules and route traffic, and that something is an Ingress controller.
We'll use ingress-nginx, which is the community-maintained controller built on NGINX. It runs as pods in your cluster, watches the Kubernetes API for Ingress resources, and rewrites its own NGINX configuration whenever one changes.
The architectural point that makes this work for preview environments is that one controller serves every namespace. Each preview environment creates its own Ingress resource. The controller picks it up, adds a routing rule for that hostname, and sends traffic to the right Service. The controller doesn't care how many environments exist.
Contrast this with what we'd otherwise do. If each preview environment used a 
LoadBalancer
 Service, every PR would provision its own Google Cloud load balancer, each with an hourly charge and its own IP address that DNS would need to know about. Ten open PRs would mean ten load balancers. With a shared Ingress controller, ten open PRs mean one.
Install it with Helm:
helm repo add ingress-nginx https://kubernetes.github.io/ingress-nginx
helm repo update

helm install ingress-nginx ingress-nginx/ingress-nginx \
  --namespace ingress-nginx \
  --create-namespace \
  --set controller.service.loadBalancerIP="YOUR_STATIC_IP" \
  --set controller.service.externalTrafficPolicy=Local



Replace 
YOUR_STATIC_IP
 with the address from Step 12.
Let's break down the flags before we go on:
--namespace ingress-nginx --create-namespace
: the controller gets its own namespace, separate from any preview environment. It's shared infrastructure, and it should never be caught up in a preview environment's teardown.
controller.service.loadBalancerIP
: tells GKE to bind the load balancer to the specific address you reserved, rather than allocating a new one. This is the line that makes your DNS record stable.
controller.service.externalTrafficPolicy=Local
: preserves the client's real source IP. Without it, Kubernetes may route a request through an intermediate node, and by the time it reaches NGINX the source IP has been rewritten to a node's internal address. Your access logs would show cluster IPs instead of real visitors.
The tradeoff is that traffic only lands on nodes actually running a controller pod, which is fine here.
Watch for the external IP to be assigned:
kubectl get service ingress-nginx-controller \
  --namespace ingress-nginx \
  --watch



It shows 
 for a minute or two while Google provisions the load balancer, then displays your static IP from Step 12. Press Ctrl+C once it appears.
Verify that the controller is healthy:
kubectl get pods --namespace ingress-nginx





Step 14: Point Wildcard DNS at the Load Balancer
This step takes about two minutes and is the piece that makes the whole pattern scale.
Go to wherever your domain's DNS is managed and create a single A record:
FieldValue
Type
A


Name / Host
*.preview


ValueYour static IP from Step 1
TTL300 (or the lowest your provider allows)
That's it. That's the entire DNS configuration for the project.
Here's why one record is enough. A wildcard DNS record matches any label in that position. 
*.preview.yourdomain.com
 resolves 
pr-1.preview.yourdomain.com
, 
pr-42.preview.yourdomain.com
, and 
pr-99999.preview.yourdomain.com
, all to the same IP, all without anyone creating a record for them.
This is worth pausing on, because it's the design decision that keeps the system simple. The obvious approach would be to have the CI pipeline create a DNS record when a PR opens and delete it when the PR closes. That means DNS API credentials in your pipeline, another thing to fail, another thing to leak, and another source of orphaned resources.
The wildcard approach eliminates that entire category of work: DNS is configured once, manually, and never touched again.
Routing to the right environment doesn't happen in DNS. Every hostname resolves to the same load balancer, and the Ingress controller reads the 
Host
 header of each incoming request to decide which namespace's Service should handle it.
Verify the record has propagated:
dig +short anything-at-all.preview.yourdomain.com



You should get your static IP back. Note that the subdomain doesn't need to exist yet. That's the whole point of a wildcard.
If nothing comes back, wait a few minutes and try again. DNS propagation is usually fast with a low TTL, but it isn't instant.
Step 15: Install cert-manager and Create a ClusterIssuer
Now for HTTPS.
cert-manager is a Kubernetes controller that automates the full certificate lifecycle. It watches for Ingress resources annotated with an issuer, requests a certificate from a certificate authority, proves you control the domain, stores the certificate in a Kubernetes Secret, and renews it before it expires. Ther eare no cron jobs, manual renewal, or expired-certificate incident at 3 am.
Install it:
helm repo add jetstack https://charts.jetstack.io
helm repo update

helm install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager \
  --namespace cert-manager \
  --create-namespace \
  --version v1.21.2 \
  --set crds.enabled=true



--set crds.enabled=true
 Installs cert-manager's Custom Resource Definitions: 
Certificate
, 
Issuer
, 
ClusterIssuer
, 
CertificateRequest
 and others. These extend the Kubernetes API with new resource types. Without them, cert-manager has nothing to watch for. (If you're following an older tutorial that uses 
installCRDs=true
, that flag was renamed in v1.15.)
Check it's running:
kubectl get pods --namespace cert-manager



You should see three pods: the controller, the webhook, and cainjector.
Create the ClusterIssuer
An Issuer tells cert-manager where to get certificates from. A ClusterIssuer is the same thing with cluster-wide scope, which is what we need. A namespaced Issuer would have to be recreated in every single preview namespace.
Create 
k8s/cluster/letsencrypt-staging.yaml
:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-staging
spec:
  acme:
    # Let's Encrypt's staging environment. Certificates from this
    # server are NOT trusted by browsers, but the rate limits are
    # far more generous. Use this while debugging.
    server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: YOUR_EMAIL@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-staging-account-key
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx



And 
k8s/cluster/letsencrypt-prod.yaml
:
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: YOUR_EMAIL@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx



Apply both:
kubectl apply -f k8s/cluster/letsencrypt-staging.yaml
kubectl apply -f k8s/cluster/letsencrypt-prod.yaml



Confirm they're ready:
kubectl get clusterissuer



Both should show 
READY: True
.
Why Two Issuers?
This isn't redundancy. It's how you avoid a frustrating afternoon.
Let's Encrypt enforces strict rate limits on its production environment. The one that matters here is 50 certificates per registered domain per week. There's also a duplicate-certificate limit of 5 per week for the identical set of hostnames.
While you're setting this up, you'll likely misconfigure something. The Ingress annotation will be wrong, or the HTTP-01 challenge won't route correctly, or DNS won't have propagated. Each failed attempt burns against your quota, and once you hit the limit you're locked out for a week with no appeal.
The staging issuer has far looser limits. Its certificates are signed by an untrusted root, so browsers show a warning, but that warning is itself proof the pipeline works. If you see a certificate warning naming "Let's Encrypt Staging," everything functioned correctly, and the only remaining step is switching issuers.
Use 
letsencrypt-staging
 until the flow works end to end, then switch to 
letsencrypt-prod
.
How the HTTP-01 Challenge Works
This is worth understanding, because it's what breaks when things go wrong.
When cert-manager requests a certificate for 
pr-42.preview.yourdomain.com
, Let's Encrypt needs proof you control that hostname. With the HTTP-01 solver, the sequence is:
  • Let's Encrypt gives cert-manager a random token.
  • cert-manager creates a temporary pod, Service, and Ingress rule that serves that token at 
    http://pr-42.preview.yourdomain.com/.well-known/acme-challenge/
    .

  • Let's Encrypt makes a real HTTP request to that URL from the public internet.
  • If the token matches, domain control is proven and the certificate is issued.
  • cert-manager deletes the temporary resources and stores the certificate in a Secret.
Three things must be true for this to work, and they're the three things to check when it doesn't: DNS must resolve the hostname to your load balancer, port 80 must be reachable from the internet (don't redirect everything to HTTPS at the load balancer level. The challenge is plain HTTP), and the Ingress controller must be routing correctly.
A Note on Scale
HTTP-01 issues one certificate per hostname, and every preview environment has a unique hostname. That's one certificate per pull request.
Against Let's Encrypt's 50-per-week limit, that's comfortable for a solo project or a small team. An active team opening more than 50 PRs a week would hit the ceiling.
The production answer is to issue a single wildcard certificate for 
*.preview.yourdomain.com
 and share it across every namespace. Wildcards can't be issued over HTTP-01. They require the DNS-01 challenge, where cert-manager proves control by creating a TXT record instead of serving a file.
With Cloud DNS, cert-manager can do this automatically using a Google service account. You'd then replicate the resulting Secret into each preview namespace with a tool like reflector.
That's more moving parts than this handbook needs, but it's the right answer once your PR volume justifies it, and it's worth knowing that limit exists before you hit it.
Step 16: Add an Ingress to the Base Manifests
Now we'll give the application a route.
Create 
k8s/base/ingress.yaml
:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: preview-app
  annotations:
    # Tells cert-manager to request a certificate for the hosts
    # listed under spec.tls, using this ClusterIssuer.
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-staging
    # Redirect HTTP to HTTPS once the certificate exists.
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - preview-host-placeholder
      secretName: preview-app-tls
  rules:
    - host: preview-host-placeholder
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: preview-app
                port:
                  number: 80



Add it to 
k8s/base/kustomization.yaml
:
You created this file back in Step 8 with two resources. Add the Ingress to it:
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

resources:
  - deployment.yaml
  - service.yaml
  - ingress.yaml



Here are the pieces that matter:
cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer
: this single annotation is what triggers the entire certificate workflow. cert-manager watches for it, reads the hostnames from 
spec.tls
, and does everything else. Note it's set to 
letsencrypt-staging
 for now. We'll switch to production once the flow is proven.
ingressClassName: nginx
: identifies which controller should handle this Ingress. A cluster can run several controllers simultaneously, and this field prevents them from fighting over the same resource. Older tutorials use the 
kubernetes.io/ingress.class
 annotation, which is deprecated.
secretName: preview-app-tls
: where cert-manager stores the issued certificate. It's created automatically in the same namespace as the Ingress, so each preview environment has its own.
preview-host-placeholder
: deliberately not a valid hostname. It appears twice: once in 
spec.tls.hosts
 and once in 
spec.rules.host
, and both get replaced per PR in the next step. Using something that obviously isn't a real domain means that if the patch ever fails, you get an immediate visible error rather than a subtle misroute.
pathType: Prefix
 with 
path: /
: matches every path on the host. Preview environments serve the whole application, not a subpath.
Step 17: Patch the Hostname Per Pull Request
Each environment needs its own hostname substituted into two places in the Ingress. Kustomize handles this with a JSON 6902 patch. A precise operation that targets an exact path within a resource.
In Step 9, the workflow generated an overlay that set the namespace and image tag. We extend that generated overlay with a patch block. Here's what the complete generated 
kustomization.yaml
 looks like for PR 42:
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization

namespace: pr-42

resources:
  - ../../base

images:
  - name: preview-app
    newName: europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev/your-project/pr-preview/preview-app
    newTag: pr-42-a1b2c3d

patches:
  - target:
      kind: Ingress
      name: preview-app
    patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/rules/0/host
        value: pr-42.preview.yourdomain.com
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/tls/0/hosts/0
        value: pr-42.preview.yourdomain.com



The patch syntax reads literally: in the resource matching 
kind: Ingress, name: preview-app
, replace the value at 
/spec/rules/0/host
, and replace the value at 
/spec/tls/0/hosts/0
.
The 
0
 indices are array positions. 
/spec/rules/0
 is the first (and only) rule. 
/spec/tls/0/hosts/0
 is the first hostname in the first TLS block. If you later add a second hostname per environment, you'd add another operation targeting index 
1
.
Why a JSON 6902 patch rather than a strategic merge patch? Because strategic merge on an array of objects is ambiguous. Kubernetes has to guess whether you mean "replace this list" or "merge into an existing entry," and the answer depends on per-field merge keys. For replacing a single value at a known position, an explicit 
op: replace
 says exactly what you mean and fails loudly if the path doesn't exist.
The workflow generates this file at runtime, so you never commit a per-PR overlay. We'll write that step in Step 19.
Step 18: Add Guardrails with ResourceQuota and LimitRange
Before we wire up the workflow, let's stop a preview environment from being able to take down the cluster.
Right now nothing prevents a pull request from deploying a manifest requesting 32 CPUs, or scaling to 200 replicas, or creating a dozen 
LoadBalancer
 Services. Someone doesn't need bad intent for this to happen. A bad merge, a copied manifest, or a typo in a replica count does it just as effectively.
Two Kubernetes resources solve this, and they work together.
Create 
k8s/cluster/namespace-guardrails.yaml
 as a template:
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: preview-quota
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "1"
    requests.memory: 1Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 2Gi
    pods: "10"
    services: "5"
    services.loadbalancers: "0"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "2"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: preview-limits
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      # Applied to containers that don't specify their own
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 50m
        memory: 64Mi
      default:
        cpu: 200m
        memory: 128Mi
      # Hard ceiling — a container asking for more is rejected
      max:
        cpu: "1"
        memory: 512Mi



What Each One Does
A ResourceQuota caps the total consumption of an entire namespace. Add up every pod's requests and limits. The sum can't exceed these numbers. A request that would push the namespace over its quota is rejected by the API server at admission time, before anything is scheduled.
The 
services.loadbalancers: "0"
 line is worth highlighting. It makes it structurally impossible for a preview environment to provision a Google Cloud load balancer, even if someone commits a manifest with 
type: LoadBalancer
. That's a direct financial guardrail: the most expensive mistake this system could make is now unrepresentable.
A LimitRange operates on individual containers rather than the namespace total. It sets defaults for containers that don't specify resources, and a hard maximum that no single container may exceed.
Why They Must Be Deployed Together
Once a ResourceQuota that constrains 
requests.cpu
 exists in a namespace, every container in that namespace must declare resource requests. A pod without them is rejected outright, because Kubernetes can't verify it fits within the quota if it doesn't know what it's asking for.
That means adding a ResourceQuota on its own will break any manifest that omits resource specs, and most manifests found in the wild do omit them.
The LimitRange fixes this by supplying defaults. A container with no resource spec gets the 
defaultRequest
 and 
default
 values injected automatically at admission time, which satisfies the quota's requirement.
Deploy one without the other, and you get confusing failures. Deploy both and the system is forgiving of incomplete manifests while still being strictly bounded.
Sizing the Numbers
The values above suit a small application like ours. To adjust them, work backwards from your node capacity.
Two 
e2-standard-2
 nodes give you 4 vCPU and 16GB total, minus roughly 15% that GKE reserves for system components. Call it 3.4 usable vCPU. With 
requests.cpu: "1"
 per namespace, three preview environments could theoretically fill the cluster.
Our application requests only 50m CPU, so in practice you'll fit far more than three. But the quota is a ceiling on what a namespace may request, and you should set it well below "one PR can consume everything."
If you expect ten concurrent environments, size the per-namespace quota at roughly a tenth of usable capacity, or add nodes.

Here's the complete 
.github/workflows/preview-deploy.yml
, with everything added in this section marked

There are a few things to understand about the new steps.
The 
~1
 in the annotation patch path: this looks like a typo and isn't:
path: /metadata/annotations/cert-manager.io~1cluster-issuer



JSON Pointer paths use 
/
 as a separator, so a literal 
/
 inside a key has to be escaped. The escape sequence is 
~1
. (And 
~
 itself escapes to 
~0
.) Since the annotation key is
cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer
, the pointer becomes 
cert-manager.io~1cluster-issuer
. Get this wrong, and the patch silently targets a path that doesn't exist.
Namespace labels: The 
app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=pr-preview
 label is what makes the reaper in Step 21 safe. A cleanup job that deletes namespaces matching a name pattern is one bad regex away from deleting something important. A job that only ever touches namespaces carrying a label it applied itself has a much smaller worst case.
Guardrails before deploy: The ResourceQuota must exist before the application deploys, not after. Applying it afterwards means the first deployment escapes it entirely, and you'd only find out when something exceeded a limit that was never enforced.
continue-on-error: true
 on the certificate wait: This is deliberate. Certificate issuance depends on Let's Encrypt, an external service with rate limits and occasional slowness. If issuance is delayed, the environment is still deployed and still works over HTTP.
So failing the entire workflow would be wrong. We note the problem and continue. The PR comment in the next step reflects whether the certificate is actually ready.
Step 20: Comment the URL on the Pull Request
The environment is live. Now it's time to tell people about it.
Add this step to the end of the deploy job:
      - name: Comment preview URL on PR
        uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const host = process.env.PREVIEW_HOST;
            const sha = process.env.SHORT_SHA;
            const ns = process.env.NAMESPACE;

            // A hidden marker so we can find our own comment later
            const marker = '';

            const body = [
              marker,
              '### Preview environment is ready',
              '',
              `**https://${host}**`,
              '',
              `Commit \`${sha}\` · Namespace \`${ns}\``,
              '',
              'This environment updates on every push and is deleted when the PR closes.',
            ].join('\n');

            const { data: comments } = await github.rest.issues.listComments({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
            });

            const existing = comments.find(c => c.body.includes(marker));

            if (existing) {
              await github.rest.issues.updateComment({
                owner: context.repo.owner,
                repo: context.repo.repo,
                comment_id: existing.id,
                body,
              });
            } else {
              await github.rest.issues.createComment({
                owner: context.repo.owner,
                repo: context.repo.repo,
                issue_number: context.issue.number,
                body,
              });
            }



So why this approach?
actions/github-script
 is maintained by GitHub itself and gives you an authenticated Octokit client with no setup. There are third-party actions that post PR comments in fewer lines, but every third-party action in a workflow with write permissions is a supply chain dependency.
Given the effort we spent in Step 5 removing a long-lived credential, adding an unaudited action that can write to your repository would be an odd trade.
The hidden marker comment is the mechanism that makes this a sticky comment. 
 renders as nothing in GitHub's markdown, but it's present in the comment body. On each run, we list the PR's comments, look for one containing the marker, and update it if found.
Without this, a PR with fifteen commits gets fifteen near-identical bot comments, and the thread becomes unreadable. Reviewers start ignoring bot comments entirely, which defeats the purpose. One comment that stays current is the difference between a useful tool and noise.
process.env.PREVIEW_HOST
: values written to 
$GITHUB_ENV
 in earlier steps are available as environment variables in the script. This is cleaner than interpolating 
${{ }}
 expressions directly into JavaScript, which can break in surprising ways if a value contains quotes or backticks.
context.issue.number
 works on 
pull_request
 events because GitHub treats pull requests as a specialised kind of issue. It's why we use the 
issues
 API to comment on a PR.
The step needs 
pull-requests: write
, which the workflow already declares.
Step 21: Build the Reaper
Here's the uncomfortable truth about the teardown workflow from Part 1: it will eventually fail to run.
The failure modes are mundane. Someone closes a PR while GitHub Actions is having an incident. A workflow file gets edited on a branch in a way that breaks the teardown job. Someone deletes a branch without closing its PR. A repository is archived with PRs still open. GitHub's event delivery hiccups.
None of these are common. All of them leave a namespace running indefinitely, consuming cluster capacity and (if it happens enough) real money. Cleanup that works 95% of the time is still a leak.
The fix is a reaper: a scheduled job that periodically compares what's running against what should be running, and deletes the difference.
Create 
.github/workflows/preview-reaper.yml
:
name: Reap Orphaned Preview Environments

on:
  schedule:
    # 03:00 UTC daily
    - cron: '0 3 * * *'
  # Allow manual runs from the Actions tab
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
  pull-requests: read

env:
  PROJECT_ID: YOUR_PROJECT_ID
  CLUSTER_NAME: pr-preview-cluster
  CLUSTER_ZONE: europe-west2-a
  # Delete environments older than this even if the PR is still open
  MAX_AGE_DAYS: 7

jobs:
  reap:
    name: Delete orphaned namespaces
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Authenticate to Google Cloud
        uses: google-github-actions/auth@v2
        with:
          workload_identity_provider: ${{ secrets.WIF_PROVIDER }}
          service_account: ${{ secrets.WIF_SERVICE_ACCOUNT }}

      - name: Get GKE credentials
        uses: google-github-actions/get-gke-credentials@v2
        with:
          cluster_name: ${{ env.CLUSTER_NAME }}
          location: ${{ env.CLUSTER_ZONE }}

      - name: Reap
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          echo "Fetching open pull requests..."
          OPEN_PRS=$(gh pr list \
            --repo "${{ github.repository }}" \
            --state open \
            --limit 500 \
            --json number \
            --jq '.[].number')

          echo "Open PRs: ${OPEN_PRS:-none}"
          echo ""

          # Only consider namespaces we created ourselves.
          NAMESPACES=$(kubectl get namespaces \
            -l app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=pr-preview \
            -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{"\t"}{.metadata.labels.preview\.pr}{"\t"}{.metadata.creationTimestamp}{"\n"}{end}')

          if [ -z "${NAMESPACES}" ]; then
            echo "No preview namespaces found. Nothing to do."
            exit 0
          fi

          NOW=$(date -u +%s)
          MAX_AGE_SECONDS=$(( MAX_AGE_DAYS * 86400 ))
          DELETED=0

          while IFS=$'\t' read -r NS PR_NUM CREATED; do
            [ -z "${NS}" ] && continue

            CREATED_EPOCH=$(date -u -d "${CREATED}" +%s)
            AGE=$(( NOW - CREATED_EPOCH ))
            AGE_DAYS=$(( AGE / 86400 ))

            REASON=""

            # Rule 1: the PR is no longer open
            if ! echo "${OPEN_PRS}" | grep -qx "${PR_NUM}"; then
              REASON="PR #${PR_NUM} is not open"
            # Rule 2: the environment has outlived MAX_AGE_DAYS
            elif [ "${AGE}" -gt "${MAX_AGE_SECONDS}" ]; then
              REASON="environment is ${AGE_DAYS} days old (max ${MAX_AGE_DAYS})"
            fi

            if [ -n "${REASON}" ]; then
              echo "DELETING ${NS} — ${REASON}"
              kubectl delete namespace "${NS}" \
                --ignore-not-found=true \
                --wait=false
              DELETED=$(( DELETED + 1 ))
            else
              echo "KEEPING  ${NS} — PR #${PR_NUM} open, ${AGE_DAYS}d old"
            fi
          done <<< "${NAMESPACES}"

          echo ""
          echo "Reaped ${DELETED} namespace(s)."



Where does 
GITHUB_TOKEN
 come from?


Unlike 
WIF_PROVIDER
 and 
WIF_SERVICE_ACCOUNT
, which you created in Step 6, 
GITHUB_TOKEN
 isn't something you set up. You won't find it on the secrets page, and you shouldn't add it there.
GitHub mints a fresh installation token at the start of every workflow run, exposes it as 
secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN
, and revokes it the moment the job finishes. It's scoped to the repository running the workflow and nothing else.
Understanding the Reaper
The reaper runs from GitHub Actions, not inside the cluster. A CronJob in Kubernetes would need a GitHub token stored as a cluster Secret to query open PRs. That's a long-lived credential sitting in the cluster, which is exactly what we avoided in Step 5.
A scheduled workflow already has 
GITHUB_TOKEN
 (scoped, automatic, short-lived) and already authenticates to GCP through Workload Identity Federation. No new secrets.
The label selector is the safety mechanism. The query is 
-l app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=pr-preview
, not a name pattern like 
pr-*
. This is a deliberate choice: a name-pattern match would happily delete a production namespace someone named 
pr-routing-service
. The reaper can only ever see namespaces that the deploy workflow explicitly labelled, which means the set of things it could possibly delete is the set of things it created.
Be careful when you adapt this. Any cleanup automation should operate on a positive allowlist it controls, never a pattern that could match something it didn't create.
We also have two deletion rules, for two different problems. Rule 1 catches the actual orphan. A namespace whose PR is closed but whose teardown never ran. Rule 2 catches the stale environment: a PR that's been open for three weeks, hasn't been touched in two, and is quietly holding cluster capacity. Seven days is a reasonable default. If someone needs their environment back, they just push a commit, and it redeploys in a couple of minutes.
set -euo pipefail
: 
-e
 exits on any command failure, 
-u
 errors on undefined variables, and 
-o pipefail
 makes a pipeline fail if any stage fails rather than only the last. In a script whose job is deleting things, silent failure is the worst outcome. If something goes wrong, stop immediately.
grep -qx
: the 
-x
 flag requires the whole line to match. Without it, PR 
4
 would match against open PR 
42
 and the reaper would spare an orphaned namespace forever. It's a small flag, but a real bug.
workflow_dispatch
 lets you run the reaper manually from the Actions tab. Do that the first few times and read the output before trusting the schedule. The log prints 
KEEPING
 or 
DELETING
 with a reason for every namespace, so you can verify the logic matches your expectations before it runs unattended.

The deployment will scale partway and then stop, with events explaining that it exceeded the quota. That's the guardrail doing its job: the namespace is bounded, and the rest of the cluster is unaffected.
Verify Teardown and the Reaper
Close the pull request. The teardown workflow fires and the namespace goes to 
Terminating
.
Then test the reaper on a namespace it shouldn't touch. Create one manually without the label:
kubectl create namespace pr-9999





Run the reaper manually from the Actions tab.
It should ignore 
pr-9999

app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=pr-preview
 label. The log won't even mention it.
Clean it up yourself:

That test matters more than it looks. You've just verified that your automated deletion job can't touch things it didn't create.

Compare that with the naïve approach of a 
LoadBalancer
 Service per environment: ten open PRs would add roughly $180/month in load balancers alone, and that's before anyone forgets to clean one up. The 
services.loadbalancers: "0"
 line in the ResourceQuota exists specifically to make that mistake impossible.
There are two ways to cut the standing cost for a personal project. Use spot nodes, add 
spot = true
 to the 
node_config
 block in Terraform for roughly a 60–70% discount on node hours. Preview environments are the ideal spot workload: if a node is reclaimed, pods reschedule, and the worst case is a preview environment briefly restarting. Or scale the node pool to zero overnight with a scheduled workflow, since nobody reviews PRs at 3 am.
Cleanup
When you're finished:
# Delete every preview namespace
kubectl delete namespaces -l app.kubernetes.io/managed-by=pr-preview

# Remove the shared infrastructure
helm uninstall cert-manager --namespace cert-manager
helm uninstall ingress-nginx --namespace ingress-nginx
kubectl delete namespace cert-manager ingress-nginx



Uninstall the Helm releases before running 
terraform destroy
. The Ingress controller's Service owns a Google Cloud load balancer that Terraform doesn't know about, because Kubernetes created it rather than Terraform. Destroying the cluster first can orphan that load balancer, leaving it billing quietly in a project with nothing else in it.
If You Plan to Rebuild This Later
Don't run a full 
terraform destroy
. Tear down only the expensive parts:
cd terraform 
terraform destroy 
-var="project_id=YOUR_PROJECT_ID" 
-var="github_repo=YOUR_USERNAME/pr-preview-envs"



Here's why. When you delete a Workload Identity Pool, Google doesn't remove it immediately. It marks it 
DELETED
 and reserves the ID for 30 days. Terraform forgets about it, but Google hasn't. Recreating the stack within that window fails with:
Error: Error creating WorkloadIdentityPool: googleapi: Error 409: Requested entity already exists



Almost all of your cost is the cluster and its nodes. The identity pool, provider, service account, IAM bindings, static IP, and Artifact Registry repository cost nothing or pennies to leave in place. Rebuilding later is then just 
terraform apply
, and your 
WIF_PROVIDER
 and 
WIF_SERVICE_ACCOUNT
 secrets in GitHub stay valid. No need to update them.
If you want to keep the cluster but stop paying for idle nodes, scale the node pool to zero instead:
gcloud container clusters resize pr-preview-cluster
--node-pool pr-preview-cluster-pool
--num-nodes 0
--zone europe-west2-a



You still pay for the GKE control plane, so this reduces cost rather than eliminating it.
If you're done for good:
cd terraform
terraform destroy
-var="project_id=YOUR_PROJECT_ID"
-var="github_repo=YOUR_USERNAME/pr-preview-envs" 



Then confirm nothing was left behind:
gcloud compute forwarding-rules list
gcloud compute addresses list



Both should be empty, or contain only resources belonging to other projects of yours. Don't forget to remove the wildcard DNS record too.
Conclusion
You've built something that most engineering teams either don't have or pay a vendor for.
You wrote a Go application that reports its own build metadata, injected at compile time through linker flags, so a running environment can always tell you exactly which commit it came from. You wrapped it in a multi-stage Dockerfile that produces a small, statically linked, non-root image
You provisioned a GKE cluster and an Artifact Registry repository with Terraform, which means the whole environment is reproducible and destroyable with a single command. You set up Workload Identity Federation so GitHub Actions authenticates to Google Cloud with short-lived OIDC tokens instead of a long-lived service account key, scoped to exactly one repository by an attribute condition.
You wrote base Kubernetes manifests once and used Kustomize overlays, generated at runtime, to deploy the same application into a different namespace with a different image tag and a different hostname for every pull request. You put a single shared Ingress controller in front of every environment and gave it a stable static IP, so one load balancer serves any number of previews. You pointed one wildcard DNS record at it, which means a new environment needs no DNS work at all: routing happens on the 
Host
 header inside the cluster. You added cert-manager so every environment gets a valid, auto-renewing TLS certificate, and made the pipeline announce itself with a sticky PR comment that updates in place.
You bounded each namespace with a ResourceQuota and LimitRange, including one line that makes the most expensive possible mistake structurally impossible. And you built a reaper that catches what the happy path misses, operating only on namespaces it can prove it created.
The result is that an isolated, production-shaped, publicly reachable environment is the default for every change, not something a developer has to request, claim in a Slack channel, or remember to clean up.
Where to Go From Here
There are a few directions you can explore. Here they are, roughly in order of how much they'd improve a real team's experience:
  • Seed data for each environment. The biggest limitation of what we built is that the application is stateless. Real applications need a database. The common patterns are a per-namespace ephemeral database seeded from a sanitised snapshot, or a shared database with per-environment schema isolation. This is the single hardest problem in preview environments and where most of the remaining engineering effort goes.
  • Run your test suite against the preview. Once the environment has a real URL, end-to-end tests can run against it in CI, a far stronger signal than tests against mocks.
  • Wildcard certificates via DNS-01. As covered in Step 15, this removes the Let's Encrypt rate limit ceiling once your PR volume approaches it.
  • Move to GitOps. Rather than the workflow running 
    kubectl apply
     directly, have it commit the rendered manifests to a repository that Argo CD or Flux reconciles. The cluster's state then has a git history, and your CI pipeline no longer needs cluster write access at all.

  • Preview environment metrics. Hook the namespaces into the cost visibility tooling you'd use elsewhere, and you can answer "what do preview environments actually cost us per month" with a number rather than a shrug.
Project File Structure
pr-preview-envs/
├── app/
│   ├── main.go                      — Go HTTP server reporting build metadata
│   ├── go.mod                       — Go module definition
│   └── Dockerfile                   — Multi-stage build with ldflags injection
├── terraform/
│   ├── main.tf                      — GKE, Artifact Registry, WIF, static IP
│   ├── variables.tf                 — Input variables
│   └── outputs.tf                   — Cluster, WIF, and ingress IP values
├── k8s/
│   ├── base/
│   │   ├── deployment.yaml          — Deployment with probes and Downward API
│   │   ├── service.yaml             — ClusterIP Service
│   │   ├── ingress.yaml             — Ingress with cert-manager annotation
│   │   └── kustomization.yaml       — Base Kustomize config
│   └── cluster/
│       ├── letsencrypt-staging.yaml — Staging ClusterIssuer
│       ├── letsencrypt-prod.yaml    — Production ClusterIssuer
│       └── namespace-guardrails.yaml — ResourceQuota and LimitRange
└── .github/
    └── workflows/
        ├── preview-deploy.yml       — Build, deploy, certificate, PR comment
        ├── preview-teardown.yml     — Delete namespace on PR close
        └── preview-reaper.yml       — Scheduled orphan cleanup



All source files for this tutorial are available in the companion GitHub repository: 
https://github.com/Amiynarh/pr-preview-envs
.

entries.title: How to Give an AI Agent Safe Access to an Internal API with MCP
entries.summary: Our on-call team keeps a small internal notes API. The web app in front of it shows who's holding the pager, which days are frozen for deploys, and where the runbooks live. A developer on that team wa
entries.content:
Our on-call team keeps a small internal notes API. The web app in front of it shows who's holding the pager, which days are frozen for deploys, and where the runbooks live. A developer on that team wanted the same search from Cursor, without opening the web app.

They set it up the way most of us would on a Friday afternoon. They copied the API base URL into the assistant settings, pasted a long-lived token from the shared ops vault into an environment variable on their laptop, and added one line to the assistant instructions: "Only read notes. Do not change anything."

On their machine it worked. They asked when the next deploy freeze was, the assistant called the search endpoint, and the right note came back.

It broke the following week, when a second developer pointed their own assistant at that same URL and that same token. The notes API can't tell those two people apart.

Both requests arrive as the ops token, so the access log says the bot searched, not either developer. The assistant can also send a search string our API treats as "match everything," because the server runs whatever text it receives. And because the notes process is open on the office network, anyone who knows the URL can call it directly and skip the sign-in screen the first developer saw in the assistant.

This tutorial rebuilds that setup in a form you can run on your laptop. You'll wrap a small notes API in a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, reject searches the assistant shouldn't be able to write, and put a gateway in front so the assistant doesn't call the notes process directly.

A later section explains how a real deployment ties each call to an account: the person who asked, or a service account for a job that runs overnight. The sample you run here stays open, so you don't need a login provider.

By the end you'll have:

  • A notes API with three functions: list, get, and search

  • An MCP server that exposes only those three tools

  • Server-side rules that reject a search the model wasn't supposed to write

  • A small gateway at 

    /notes/mcp

  • A script that lists the tools, runs a valid search, and proves an invalid search is rejected

The example is deliberately small. You can swap the notes list for a ticket system, a git host, or any HTTP API you already run.

Table of Contents

  • What Goes Wrong When an Agent Calls an API Directly

  • What You Will Build

  • Prerequisites

  • How to Build a Tiny Internal API

  • How to Keep the Model From Writing the Query

  • How to Wrap the API in an MCP Server

  • How to Put a Gateway in Front

  • How to Test tools/list and tools/call End to End

  • How to Attach Identity (Person or Service Account)

  • What the Gateway Does Not Check

  • Conclusion

What Goes Wrong When an Agent Calls an API Directly

A coding assistant that speaks MCP is another program making HTTP calls. Your notes API was written for two callers: the web app your team already uses, and backend jobs you wrote yourself. Both of those callers send a known shape of request. A person clicks Search, or a script calls one endpoint you reviewed.

A model is a different caller. It chooses the next request from the text in front of it. That's fine when the only thing it can choose is one of a few functions you defined. It's not fine when it can do any of the following:

  • Send every call with one shared token, so the API logs "the bot" instead of a person or a job

  • Send a raw query, or call a tool named 

    http_request
    that forwards any path and any body

  • Reach the API process on a URL that has no login in front of it

  • Receive secrets or personal data in the tool result, then carry that text into the next prompt

  • Leave no record of which tool ran, or for whom

Those aren't things the notes API was asked to prevent. It checks a token and runs the search you send. It doesn't know that the text was written by a model, and it doesn't know that the token is shared by every assistant in the company.

Signing in to the chat window doesn't fix that. When you open Cursor, Claude, or your own chat UI, you may see an OAuth screen. OAuth there proves who opened the chat. It doesn't, by itself, change the HTTP request that searches notes. That request still needs its own credential, and the notes API still needs to know which account that credential belongs to.

That account is the principal. A principal is the identity the API should record and authorize for this call. It's either a person (whoever asked the assistant) or a service account you created for a job that runs when nobody is at the keyboard. "The bot" isn't a principal you can grant, revoke, or explain in an audit.

The prompt doesn't do this job either. "Be careful" is text. The server has to be the thing that refuses a bad search.

What You Will Build

Coding assistant
    |
    |  http://127.0.0.1:8090/notes/mcp
    v
Teaching gateway
    |
    v
Notes MCP server on port 8091
    |
    v
Notes functions (list, get, search)

You'll follow three rules for this notes service, and the same three rules the next time you wrap an internal API.

  • The assistant calls the gateway, not the MCP server. The server stays on a URL only the gateway should use. That way login, limits, and logs have one front door. If the assistant can open port 8091 directly, it can skip that front door.

  • Every call runs as a named principal: a person, or a service account for a job that runs overnight. You don't put one long-lived admin token in the assistant and share it with every laptop. If you do, you can't tell who searched, and you can't take one person's access away without breaking everyone else.

  • The model sends what it wants, and your code builds the search. A keyword such as 

    deploy
    is allowed. A string such as 
    title:* OR body:*
    is not, because that is the model trying to write the query itself. The check lives in Python, so it applies to every caller, not only to a well-behaved prompt.

Prerequisites

This isn't a first Python tutorial, and it's not an introduction to large language models. You should already be comfortable with the following:

  • Python 3.10 or newer, including functions, dictionaries, and virtual environments

  • HTTP: a URL, a JSON body, and what a request header is

  • The idea of an API token: a secret the server checks before it runs your request

  • What a coding assistant is, and that it can call functions (tools) you expose to it

You should know that MCP is the protocol many assistants use to discover those tools and call them. You don't need to have built an MCP server before. You also don't need a paid model, a cloud account, or Docker. Everything here runs on your laptop.

Install Python 3.10 or newer, then create a folder and a virtual environment:

mkdir notes-mcp-demo && cd notes-mcp-demo
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate

On Windows, activate with 

.venv\Scripts\activate
.

Install the libraries this tutorial uses. The official MCP Python package moved its FastMCP import in version 2, so stay on 1.x:

pip install "mcp>=1.0.0,<2.0.0" httpx uvicorn pytest

How to Build a Tiny Internal API

The "internal API" in this tutorial is three notes stored in a Python list, plus three functions your own web app might already have.

  • list_notes
    returns every note, or only the notes for one owner. 

  • get_note
    returns one note by id, such as 
    n2
    . 

  • search_notes
    finds notes whose title or body contains a word, optionally limited to one owner, and it stops after 
    limit
    rows.

Create 

notes_api.py
:
from typing import Optional

NOTES = [
    {"id": "n1", "owner": "oncall", "title": "on-call rotation", "body": "Pager is in #ops"},
    {"id": "n2", "owner": "oncall", "title": "deploy window", "body": "Fridays are frozen"},
    {"id": "n3", "owner": "platform", "title": "ssh keys", "body": "Rotate bastion keys in May"},
]


def list_notes(owner: Optional[str] = None) -> list[dict]:
    if owner is None:
        return NOTES
    return [n for n in NOTES if n["owner"] == owner]


def get_note(note_id: str) -> dict | None:
    return next((n for n in NOTES if n["id"] == note_id), None)


def search_notes(query: str, owner: Optional[str] = None, limit: int = 20) -> list[dict]:
    q = query.lower()
    rows = [
        n
        for n in NOTES
        if q in n["title"].lower() or q in n["body"].lower()
    ]
    if owner:
        rows = [n for n in rows if n["owner"] == owner]
    return rows[:limit]


search_notes
trusts its arguments. If you pass 
deploy
, it looks for that substring. If you pass 
title:* OR body:*
, it also looks for that substring. It doesn't interpret 
*
as "everything," but a real search API often would. That's why the next file exists. This file is the stand-in for the API you already operate. Keep it boring.

Don't put a single MCP tool in front of it that accepts an HTTP method, a path, and a body. That tool is a generic proxy. The model can then call any route the process will answer, including routes you added for admins and forgot to mention. A short list of named functions is a list you can review. A pass-through HTTP tool is the whole API, with a model choosing the request.

How to Keep the Model From Writing the Query

If the model can put any string into search, you have given it a query language. On a real notes service, 

title:* OR body:*
can mean "return every note."

owner=oncall; DROP TABLE notes
is the same class of problem: the model is writing the query, not asking for a keyword.

You want the opposite. The model may ask for the word 

deploy
, owned by 
oncall
. Your server decides whether that request is allowed, then builds the search itself.

Create 

safe_search.py
:
import os
import re


class SafeSearchError(ValueError):
    pass


MAX_RESULTS = min(int(os.getenv("NOTES_MAX_RESULTS", "20")), 100)
OWNER_ALLOWLIST = {
    name.strip()
    for name in os.getenv("NOTES_OWNER_ALLOWLIST", "oncall,platform").split(",")
    if name.strip()
}
QUERY_OK = re.compile(r"^[a-zA-Z0-9 \-]{1,64}$")


def build_search(query: str, owner: str | None, limit: int | None) -> dict:
    if not query or not QUERY_OK.match(query):
        raise SafeSearchError("query must be 1-64 letters, numbers, spaces, or hyphens")

    if owner is not None and owner not in OWNER_ALLOWLIST:
        raise SafeSearchError("owner is not on the allowlist")

    cap = MAX_RESULTS if limit is None else min(int(limit), MAX_RESULTS)
    if cap < 1:
        raise SafeSearchError("limit must be at least 1")

    return {"query": query.strip(), "owner": owner, "limit": cap}

Here's what that file does.

MAX_RESULTS
defaults to 20 and won't go above 100 even if someone sets the environment variable higher. 
OWNER_ALLOWLIST
defaults to 
oncall
and 
platform
. 
QUERY_OK
allows only letters, numbers, spaces, and hyphens, and only 1 to 64 characters.

build_search
then checks the three arguments the model is allowed to send:

  • query
    must match 
    QUERY_OK
    . 
    deploy
    matches, because it's only letters. 
    title:* OR body:*
    does not, because 
    *
    and 
    :
    aren't letters, numbers, spaces, or hyphens. The function raises 
    SafeSearchError
    and never searches. 

  • owner
    , when the caller sends one, must be 
    oncall
    or 
    platform
    . Any other name is rejected. 
    None
    means "don't filter by owner." 

  • limit
    , when the caller sends one, is reduced to 
    MAX_RESULTS
    . A request for 9999 rows becomes 20. A limit below 1 is rejected.

So 

{ "query": "deploy", "owner": "oncall" }
is a keyword plus an owner on the list. 
title:* OR body:*
is the model trying to write a match-everything query. Both strings would be harmless as plain substring searches in this toy list. The check is here so the same function still refuses them when you later point 
search_notes
at an API that treats 
*
as a wildcard.

Create 

test_safe_search.py
so you can see those three cases fail or pass without starting a server:
import pytest
from safe_search import SafeSearchError, build_search


def test_happy_path():
    out = build_search("deploy window", "oncall", 10)
    assert out["limit"] == 10
    assert out["owner"] == "oncall"


def test_rejects_query_language():
    with pytest.raises(SafeSearchError):
        build_search("title:* OR body:*", None, 10)


def test_caps_limit():
    out = build_search("keys", "platform", 9999)
    assert out["limit"] == 20


test_happy_path
is the allowed call: a normal phrase, an owner on the list, and a limit under the cap. 
test_rejects_query_language
expects 
SafeSearchError
for the wildcard-style string. 
test_caps_limit
asks for 9999 rows and checks that the function returns 20, which is the default cap.
pytest -q test_safe_search.py

You should see 

3 passed
.

How to Wrap the API in an MCP Server

The MCP server is the process the assistant talks to. It doesn't add new notes behavior. It publishes three tools, and each tool calls one function you already wrote.

Create 

server.py
:
import json
import os
from typing import Optional

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
from starlette.responses import JSONResponse

from notes_api import get_note, list_notes, search_notes
from safe_search import SafeSearchError, build_search

mcp = FastMCP("notes-mcp-server")

ALLOWED_OWNERS = {
    name.strip()
    for name in os.getenv("NOTES_OWNER_ALLOWLIST", "oncall,platform").split(",")
    if name.strip()
}


@mcp.custom_route("/health", methods=["GET"])
async def health(_request):
    return JSONResponse({"status": "ok", "server": "notes-mcp-server"})


@mcp.tool()
def list_notes_tool(owner: Optional[str] = None) -> str:
    """List notes. Optional owner filter must be on the allowlist."""
    if owner and owner not in ALLOWED_OWNERS:
        return json.dumps({"error": "owner is not allowed"})
    return json.dumps(list_notes(owner))


@mcp.tool()
def get_note_tool(note_id: str) -> str:
    """Get one note by id."""
    note = get_note(note_id)
    if note is None:
        return json.dumps({"error": "not found"})
    return json.dumps(note)


@mcp.tool()
def search_notes_tool(query: str, owner: Optional[str] = None, limit: Optional[int] = None) -> str:
    """Search notes. The server builds the query. The model only sends intent."""
    try:
        cleaned = build_search(query=query, owner=owner, limit=limit)
    except SafeSearchError as exc:
        return json.dumps({"error": str(exc)})
    rows = search_notes(
        query=cleaned["query"],
        owner=cleaned["owner"],
        limit=cleaned["limit"],
    )
    return json.dumps(rows)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    host = os.getenv("HOST", "0.0.0.0")
    port = int(os.getenv("PORT", "8091"))
    mcp.settings.host = host
    mcp.settings.port = port
    print(f"MCP endpoint: http://{host}:{port}/mcp")
    mcp.run(transport="streamable-http")


FastMCP("notes-mcp-server")
creates the server and the name the client will see after it connects. Each 
@mcp.tool()
function becomes one tool. The docstring is the description the assistant reads when it lists tools. The arguments become the tool's inputs. There's no tool that accepts a URL.

/health
is a normal HTTP route so you can check that the process is up. It's not an MCP tool.

list_notes_tool
refuses an owner who's not on the allowlist, then returns the matching notes as JSON text. 
get_note_tool
returns one note, or an error if that id doesn't exist.

search_notes_tool
is the important one: it calls 
build_search
before 
search_notes
. If the query is 
title:* OR body:*
, the tool returns 
{"error": "query must be 1-64 letters, numbers, spaces, or hyphens"}
and doesn't search.

The block at the bottom is required. Setting 

HOST
and 
PORT
in the shell does nothing until you copy them onto 
mcp.settings
. 
streamable-http
serves the MCP endpoint at 
/mcp
.

Start it:

HOST=127.0.0.1 PORT=8091 python server.py

In another terminal, with the virtual environment activated:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8091/health

You should see 

{"status":"ok","server":"notes-mcp-server"}
.

You didn't add 

http_request
or 
run_sql
. If a tool isn't in this file, the assistant can't call it.

How to Put a Gateway in Front

Right now, the assistant can open 

http://127.0.0.1:8091/mcp
. That port is the MCP server itself. "Skipping the edge" means skipping every check you meant to run in front of that server: who's calling, how often they call, and the log of what they called. On a laptop, that's only you. On a shared network, it's anyone who can open the port.

The gateway is a second process. The assistant calls 

http://127.0.0.1:8090/notes/mcp
. The gateway forwards that call to port 8091. The MCP server shouldn't be the URL you put in the assistant's settings.

A production gateway also does the sign-in (OAuth), slows callers down when they send too many requests, and writes an audit log. This teaching gateway doesn't do those yet. What it does share with that production gateway is where it sits: clients talk to it, and it's the program that talks to the MCP server.

Create 

gateway.py
:
import json
import os
from urllib.parse import urljoin

import httpx
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.responses import JSONResponse, Response
from starlette.routing import Route

UPSTREAM = os.getenv("NOTES_MCP_URL", "http://127.0.0.1:8091").rstrip("/") + "/"
FORWARD = {
    "accept",
    "content-type",
    "mcp-session-id",
    "mcp-protocol-version",
    "last-event-id",
    "authorization",
}
MAX_DESCRIPTION = 280
BLOCKED_PHRASES = (
    "ignore previous",
    "system prompt",
    "jailbreak",
    "exfiltrate",
)


def scrub_tools_list(payload: dict) -> dict:
    """Drop tools whose description is too long or looks like an instruction to the model."""
    result = payload.get("result")
    if not isinstance(result, dict):
        return payload
    tools = result.get("tools")
    if not isinstance(tools, list):
        return payload
    kept = []
    for tool in tools:
        if not isinstance(tool, dict):
            continue
        description = tool.get("description") or ""
        lowered = description.lower()
        if len(description) > MAX_DESCRIPTION:
            continue
        if any(phrase in lowered for phrase in BLOCKED_PHRASES):
            continue
        kept.append(tool)
    result["tools"] = kept
    return payload


def filter_tools_list(request_body: bytes, response_body: bytes) -> bytes:
    try:
        request = json.loads(request_body or b"{}")
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return response_body
    if request.get("method") != "tools/list":
        return response_body

    text = response_body.decode()
    if text.startswith("event:"):
        lines = []
        for line in text.splitlines():
            if line.startswith("data: "):
                data = scrub_tools_list(json.loads(line[6:]))
                lines.append("data: " + json.dumps(data))
            else:
                lines.append(line)
        rewritten = "\n".join(lines)
        if text.endswith("\n"):
            rewritten += "\n"
        return rewritten.encode()

    try:
        payload = json.loads(text)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return response_body
    return json.dumps(scrub_tools_list(payload)).encode()


async def health(_request):
    return JSONResponse({"status": "ok", "gateway": "notes-gateway"})


async def proxy_notes(request):
    target = urljoin(UPSTREAM, "mcp")
    headers = {
        key: value
        for key, value in request.headers.items()
        if key.lower() in FORWARD
    }
    body = await request.body()
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=30.0) as client:
        upstream = await client.request(
            request.method,
            target,
            headers=headers,
            content=body,
        )
    filtered = filter_tools_list(body, upstream.content)
    out_headers = {
        key: value
        for key, value in upstream.headers.items()
        if key.lower() in {"content-type", "mcp-session-id", "mcp-protocol-version"}
    }
    return Response(filtered, status_code=upstream.status_code, headers=out_headers)


app = Starlette(
    routes=[
        Route("/health", health, methods=["GET"]),
        Route("/notes/mcp", proxy_notes, methods=["GET", "POST", "DELETE"]),
    ]
)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import uvicorn

    host = os.getenv("GATEWAY_HOST", "0.0.0.0")
    port = int(os.getenv("GATEWAY_PORT", "8090"))
    uvicorn.run(app, host=host, port=port)


UPSTREAM
is the MCP server from the previous section. 
FORWARD
is the small set of headers the gateway will pass through.
